Summary

“Oh, no, you definitely don’t want to do that,” Kara said, picking up a paper cup and dumping a teabag in it.

The woman next to her looked up, surprise etched onto her pale, drawn face. “Excuse me?” she rasped.

Kara nodded at the coffee pot the woman had picked up and wrinkled her nose. “You’d get better coffee at the 7-Eleven across the street and that’s saying something. I’d stick with tea.”

“Oh. Oh … okay.”

“First time?” Kara asked, glancing sideways at the woman.

She was striking, her medium height made a fraction taller by her heels, the tailored cut of her clothes precise, her makeup perfect and her dark hair long and sleek. In her scrubs and denim jacket, bare-faced and dishevelled, Kara felt positively inadequate. And yet, there was the same hollowed out look to the newcomer's face, a sadness in her green eyes, a weary slump to her shoulders that was recognisable.

“Yes.”

Picking up a glazed donut, Kara took a bite and gave her a strained smile. “I’d say it’s good to have you here but … well, obviously not.”

    Chapter 1

                “Get up.”

     

                Kara blearily blinked as the blankets were torn off her, a groan at the back of her throat as she squeezed her eyes shut and exhaled into the pillows.

     

                “Get the fuck out of bed,” Alex brusquely ordered her, dragging the pillow out from under Kara’s head.

     

                “Alex,” Kara snapped, pushing herself up slightly to glare at her sister. “Stop it.”

     

                “It’s seven o’clock; go to work. Go for a walk, just … do something.”

     

                Early morning sunlight filtered in through the slatted blinds and Kara ran a hand over her face before slumping back onto the mattress. Her whole body felt heavy and she fumbled for the edge of the quilt to drag it back over herself so she could sleep for a few more hours, but Alex tugged it even further down.

     

                “Leave me alone.”

     

                “No,” her sister bluntly retorted, “you can’t just … live like this forever. This is my apartment and I love you but … you’re just- you’re not doing anything to help yourself. Staying in bed won’t make you feel better and it’s making it harder for me-“

     

                Kara snorted and pushed herself up, her eyebrows rising as a caustic laugh escaped her. “Are you serious? Did you really just say that my husband being dead is making it hard for you?”

     

                “I didn’t mean it like that,” Alex sighed, her mouth turning down at the corners. “You know that’s not what I meant.”

     

                “It’s what you implied.”

     

                “Kara, I’m trying to adopt a fucking child and I’ve got you holed up in here all day, every day while you try and sort your shit out. But you’re not even trying to sort your shit out. When are you going to sort out his things?”

     

                Drawing her knees to her chest, Kara swallowed thickly, closing her eyes as she rubbed at her forehead. Her mood had already soured for the day and she could feel a headache blossoming. There was that familiar hollowness inside her as well as the ocean of grief inside her opened up to swallow her.

     

                “It’s only been three months,” she whispered.

     

                “You can’t put it off forever,” Alex gently replied, her voice weary and resigned.

     

                “It’s only been three months,” Kara snapped as she repeated herself. “Sorry that I haven’t fucking moved on yet, I’m sorry that’s such an inconvenience for you.”

     

                Alex scoffed, giving her sister a disappointed look as she shook her head. “Get up. Go and shower; you look a mess.”

     

                Moving to sit on the edge of the bed for a moment, Kara let out a heavy sigh and rubbed at her eyes before she slowly climbed to her feet. The spare room was small and filled with boxes of Alex’s clutter, interspersed with the mess of Kara’s things, the suitcase she’d packed for a week spilling her clothes onto the creaking floorboards. She’d overstayed her welcome by a couple of months now, yet the thought of going home to her empty apartment was terrifying.

     

                Watching as she rose to her feet and moved over to the blinds to open them, the windows of the third-floor unit just level with the tops of the ginkgo trees outside, Alex waited patiently. Bracing her hands against the windowsill, Kara hunched her shoulders and swallowed, the weight of her sister’s gaze falling heavily on her back.

     

                “Are you going to group tonight?”

     

                “It’s Thursday, isn’t it?” Kara curtly replied.

     

                Alex’s sigh was soft and she hesitated a moment, feet scuffing on the floor, and walked out. “Go to work.”

     

                Shaking her head, looking pale and exhausted, Kara ran a hand through her lank blonde hair. She couldn’t even remember the last time she’d washed it and she knew work would soon pull her aside to check in on her, the vacant look in her eyes, the missed shifts and dishevelled appearance a concern for them. 

     

                She didn’t bother making the bed and shuffled down the hallway to climb into the shower. Robotically washing her hair, she scrubbed herself and then stood beneath the hot water, letting it douse her as she wasted water until Alex banged on the door to get her out.

     

                Sighing heavily, Kara shut off the water and climbed out, wrapping a towel around herself and wiping the condensation from the mirror. Looking at her lifeless gaze in the mirror as she brushed her teeth, damp hair straggling around her face as she squinted through her poor eyesight.

     

                Padding back to the bedroom, she rifled through the pile of laundry that Alex had placed there a few days ago and pulled out a pair of sky blue scrubs before she got dressed. Lacing on her running shoes, she ran a brush through her hair and pulled it back. 

     

                The sound of her sister getting ready for work sounded further in the house and she emerged to find Alex kissing Kelly goodbye. Looking away as a lump rose in her throat, Kara fiddled with her fingers. 

     

                “Morning,” Kelly warmly greeted her, already dressed in her scrubs for her shift at the hospital. 

     

                She was a psychiatrist at National City General Hospital, and while Kara also wore scrubs, she dealt with patients of another kind. Giving her a ghost of a smile, Kara made for the coffee pot and poured herself some into a mug.

     

                “I’ll see you later,” Alex said, giving her sister a grim look. “Do you want me to pick up anything in particular for dinner?”

     

                Lips twisting slightly, Kara didn’t meet her eyes. “I’ll get something after group.”

     

                Alex nodded and then kissed Kelly goodbye again before breezing out of the apartment, leaving Kara alone with her soon-to-be sister-in-law.

     

                “How’s group going?”

     

                Gesturing vaguely as she let out a short laugh, Kara’s eyes creased at the corners behind her glasses, although her amusement didn’t quite reach them. “I get a free donut out of it, so that’s nice.”

     

                “If you want to see someone private-“

     

                “What are they going to say, Kelly?” Kara asked as she softly sighed, a thin smile on her lips. “Nothing is going to make me not a widow, so …”

     

                “I know how you feel. It gets easier.”

     

                “Doesn’t feel like it.”

     

                “Kara, I-“

     

                “I’ve got to get to work,” she blurted out.

     

                Brow creasing slightly, Kelly’s mouth thinned. “Oh. Okay, well … have a good day.”

     

                Smiling in her general direction, Kara grabbed her denim jacket off the coat rack and slipped it on. “You too.”

     

                Picking up her work backpack, she slung it over her shoulder and stepped into the hallway. Jogging down the two flights of stairs, Kara untangled her earphones and put on a podcast as she walked to the bus stop, hands in her pockets and a tense set to her shoulders.

     

                It was fifteen stops to the clinic and she sat by the window, the motion of the bus jostling her as it started and stopped, brakes hissing and doors shuddering open to admit and expel passengers. She ignored it all, staring at the blur of houses and convenience stores, tattoo parlours and vape shops. She ended up getting off a stop early and going to Noonan’s, her favourite coffee shop, to buy a caramel latte before she idled, already running late for work and in no hurry to go.

     

                It wasn’t that she didn’t enjoy her job - Kara loved it - but dealing with death had become unbearable since Mike had died. She took her time walking down the street, draining the rest of her coffee and tossing the empty cup into a trash can, before she crossed the parking lot at the small complex of varying businesses and pushed open the door.

     

                The waiting room was occupied by an elderly woman with a cat carrier set on the floor before her and a young couple with a new puppy writhing in their arms as its tail wagged. Kara smiled slightly at the sight and greeted Eve, the receptionist, before making her way down the hall to the communal kitchen at the end and putting her jacket and bag into her locker.

     

                “You’re here.”

     

                “Hey, James.”

     

                “Didn’t think you were coming in today.”

     

                Kara glanced over at him, taking her stethoscope from her locker. “I’ve got a surgery at one for a cat to be spayed.”

     

                “I’ve already rebooked it for myself at eleven.”

     

                “I can-“

     

                “No,” James gently cut her off. “How about you take my afternoon appointments instead?”

     

                She nodded and shut her locker, not up for arguing. James moved over to the coffee percolator and rinsed out the chipped mug displaying the logo from the gym he frequented down the block. 

     

                “Coffee?”

     

                Despite her already having a cup on the way in she murmured her agreement and took the mug that James held out to her. He was eight years older than her and had been her mentor when she’d still been at college, studying Veterinary Medicine. He’d offered her the job upon graduating and she’d stayed ever since, the small clinic with its constant flow of new and old patients over the last nine years offering her the perfect environment to manage the life she’d wanted.

     

                It had been perfect, or, rather, as perfect as she’d hoped for, which wasn’t saying a lot with her low expectations for what Kara imagined for her life. She’d always wanted to be a vet, wanted to get married and maybe have a kid or two, a small home. At thirty-three, she’d managed two out of the four, never quite able to save enough for a down payment on a house, and never quite in a position where she and Mike were ready for a kid. 

     

                But they’d had their group of friends; Alex about to marry Kelly, Nia and Querl with their on-and-off-again relationship and James with his contented life as a bachelor. Then there had been Alex’s boss, J’onn, who’d been an Attending when she’d started as an intern at the hospital, and had taught her everything he knew about being an elite Cardiothoracic surgeon. They all brought more people to the group; flings and out of town friends, Mike’s friends from work who never seemed to mesh well but were always welcome. They would go out weekly, host game nights and dinners, spend the holidays together for whoever didn’t fly to see family. 

     

                Now, Kara felt so removed from it all. It was strange in a way, how the loss of one person, independent of the group, only welcomed by his marriage to Kara - a sensitive topic for her friends, if she was honest - had completely ruined that circle for her. She didn’t go to game nights anymore, partnerless and wallowing in her grief, she only went out for drinks to get plastered and piss off Alex when she spent the entire next day occupying the toilet as she nursed her hangover. Kara had completely disconnected from the life she’d made for herself over the death of him and it was hard. 

     

                She felt like no one really understood just how hard it was - except Kelly. And the truth was she was angry. They hadn’t been a good match, that much she knew on some subconscious level, always arguing about something, always snapping and annoyed and disagreeing. But they’d loved each other and that had felt like enough, especially when things were going well. If she was being honest with herself, she found him a little predictable, like a generic cutout of the all-American husband he should have been.

     

                Even now, Kara could see the future they should have had. He would work all day at his job at a tech start-up, coming home exhausted and eating dinner alone, the kids already in bed and Kara doing all of the housework that had been left while she’d been at work all day too. He’d watch the NFL with the guys on the weekend, mow the lawn on Sunday’s and control the barbecue at get-togethers. Kara hadn’t realised how badly she didn’t want that life until he was dead.

     

                The thought made her wince and James gave her a concerned look as she was slammed back into the moment. It never ceased to make her feel bad to think those silent, critical thoughts of her husband. She’d loved him, she had, but in a way that would have inevitably broken down, and perhaps had already started to. He didn’t make her laugh very hard and he didn’t blow her mind in bed. She didn’t like how often he would simply refuse to do something that he wasn’t immediately good at.

     

                But he’d loved her, had been dependable and a constant amidst a life that had thrown her so many curveballs since childhood. Kara hadn’t imagined he’d be another death to add to the mountain of grief she was still struggling to process. He’d seemed like a ticket to normal life and now that had been ripped away from her too. 

     

                “I’ve got a patient,” James slowly said. “You going to be alright?”

     

                Rubbing at her brow, Kara made a low sound of agreement at the back of her throat. “Yeah. Yeah, I’ve got patients too.”

     

                He knew that she didn’t, having rescheduled half of them on the chance that she didn’t come in and left them swamped with too many patients and not enough vets. Still, she took one of William’s ones, the puppy in the waiting room who needed its first vaccines. 

     

                It was a slow day, putting the plaster on the broken leg of a Golden Retriever after taking x-rays and confirming the fracture, setting a particularly lethargic bunny up on a drip and keeping it in for observation, and the prescribing of half a dozen different medications to different clients over the course of her morning. 

     

                The afternoon seemed to drag by and she took an extra-long lunch, sitting in the park across from the deli where she’d bought her sandwich as she ate it and basked in the warmth of the sun. When she got back to the clinic she sat through an hour of explaining the nutritional benefits of a good diet for a woman’s corgi, recommending brands and informing her which ones to steer clear of while she outlined what her dog needed, and then a teenager came in with his mom for her to inspect the inflamed wound of his lizard, which had been bitten by the other lizard they owned.

     

                When everyone else left for the day, Kara lingered behind with the promise to lock up, spending a little extra time with all of the animals in cages as they were kept there to rest or await procedures. Stroking the nose of a kitten who’d been born with her organs outside of her abdomen, Kara murmured soft reassurances to the mewling kitten until it was late enough for her to grab dinner and make it to grief group.

     

                It was already growing dark outside, past six o’clock, and she bought two slices at a pizza parlour and ate them on the front steps before wiping her greasy fingers on the thighs of her pants and climbing to her feet. Riding the bus three stops down near the local Y, one of the recreation rooms used for their group therapy sessions every Thursday.

     

                Making her way inside, the bleak industrial carpet floor and off-white walls with years of wearing and chipping illuminated by the humming fluorescents set into a water-stained ceiling, Kara dumped her bag at the foot of a plastic chair.

     

                A long trestle table was set up along one wall with an urn of hot water and a pot of coffee and Kara made her way over to it. There was already a woman there, looking completely out of place in the shabby room. She was making her own drink and Kara’s lips twitched with faint amusement. Definitely new.

     

                “Oh, no, you definitely don’t want to do that,” Kara said, picking up a paper cup and dumping a teabag in it.

     

                The woman next to her looked up, surprise etched onto her pale, drawn face. “Excuse me?” she rasped.

     

                Kara nodded at the coffee pot the woman had picked up and wrinkled her nose. “You’d get better coffee at the 7-Eleven across the street and that’s saying something. I’d stick with tea.”

     

                “Oh. Oh … okay.”

     

                “First time?” Kara asked, glancing sideways at the woman.

     

                She was striking, her medium height made a fraction taller by her heels, the tailored cut of her clothes precise, her makeup perfect and her dark hair long and sleek. In her scrubs and denim jacket, bare-faced and dishevelled, Kara felt positively inadequate. And yet, there was the same hollowed out look to the newcomer's face, a sadness in her green eyes, a weary slump to her shoulders that was recognisable. 

     

                “Yes.”

     

                Picking up a glazed donut, Kara took a bite and gave her a strained smile. “I’d say it’s good to have you here but … well, obviously not.”

     

                The woman let out a surprised laugh and gave Kara a rueful smile in reply as she grabbed a tea bag and poured hot water into her cup. Kara followed suit and then carried her tea over to her seat and sat down. The woman sat down just to the left of directly across from her on the circle and Kara looked at her with interest.

     

                Group started at seven and Kara always got there with just enough time to get her tea and a donut from the box. The weekly group was led by Thomas Coville, a middle-aged man with a quiet demeanour who’d once been a lawyer until his wife cheated on him and left, leading him to heavy drinking and disbarment. He’d since turned things around and had slowly built up a new career for himself as a motivational speaker and part-time therapist for the community centre. 

     

                Kelly had tried to convince Kara on more than one occasion to speak to someone who was fully qualified, offering up a slew of names and options she was acquainted with through work, but Kara always refused. She’d only been coming to the Y for the past six weeks, and while the building was decrepit and the smell of chlorine from the public pool seeped into the space, there was a comfort to it. Even if she didn’t speak much, there were other people there too, other people who had lost family members, and that made her feel a little less alone. The thought of sitting in an artfully arranged room, on a stiff couch with some big shot therapist who scrawled notes was unbearable.

     

                “Good evening, everyone,” Thomas started, leaning forward as he rested his elbows on his knees. “Thank you all for joining me here. It’s good to see so many familiar faces - and new ones too. Welcome.”

     

                There was an oppressiveness to the silence of the space, the sound of the plastic chairs shifting and someone sniffing filling the place. He cleaned his throat, a faint smile on his lips as his eyes went around the circle.

     

                “Who would like to start first today?”

     

                A middle-aged woman who had lost her son from cancer went first, a glazed look in her eyes as she spoke haltingly, in between sobs. Someone passed her a box of tissues and she blew her nose loudly. Kara’s throat tightened and she chewed her donut as she avoided looking at the woman, uncomfortable by her evident grief as she tried to suppress the tide of her own.

     

                They all went around and spoke, and Kara restlessly bounced her knee as she waited for her turn. Some of them told the same stories about the people they’d lost; the sixty-year-old man who’d lost his wife last year to a stroke, the fifty-year-old woman whose father had died after a long battle with MS, the woman in her forties whose husband had collapsed from a heart attack. Kara and the newcomer were the youngest in the room by about a decade, the other dozen from their mid-forties to one old man in his early eighties who had to use a walking frame to make it into the room. All of them were equally pitiful.

     

                “Would you like to go next?”

     

                Kara glanced up to see who Thomas was speaking to, her eyes straying over to the newcomer, who blanched at the thought of speaking. She nodded stiffly, her knuckles whitening in her lap as she gripped the paper cup too tightly.

     

                “I- my name’s Lena.”

     

                “You’re very welcome here, Lena. How about you tell us a little more about your story.”

     

                She swallowed thickly, nodding again as she stared at the carpet. Kara watched her closely, the struggle a familiar sight. It was hard to talk about the loss, she’d had three months to bear it and it was still unbearably hard. Even talking about the things she didn’t like about him, the things that still sent a prickle of anger through her, were hard to talk about without crying.

     

                “My wife … she-“

     

                Cutting off, Lena shifted in her seat, her face hard and angular, a muscle twitching in her jaw.

     

                “She was sick for a long time. Last month … I miss her.”

     

                “Why don’t you tell us about her so that we can miss her too.”

     

                Shaking her head as her chin wobbled, teeth chattering slightly as she suppressed the urge to cry, struggling with the process, Lena pressed her lips into a hard line. Kara watched as she wiped a tear off her cheek, blending the grey smudge of mascara in with her thumb.

     

                “It’s okay, take your time. You still have a few minutes.”

     

                “I don’t really want them.”

     

                Lena’s voice was cold and angry and Kara blinked in surprise. It wasn’t uncommon for there to be anger expressed in the group but it was usually at the deceased, amidst tearful, helpless monologues about how they couldn’t be gone, how they shouldn’t have left - regardless of whether an illness had taken them or not. The old man who had lost his daughter in a car accident was angry at the drunk driver who’d slammed into her, the old woman was angry at the surgeon who hadn’t been able to get the tumour out. And Kara - Kara was angry at Mike for going on that hike and leaving her guessing whether the fall had been an accident or not.

     

                “Remember, if you’re not talking about it, you’re storing it, and that gets heavy,” Thomas gently cautioned her.

     

                With a choked laugh, sharp and humourless, Lena arched an eyebrow.

     

                “What makes you think talking about it would bring me any comfort?”

     

                “You came to group,” he said, sitting back as he spread his hands, “you’re here, with all of us who have lost someone. It will take time, Lena, and pain and patience and anger, but we’re all here to support each other.”

     

                Kara thought she looked like she was about to laugh but Lena just nodded and Thomas looked placated. He looked around and the silence in the room was thick.

     

                “Let’s take five before we continue.”

     

                Lena shot to her feet and walked over to the door leading out to the hallway. Kara went to make herself another cup of tea, stirring in the milk with a wooden stick before reclaiming her seat. She sipped it as the clock on the wall ticked away each second.

     

                Once everyone had refilled their cups and taken a bathroom break, they rejoined the circle. Lena was last to come back in, the smell of her perfume heady as she breezed past Kara’s seat and made for her own on the opposite side. Kara was surprised she’d returned at all, left with the distinct impression that she didn’t want to be there.

     

                Then again, neither did Kara. It was only for the charade of feeling like she wasn’t alone for the brief hour within the shitty recreation room, for the free donut and an hour away from Alex’s that got her sister off her back, that Kara went. She didn’t think it was beneficial, didn’t think it was going to heal her grief, but it was something.

     

                Eventually, it was her turn and she felt even more jittery. Palms clammy and her throat dry, despite the tea, Kara’s knee bounced as she bit her nails, hunched forward.

     

                “Kara? How’s this week been for you?”

     

                “My sister has been trying to get me to get back into a normal routine; she said it’s hard for her but … she doesn’t know how it feels to lose the person you married,” she said, her voice low and trembling. “I think maybe if- if she knew, she wouldn’t be so angry with me.”

     

                “Do you think you’re ready to get back into a normal routine?”

     

                “No,” she whispered, her vision blurring as she quickly ducked her head down.

     

                “What’s stopping you?”

     

                Her mouth twisted at his question and she shrugged as she kept her head ducked down. Letting out a shaky breath, she kept bouncing her knee and hoped that he’d move on to someone else. Instead, after a long minute, he spoke again.

     

                “You don’t have to tell us.”

     

                She felt the full force of the room on her, her eyes limned with tears, her lips slightly parted as Thomas spoke.

     

                “I know talking about it won’t undo any of it. But not talking about it won’t either, and if there's anything you need to say, you can. Even if it’s just your favourite thing about him, you can say it.”

     

                Her mouth tightened into a knot, trembling slightly as her eyes tightened at the corners, trying to keep the tears at bay, before she finally spoke. “His laugh. He snorted when he laughed.”

     

                She let out a choked laugh and wiped at her nose as tears spilled down her cheeks. Laughing again, Kara reached up to wipe the cuff of her jacket across her pale cheeks.

     

                “Thank you for sharing with us.”

     

                It was another ten minutes of sharing before they wrapped up with Thomas giving a small closing speech, full of hope and reflection on their situations. Kara had to swallow the scoff that built in her chest, rubbing at her face as she waited to go.

     

                They all murmured their goodbyes once the session was over and Kara lingered a minute to help stack the chairs before she walked out. Her bus was just down the block and wasn’t due for another fifteen minutes so she lingered on the sidewalk outside for a minute, tipping her head back and inhaling deeply. 

     

                When she lowered her head and opened her eyes, she caught a flicker of movement out of the corner of her eyes and she looked to find someone still lingering. It was the newcomer, Lena, and Kara watched her as she paced, before their eyes met and Lena stopped.

     

                Ducking her head as she hitched the backpack higher on her shoulder, the yellow light of the Y spilling out and illuminating her, she carried on past the woman and made for the bus stop.

    Chapter 2

                The next week dragged on much the same as the last few had. Kara lingered at Alex’s, laying in bed all day, occasionally waking when it was still dark and going for a jog, sometimes putting in an appearance at work. On Sunday she walked to a café and sat by herself, drinking a caramel latte and picking at a bagel as her appetite evaded her, much like she evaded her sister’s attempt to force her back into the routine of her normal life.

     

                She’d skipped drinks again on Friday, feigning a headache and spending the night in her sweats, eating dry cereal from the box as she stared at the ceiling. By the time Thursday came around again, Kara mustered the energy to dress in her scrubs from Monday, dug out of her overflowing laundry basket, and made the trip to work. 

     

                Arriving early, she surprised James and was handed a cup of coffee by William before she lingered in the kitchen for a while doing paperwork. Making herself another cup of coffee, Kara slipped out the back and made small talk with one of the vet nurses, Eve, checking in on a litter of abandoned puppies and reading over charts for the patients that weren’t even hers.

     

                For lunch, she went out with James to get gyros and they walked around the block, the grey skies and cool weather adding to Kara’s already gloomy mood.

     

                “How’re you holding up?”

     

                She shrugged, unwashed hair pulled back, bare face pale and exhausted and her scrubs wrinkled. Taking a bite of her food, she watched a couple walk hand-in-hand on the opposite side of the road.

     

                “I’m fine.”

     

                “You going to be at work tomorrow?” James asked, looking down at her.

     

                Lips twitching ruefully, Kara glanced up at him and then sheepishly looked away. “Yeah.”

     

                “Three days in one week? That’s … good,” James lightly replied. “Getting back into things.”

     

                “You sound like Alex.”

     

                “I’m not going to push you. He was my friend too.”

     

                “Kind of.”

     

                James smiled thinly. “Kind of. But you were always bigger than him. You were the link for us all. I know it’s hard for you, especially with everyone hounding you about hanging out, but … we just miss you.”

     

                Taking another bite of food as she walked alongside him, Kara chewed slowly and then swallowed. Staring stoically ahead, her mouth turned down at the corners as she frowned faintly.

     

                “And I miss him.”

     

                James clapped a hand on her shoulder and gently squeezed in a reassuring manner, although Kara was anything but comforted by the gesture. He didn’t reply for a few minutes and Kara finished off her lunch and dumped the wrapper in a trash can they passed by.

     

                “You still going to that grief group thing?”

     

                “Mhm. Got one tonight.”

     

                “How’s that going?”

     

                Kara let out a humourless laugh, wiping her hands on the thighs of her pants. She’d had to cinch the drawstring of the scrubs in a little tighter that morning.

     

                “Yeah, it’s super. Nothing says healing quite like some dingy Y led by a preachy middle-aged man and a dozen strangers.”

     

                “Kelly said she offered to set you up with someone-“

     

                “Yeah, no offence, James, but just because that helped your sister out, it doesn’t mean that it’s going to work for me. I’m fine. Really. Except for the part where being a widow sucks.”

     

                “We’re just trying to help.”

     

                “It’d help a hell of a lot more if everyone just stopped,” Kara muttered. “Just because everyone else wants to move on, it doesn’t mean that I have to.”

     

                “Come on, you know that’s not it.”

     

                “Isn’t it?”

     

                “Kara-“

     

                Biting back an impatient sigh, she turned around. “We should get back to the clinic; don’t you have that TECA surgery for that dog at one?”

     

                Glancing down at the watch on his wrist, James hummed in agreement and followed after her. She ended up scrubbing in on his surgery and ran a few x-rays on a pet parrot with a broken wing once she was out. Her last patient of the day was a wounded rescue brought in for medical treatment, the mangy stray terrified and aggressive as Kara tried to soothe it, bribing him with dog treats and then sedating him so she could clean out the wounds and set the broken bones with casts.

     

                She clocked out just past five and rode the bus past the Y so she could pick up takeout for dinner before she made her way back. The inside of the community centre reeked of chlorine and she could hear the splashing of water from the cavernous room with the pool and the squeak of shoes and pounding of a ball on the basketball court from the other side. Lingering on a bench, she ate half of her dumplings and put the rest in her backpack for later while she waited for Thomas Coville to show up.

     

                Early, she walked in with him and helped unstack chairs while he set up the coffee and tea station, opening the boxes of donuts he’d brought with him. Because she was so early, Kara helped herself to one before the others had even started to arrive and took a seat as she pretended to be busy on her phone, while Thomas laid out his flyers and pamphlets near the sugar and milk. Kara hadn’t even entertained the thought of reading through them over her weeks of attending sessions. She didn’t think a nature retreat or horseback riding would help revive her husband from the dead.

     

                People slowly trickled in after that and Kara joined the queue to make herself a cup of tea, sneaking another donut while she was there. Scrawling her name onto a sticker and slapping it on her chest, she reclaimed her seat and excluded herself from the quiet chitchat of people greeting each other and catching up on their week. The newcomer, Lena, was the last to arrive and Thomas shut the doors behind her while she made her tea and took a seat to Kara’s left.

     

                She met Kara’s eye for a brief moment before taking a sip of her scalding tea and they didn’t speak at all as Thomas launched into his usual welcome spiel. They all responded with varying levels of enthusiasm and listened to his inspiring speech on strength and resilience. Kara felt she was quite lacking in both. What she was was exhausted.

     

                As usual, they took it in turns to go around and talk about their week, about their grief and what they missed, what was difficult, what they were doing to fix it. Hearing other people talk about their lives, what they were doing to move forward, to heal, made her feel like a failure and it took her a moment to speak when it was her turn.

     

                “I … I made it to work three times this week. That’s the most since he … passed. My family, my friends, are kind of over it now; they think I should be back to my usual self. They miss me. Sometimes I feel like I’m talking to a brick wall with them. Does that make sense?”

     

                Thomas gave her a small encouraging smile. “Loss can cause a rift between us and those we love who can’t understand. But it’s not a unique experience; talk, and all of us here will listen.”

     

                “I just think … I’m a bit … lost,” Kara said as her forehead furrowed. “I never really had the chance to develop my own person outside of him. And now I’ve been forced to and I just- I can’t figure out a way to be normal. My friend today said that I was the link. I don’t even know what that’s supposed to mean.”

     

                “Do you think you’ve pulled away from your social circle since your husband has passed?”

     

                Shrugging, Kara tapped the side of her paper cup. “I’m just … tired. I can’t even think about going out for drinks with them when I can barely get out of bed. The only time I feel like I can escape is here. Do you ever feel like a stranger cares more than your family or friends?”

     

                “All the time.”

     

                The reply came from beside her and Kara turned to look at Lena, who was staring blankly back at her, green eyes flat and lifeless. She looked tired, defeated, and Kara’s lips twitched with a faint smile of understanding.

     

                “It’s exhausting, isn’t it?”

     

                Lena dipped her head in a nod and Kara found herself done with speaking. It moved on to the next person who piped up with a hesitant explanation of their own recent feelings, and Kara tuned it out as she stared at the man without really seeing him.

     

                When the session ended, she helped stack the chairs and made her way outside. It was raining and her bus wasn’t due for another fifteen minutes so Kara lingered on the stoop of the building in the hope that the rain would let up soon, nodding and murmuring goodbyes to those that passed her by.

     

                Alone, she watched cars pull out, except for one that lingered, the headlights on but the engine not running. She’d watched Lena climb into that one, her sleek yet understated fashion suiting the matching car, and Kara stepped out into the rain, telling herself she’d walk to the bus stop now but cutting past the other woman’s car as she walked. She could tell that she was crying, the shadowed outline of her shaking as she bowed her head and Kara felt like she was intruding in on something deeply personal. She also felt like she should say something though, knowing how raw the pain felt during the first few weeks.

     

                Hesitating, Kara crossed over to the window and tapped on it, startling the woman, who shot her a scowl, bloodshot eyes wary and wet. She wiped at her face with the cuff of her coat and then rolled the window down, Kara blocking the worst of the rain.

     

                “Can I help you?” she asked, her voice brittle and slightly hoarse.

     

                Feeling suddenly uncomfortable, Kara opened and closed her mouth, a pained smile faintly curling her lips. “I just … I wanted to see if you were okay.”

     

                “Obviously not.”

     

                “Yeah. Stupid question. Sorry.”

     

                Staring straight ahead as she gripped the steering wheel in a white-knuckled grip, Lena swallowed thickly, blinking back tears. Neither of them spoke for a moment and Kara ducked down a little more, feeling the light rain patter against the back of her neck.

     

                “I’m Kara.”

     

                “Lena.”

     

                “I know who you are.”

     

                Glancing sideways at her, Lena gave her a bitter smile, “I know you too. Your husband is dead.”

     

                Wincing, Kara pulled back a fraction. “Yeah. He is.”

     

                “Why’re you standing in the rain?”

     

                Kara glanced back over her shoulder and her face furrowed slightly, nose wrinkling as rain dotted her glasses.

     

                “Oh. I’m hanging around for my bus.”

     

                “Do you want a ride?”

     

                Hand on top of the car roof, Kara stooped and smiled crookedly. “No, it’s alright. I’ll get your seats wet.”

     

                Lena snorted and wiped at her face. “We’re outside some shitty Y after grief group and you think wet car seats are my biggest problem?”

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Kara let out a choked laugh, the knot in her chest tightening a fraction. “Yeah, good point.”

     

                “Get in. I’ll drive you.”

     

                She was going to protest further but Lena wound the window up and brought the engine to life, headlights illuminating the light sheeting rain pattering the asphalt parking lot. Shallow puddles reflected the neon lights of the city and Kara walked around to the passenger side, opening the door and climbing inside. 

     

                It wasn’t lost on her that it was an extremely nice car, the smell of brand new leather and the digital dashboard too expensive for her. Hell, Kara didn’t even own a car, not even a shitty one to drive to work. She was mostly dry though and wedged her backpack near her feet.

     

                “Nice car.”

     

                “Thanks,” Lena muttered as she put the car into drive and eased them out of the parking lot.

     

                Kara had always been good with strangers - or used to be anyway - which had always made her so good at her job, meeting new clients with her little patients every day, but the past few months had dampened that charm she’d used to exude. Now, she was flatter, monotone, unable to muster the effort to make small talk or put people at ease. But she was still forthright, so she talked, even if Lena didn’t want her to.

     

                “What do you do?”

     

                “Excuse me?”

     

                “What do you do for a living?“

     

                “Oh. I own my own architecture firm.”

     

                “Interesting.”

     

                Lena made a vague sound of agreement at the back of her throat as she slowed in the traffic at a red light. The sound made it seem like she thought it was anything but interesting.

     

                “You’re a doctor, I presume?”

     

                Snorting, Kara looked down at her scrubs, a wry smile twisting her lips. “Technically I’m Doctor Kara Danvers, but I’m a veterinarian, so not the kind that gets you any respect.”

     

                “If it’s any consolation, I don’t respect doctors, so …”

     

                Letting out a quiet laugh, Kara stared at Lena from the corner of her eye, taking in the haughtiness of her hard face, her pale skin that was bathed in the light of whichever neon sign they were passing by. 

     

                “Well, if you have a pet that needs updated booster shots, you know who to come to. I’ll even throw in a discount for a fellow grief group member. You know, on account of the rest of our lives being shit.”

     

                Lena let out a rough laugh. “How long have you been going?”

     

                “This was … my seventh week. Eighth? I don’t know.”

     

                “Does it help?”

     

                With a huff of laughter, Kara leaned her head back against the headrest and stared at Lena’s side profile. There was a sadness to her gaze as her wan amusement vanished and she became quiet.

     

                “Not really. But … you just- you go so the people in your life stop worrying. Nagging. It makes them feel better.”

     

                “I don’t have anyone to pander to,” Lena muttered.

     

                “Then you’re lucky. In the beginning, everyone sends you flowers and they- they’re understanding, but then they move on because it’s not their life and they just- they get angry that you haven’t moved on. He was my fucking husband.”

     

                “I get that.”

     

                “Yeah?” Kara murmured, a hopeful note in her voice.

     

                Lena glanced over at her for a brief moment, her eyes piercing in the dimness of the car, and there was a flicker of surprise on her face. She looked back to the road and Kara saw the corner of her mouth twitch.

     

                “I don’t have anyone because they’ve all moved on. Or they never even got caught up on it in the first place. It’s- it’s only been a month and I-“

     

                “I’m sorry.”

     

                Straightening as she cleared her throat, Lena gestured vaguely ahead. “Were you planning on telling me where you were going? Just so we’re not driving around all night.”

     

                “Oh, shit. Sorry, um … take a left here. Follow it to Thirty-First and then make a right.”

     

                “How long ago did your husband die?”

     

                “Three months.”

     

                “How’d it happen, if you don’t mind me asking.”

     

                Kara grimaced slightly as she looked at Lena, who was purposely staring straight ahead. “Hiking accident. Of all the ways to go. Weekend camping trip with the boys and they just- they drank too much and went hiking at night. The next thing I know, I’m getting a call at the crack of dawn from the hospital telling me my husband’s in a coma. He was gone before I got there. Idiots.”

     

                She said it with bitterness, her anger at Mike flooding back in. He was always so reckless, so immature, and she’d clung to the naïve hope that he’d grow up eventually. 

     

                “I’m sorry.”

     

                “What about your … wife?”

     

                “She was sick for a long time. It wasn’t unexpected.”

     

                “Still … a month-“

     

                “I’m used to it.”

     

                Kara fell silent after that, except for the occasional direction as Lena drove her home, passing further out of the city centre. 

     

                “On the right. Here.”

     

                Putting the car into park, Lena looked out the window at the yellow glow of the lobby. “This is where you live?”

                

                “My sister,” Kara awkwardly explained. “I’ve been staying with her ever since … I can’t go home with all his things, you know?”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “Are you still at your place?”

     

                Lena’s mouth thinned slightly and she made a rough sound of agreement, raking a hand through her hair. “Yeah. I wouldn’t have had anywhere to go anyway, but … I mean, it doesn’t matter where I go, I wouldn’t be able to get rid of her.”

     

                “Fair point,” Kara murmured.

     

                They sat there in silence for a long minute, surprisingly not uncomfortable despite them practically being strangers, and she eventually sighed. Turning to look at Lena, who met her gaze, Kara gave her an uneven smile.

     

                “Thanks for the ride.”

     

                “Any time.”

     

                “And … it does get better, you know. Or, well, you get used to it, and that’s pretty much the same thing.”

     

                Nodding, Lena swallowed thickly and reached for the gearstick, shifting the car back into drive. “I’ll see you next week.”

     

                “Yeah. See you.”

     

                Climbing out of the car, Kara hauled her backpack onto her shoulder and made for the lobby, turning to raise a hand in farewell as Lena pulled out into the street. Shouldering open the door, Kara grabbed the spare set of keys from the front pocket of the bag and walked upstairs to Alex’s apartment, working the key into the lock and kicking off her running shoes as she stepped over the threshold.

     

                Alex looked up from where she was finishing up the dishes in the kitchen, a look of mild surprise crossing her face before she frowned. Shaking off soap suds, she grabbed a dish towel and wiped her hands.

     

                “You’re home early. Did you bail on grief group?”

     

                “No. One of the women there dropped me home,” Kara murmured, bending down to pick up her shoes.

     

                “Oh. Well … that’s good. You’re making friends there at least.”

     

                Kara snorted and rolled her eyes. “She’s not my friend. She just has a dead wife.”

    Chapter 3

                Over the next four weeks, Kara only missed five days of work and attended all four sessions of grief group. She always got there early after work, helping set up and making her tea and snagging a donut while they were still relatively fresh. Lena would only appear right before they were about to start, and Kara started saving a seat for her in the spot next to her, her backpack placed on the plastic chair to deter anyone else from claiming it.

     

                Afterwards, Lena would always exit slowly, dressed in some form of stylish business attire - fitted shirts and cropped cigarette pants, blazers with wide-legged pants or turtlenecks and pencil skirts - looking far too out of place for such a grim place. Kara didn’t ask, but she imagined the architect had enough money to afford private sessions with the best shrinks in the city, especially if she owned her own firm, but Lena showed up every week and had taken to catching Kara outside and offering her a ride home.

     

                In the fifth week, more than four months after Mike had died, Kara hitched her backpack higher on her shoulder as her running shoes squeaked on the concrete steps of the Y as she left. The smell of chlorine had been overwhelming all session and the fresh air was welcome as she stepped out into the dark. Lena was standing to the left of the steps, handbag slung over one arm as she stiffly waited.

     

                “Need a ride?” she asked when Kara appeared at the tail end of the group, knowing that she did.

     

                “If it’s not a bother.”

     

                It had become something of an awkward routine between them, with Lena offering and Kara hesitantly offering before they walked to her car. Kara would climb into the passenger seat and they’d make stilted small talk on the drive out to Alex’s apartment.

     

                “Still at your sister’s?” Lena asked as the quiet engine purred to life, headlights illuminating a wide swathe of the parking lot.

     

                Kara’s lips twisted ruefully as she gave Lena a sheepish look. “Still there.”

     

                Nodding without any judgement, Lena pulled out into traffic and fiddled with the radio, soft music set to background noise as they caught the red light. Kara stared out the window and relaxed into the leather seats, used to the silence between them on their rides, knowing that if one of them wanted to speak, they would. It was comforting in a way, to sit next to someone in the same boat, at the same level of grief, without any expectations to pretend like everything was fine.

     

                Once the light turned green and Lena accelerated, she cleared her throat and glanced sideways at Kara, who turned her head to meet her gaze. There was a wariness to the stiffness of Lena’s pale face and she gripped the steering wheel a little tighter.

     

                “You know … if you’d like help … well, I imagine it would be easier to sort through things with a stranger than people with … you know, opinions and all of that. So … when you’re ready, I can always- I can help.”

     

                Kara stared at Lena for a long moment, the sound of the car rushing down the street, lights blurring beyond the windows and the silence almost stifling after Lena’s hesitant offer, and her face crumpled with confusion. Chewing on her lip, she considered it for a moment before replying.

     

                “Why?”

     

                “Because … I’d like to think someone would help me through the hard stuff when I’m ready for it.”

     

                “Oh. Thank you.”

     

                Lena nodded, eyes fixated back on the road. “No rush, of course.”

     

                “I’ll make you a deal,” Kara murmured after a pause. “You do it for me, and when you’re ready I’ll do it for you.”

     

                A small smile dimpled Lena’s cheek as she let out a quiet huff of laughter. “Sure, Kara.”

     

                They descended into silence once more for a few minutes but Kara felt the burning urge to admit the truth, the thing she was scared to confront.

     

                “It always smelled like bread in the mornings because of the bakery downstairs,” she murmured. “I miss it there; I want to go back every day, I just- I’m scared of what it’ll be like without him.”

     

                Turning slightly, although her eyes stayed on the road, Lena gave her a rueful smile. “It’s exactly like you think it’ll be. It’s lonely but everything is the same. You still have … the same bed, the same dishes you ate out of every night, you use the same detergent and … sometimes, you still expect to hear the key in the lock and the sound of them coming home. You’ll forget, a lot, because it feels so familiar but the loneliness-“

     

                She faltered there, a flicker of pain crossing her face as a muscle twitched in her jaw. Shaking her head, Lena quietly snorted.

     

                “But to get better, it has to get worse.”

     

                “Do you believe that?”

     

                Hesitating, Lena smiled thinly. “I’m not an optimist, but … it can’t always be like this, can it? Even if we never get over it … it can’t always be like this.”

     

                Kara made a dubious sound of agreement and leaned her head against the window, the vents pumping out warm air as she thought. She couldn’t imagine a day would come when it wouldn’t hurt, when she wouldn’t miss him, for all his flaws and the frustrating things that made her doubt the longevity of their marriage. She’d never know if she might’ve tried to make things work - she’d just be permanently left with the inadequate feeling of a mediocre marriage that left her in the lurch. But Kara wouldn’t imagine she’d ever make it to the point where she’d walk back inside their apartment; she couldn’t even imagine walking to the front door. There was simply too much sadness there.

     

                Lena dropped her off and they said goodnight and Kara spent a sleepless night wallowing in her feelings and wondering about how things could ever change. The lack of sleep, the infrequent meals and just the general heaviness of grief left her feeling listless and hollow. She’d always been so vibrant before, had so much to give, but she felt so empty that the thought of holding someone else’s feelings as well as her own was just exhausting. 

     

                At work, she was like an emotionless zombie, offering patients their diagnoses and news as if she was reading them her shopping list, so flat and unfeeling. But then they’d had to put down the twelve-year-old Labrador and Kara had burst into tears as she was left to tell the owner his dog’s fate. Her numbness was all-encompassing, except when emotion came for her at the strangest of times.

     

                On Saturday, she’d cried the whole bus ride home after she’d dropped her bag of groceries, no one there to help carry them, no one there to eat the Sour Patch Kids flavours she didn’t like or to bicker about whether they should buy the ground coffee beans or do it themselves at home so their coffee would taste better. It was always the little things. It didn’t matter that it had driven Kara insane that he’d put empty ketchup bottles back in the fridge, that he’d rarely cooked but always argued about what to have for dinner that week. All of the little things that had annoyed her, made her angry and resentful at times, were just things she missed about him now, if only because he’d been there to make her feel something.

     

                The fifth month rolled around and she felt absolutely nothing. 

     

                Living with Alex and Kelly was starting to become unbearable though. She was grateful they let her stay there but being around two people in love was more than she could handle at times, catching sight of the fleeting touches, the adoring glances and quiet whispers, so intimate and so painful. It made Kara resentful and she hated that she felt that way about her sister’s happiness, knowing that it wasn’t really about them being happy together, only that Kara wasn’t happy with anyone. The following Thursday night, in Lena’s car after group had finished, Kara swallowed thickly and stared out the window as she spoke.

     

                “I think … I’m going to move back into my apartment.”

     

                “Oh,” Lena murmured with faint surprise, glancing over at her. “Do you want help?”

     

                Turning to face her, Kara gave her a strained smile. “If you’re not busy.”

     

                “Saturday,” Lena firmly replied. “Get it out of the way. I’ll pick you up at eight.”

     

                Kara let out a strangled laugh, raising her eyebrows slightly. “Don’t you have better plans for the weekend?”

     

                “What gives you the impression I have any sort of social life,” Lena snorted, her lips twitching.

     

                “I don’t know, you just- you seem remarkably put together.”

     

                “What does that mean?”

     

                Shrugging, Kara tilted her head to the side and twisted in her seat as she leaned it against the headrest, taking in Lena’s side profile. She really was beautiful and so cool and impassive that you might have never known she was silently suffering through the loss of a dead wife if you didn’t know how to pick up on the subtle signs of grief. Unfortunately, Kara was well-versed in that and could see through the polished veneer of Lena’s mask.

     

                “You just- you hide it so well that I can imagine that you’d be able to bring yourself to have drinks with friends, even while you fell apart on the inside.”

     

                Lena’s throat bobbed as she swallowed and her voice was hoarse when she replied. “I don’t have friends. I never have. I had her and that was it.”

     

                “Well, if you feel like you need a friend now … I’d understand, you know.”

     

                “Yeah,” Lena muttered. 

     

                The rest of the drive continued in silence until Lena pulled up outside Alex’s, both of them rehashing their plans for Saturday before Kara went upstairs and shut herself in the bedroom. She fell asleep in her scrubs, smelling of antiseptic and wet dog and feeling sluggish when she woke late that morning. Rushing to make it to work, she was ten minutes late, but James was just pleased she’d shown up at all, five consecutive days for the first time in five months. It didn’t feel like the victory he was making it out to be; Kara was simply bored and looking for a distraction. 

     

                That didn’t necessarily have to be through work, but she hadn’t felt like skipping work to walk the streets with a coffee, knowing she’d have to face Alex’s judgement when James told her she skipped another day of work. The following day would be hard enough without the frustration of dealing with her uncompromising sister who thought pushing her was the best way to get past her grief. Kara just wanted to avoid it all but she knew she had to get out of that spare room too, perhaps even more. Still, she hadn’t told Alex, didn’t want the infantilising delight of everyone applauding her for throwing out Mike’s things, bordering on patronising. 

     

                Work dragged on and she volunteered to stay late, doing the duties of the vet technicians as she restocked gauze and sealed needles and bandages, stacked the shelves at reception with the variety of treats and shampoos that they sold. It was late and she was hungry when she left, walking to an Indian takeout place that sold trays with rice, daal and curry and eating it at the back of the bus. The light overhead flickered and she had the odd sensation that she was drunk as she swayed along with the motion.

     

                Sleep eluded her for most of the night, tossing and turning in the bed until she woke just after five and started doing laundry to keep herself busy. She’d have to take it all with her when she moved back home anyway, so it felt somewhat purposeful as she sipped coffee and leaned against the counter in the laundry room, watching the suds as the barrel turned. Kelly poked her head in just after six, blearily blinking in the light.

     

                “You’re up early.”

     

                “Couldn’t sleep.”

     

                “Breakfast?”

     

                Her stomach felt too tied in knots to even consider eating but she agreed to please her sister-in-law and Kara made herself useful by putting away the dishes from the night before as Kelly scrambled eggs for omelettes.

     

                “How was group?”

     

                “Fine.”

     

                “Making any progress?

     

                Shrugging indifferently, Kara sorted the cutlery into the compartments in the drawer. “Maybe.”

     

                Kelly didn’t seem bothered by her curt, nothing answers, just nodded encouragingly and kept cooking. Alex woke a while after that and Kara silently shuffled eggs around her plate as she listened to the conversation about the adoption application, both women speaking with a calmness that belied their excitement about starting a family. Kara was happy for them but couldn’t muster the energy to include herself in the conversation. 

     

                At seven, she hopped in the shower, washing her hair and pulling on a plaid shirt and worn jeans, thinking practical clothes would be best for all the work she’d be doing. Alex and Kelly kept giving her sidelong glances as she dressed, brushed her teeth and dried her hair, all of her bustling around the apartment filled with a purpose she’d lacked for a while now. When they hesitantly asked where she was going, her answer was evasive and nonchalant.

     

                She’d been waiting outside for ten minutes when Lena pulled up outside in her sleek car, and Kara pushed off the wall of the building as she walked over to the car and slid into the passenger seat. Buckling herself in as she murmured a greeting to Lena, who looked far too dressed up for someone who would be sorting through a stranger’s clothes in a dusty apartment no one had set foot inside in months.

     

                As she pulled out into traffic with one hand on the wheel, she reached for the centre console with her other hand and picked up a paper cup. “I wasn’t sure how you had your coffee so I got you a tea - I know how you have that.”

     

                Kara chuckled quietly, accepting the warm cup in her cool palms. “Thank you.”

     

                “What’s the address?”

     

                She rattled it off in a monotone voice as Lena plugged it into the digital dashboard, a map showing the route through the city, and they listened to the morning radio as they drove, the windows wound down a fraction for a flow of gasoline-tainted cool air to stream inside. It was a clear day, the sky a pale blue, and Kara felt the swooping sensation of nerves inside her as she tried to whet her parched throat with tea, her hands clammy on the cup and a hollow shakiness to her body. She felt physically weak, as if she’d black out if she tried to stand up, and she breathed slowly, trying to quell the panic as the city blocks became increasingly familiar.

     

                The arcade they’d played bowling and pool, the cheap diner they sometimes got pancakes on a Sunday, the local bodega, the convenience store Kara would stop by for milk when they were out. It was a suffocating blur of overlapping memories and she almost asked Lena to take her back to Alex’s.

     

                In the end, she was silent until they pulled up outside the designated building, that little bakery still there as the smell of freshly baked bread slammed into her as it crept through the gap in the open windows. Lena cut the engine and turned to look at Kara, a mild look of expectation on her face.

     

                “Is this it?”

     

                Kara couldn’t make herself speak, her throat tightening with each attempt to vocalise, and she settled for a weak nod and a vague sound of affirmation at the back of her throat. They both sat in silence for a few minutes and Kara was grateful that Lena didn’t rush her, the silence relatively comfortable as they listened to the passing traffic and waited. When she finally unbuckled her seatbelt and opened the door, Lena followed after her.

     

                Hands shaking as she fished out her keys and set them into the lock of the door in a small alcove beside the bakery, Kara hesitated before pushing it open. A narrow flight of stairs went up to the door to their apartment on the right, another door on the left to her old neighbours. At the top of the stairs, she had to pause for a while longer before putting the key into the lock, her hands shaking so badly that Lena itched to do it for her but knew it was something Kara had to do for herself. She hovered on the staircase, not enough room for them both at the top, and eventually, Kara let them inside.

     

                The living room was spacious, with dead potted plants on the bookcases, dried leaves trailing over the spines of books. It was full of the clutter of an ordinary life that had been ripped to pieces in wake of Mike’s death and Kara looked around at the thick layer of dust that blanketed everything. There was a fetid smell in the air from groceries that had been left to putrefy in the fridge and she breathed shallowly through her mouth as she looked around. Beneath the blanket of untouched dust and disarray from abandonment, it was the same old apartment. 

     

                The air rushed from Kara’s lungs as she warily stepped further inside, kicking up a cloud of dust. Lena tried to muffle a cough as she followed behind, the door hinges squeaking as it was shut behind them. Eyes locking onto the sight of Mike’s jacket hanging in its usual spot just inside the door, Kara let out a choked sound, her eyes stinging with tears.

     

                “Oh.”

     

                She pulled it off, buried her face into it, the fading smell of his aftershave and soap a familiar comfort that opened new wounds. Sniffing as she hugged it to herself, trying to blink back the tears as she hunched her shoulders, cheeks pink with embarrassment, she turned her head slightly to speak over her shoulder.

     

                “Sorry, I-”

     

                “Don’t apologise,” Lena murmured, firm despite the awkwardness of intruding on something so personal. “You don’t have to apologise to me.”

     

                Nodding, Kara swallowed and stayed that way for a few minutes. In the meantime, Lena brusquely moved through the apartment and jerked open every stiff window, dispelling the stuffy air inside along with the foul odour of rotten food. Letting out a choked breath, Kara wiped at her face and set the jacket back on the hook before moving further through the space.

     

                Lena was in the kitchen, the neck of her thin cashmere drawn up over her nose and mouth as a severe frown clouded her face, the trash can at her feet as she tossed things that didn’t resemble food anymore into it. Even the jars of pickles and spreads went in, and Kara didn’t bother to argue that they were fine. She wanted the entire place gutted. Still, she tried to take over but Lena gave her a dismissive wave of her hand and continued.

     

                Standing there for a moment, Kara turned and slowly went to fetch the vacuum. Neither of them spoke for a while as they worked independently, Kara vacuuming up as much of the dust as she could while Lena scrubbed down the kitchen surfaces and appliances, the smell of citrus and bleach chasing away any malingering odours. By the time she was down, the fridge was spotless and she looked revolted as she held a trash bag aloft.

     

                Kara took it from her and walked out of the apartment to the garbage chute set in the back wall at the top of the stairs. She felt a little embarrassed to have let her place fall into such disarray but after the news she hadn’t gone back to it, leaving Alex and Kelly to fetch her funeral clothes for her and all of her other things, and she couldn’t fault them for not throwing out her trash.

     

                The morning passed by quickly, all of the surfaces wiped down and polished, the dust motes caught in shafts of sunlight through the open windows thinning out as they tackled each room. It wasn’t a large apartment - an open kitchen and living area, two bedrooms, one of which was used as an office and storage room, a laundry room and the bathroom - and once Kara had finished bleaching the bath and shower, cleaning the grout and polishing up the stainless steel taps, it was time to move onto the main purpose. 

     

                Lena wrung out the mop in the bucket and emptied the greyish water down the sink of the laundry room and cautioned Kara against walking on the wet floors. She’d been relatively silent, content to work without talking, but there was an air of command around her as if she was used to ordering people about, and Kara imagined she didn’t often wield a mop and bucket or clean out spoiled food. Just from looking at her, Kara could tell she was far too rich to not have a housekeeper.

     

                “Where do you want to start?” Lena asked.

     

                “I don’t know.”

     

                Nodding, Lena tilted her head to the side and thought. She was good at executing plans and delegating tasks, probably thanks to her work running her own business, and she nodded to herself a moment later, fixing Kara with a level stare, her eyes so green that Kara couldn’t help but stare back.

     

                “You strip the bed and put the sheets in the wash; if you have spare ones, make the bed. I’ll get the boxes.”

     

                “I don’t have any boxes.”

     

                “I know, I brought some with me.”

     

                “Oh. Thanks.”

     

                Lena nodded again and slipped outside, taking Kara’s keys with her to let herself back in. Peering out the window, Kara watched her unlock her car and open the trunk, pulling out flat-packed boxes. She wished she was so composed but she also knew that Lena was probably using this as a distraction from her own pain, focusing on helping Kara through hers as a means to ignore her own loss. She’d never known Mike so it wasn’t personal for her.

     

                Turning from the window, Kara made her way into the bedroom and started stripping off the sheets. Carrying an armful to the laundry room, she set the washing machine on and fetched clean sheets from the laundry closet and went back to make the bed. She struggled alone for a minute until Lena appeared and was suddenly helping her wrestle the fitted sheet on. In short order, they had the bed made and the bedroom looking remarkably tidier and fresher. 

     

                Out in the living room, they assembled the cardboard boxes and Kara held down the flaps as Lena reinforced them with tape, both of them working quickly and Lena surprisingly efficient - although Kara found it wasn’t that surprising; she seemed like the type of person who was proficient at everything, including helping widows throw out their dead husband’s belongings. Since they were already in the living room, they started there, Kara kneeling on the wooden floor before the TV console as she pulled out a CD.

     

                “He loved Bon Jovi,” Kara snorted, shaking her head as she turned over the CD. “Of all bands, Bon Jovi . He’d play it in the morning, at night, in the car, at karaoke night, when we argued. If there was ever a band I hated, it was Bon Jovi.”

     

                Lena chuckled, perching on the edge of the sofa with her elbows on her knees. “Andrea liked NSYNC. And not in the way that she liked them when she was younger, no, she listened to them now . It drove me insane.”

     

                Kara choked on a laugh as she closed her eyes and pressed her lips together to fight back a smile. “I love NSYNC.”

     

                Quietly groaning, Lena shook her head and rolled her eyes. “You know what, that doesn’t surprise me.”

     

                “What’s that supposed to mean?”

     

                “I can imagine what you were like before.”

     

                “How’s that?”

     

                Shrugging, Lena cocked her head to the side and gave her such a scrutinising look that Kara flushed slightly beneath the intensity of her stare. “I don’t know, you just- you seem so devastated that it’s easy to believe that you had a good life before. You probably laughed a lot, were happy a lot, and then you were blindsided.”

     

                Kara looked down at her lap, swallowing thickly as she fiddled with the cracked CD case. “You’re right, I was. But this isn’t the first time I- my parents died when I was thirteen. Both of them so … well, I thought I was done losing people for a while anyway.”

     

                “I watched my mom drown when I was four. I thought that was going to be the worst thing that would ever happen to me.”

     

                Exhaling heavily, an ache in her chest and a sorrowful look on her face as she glanced at Lena, imagining what she’d been like at four years old, just as serious and aloof, her wide green eyes still so innocent to the awful things that could happen in life. That was a brutal lesson to learn at such a young age and Kara pitied her. 

     

                Neither of them spoke for a moment as Kara fiddled with the CD in her hands until Lena softly sighed and jerked her chin towards it. “Put it on.”

     

                “What?”

     

                “Put the CD on. It’ll make you feel better, just for a little bit.”

     

                Hesitating, she nodded and swallowed thickly, pulling the CD from the case and turning on the small stereo as she put the disc inside and turned the volume up. The first notes started playing and she let out a quiet scoff, shaking her head and rolling her eyes. They prickled with tears and she smiled wryly at Lena as she tossed the CD onto the rug.

     

                “Still just as bad.”

     

                A slow smile spread across Lena’s face and they started to sort. Rifling through the CDs, she removed any of Mike’s and stacked them in the box, the collection sparse by the end of it and critiqued by Lena as she eyed the Britney Spears, Taylor Swift and Backstreet Boys albums lined up. Next was the bookshelves, thick volumes about business and the economy interspersed with science fiction paperbacks and Stephen King horrors. Kara’s were mostly books to do with animals and work-related, with a few memoirs and contemporary fiction and she freed up a few shelves once all of Mike’s were packed away into two boxes. 

     

                Lunchtime came around quickly and they took a break, walking to a cafe together to buy paninis and more coffee, sitting in the fresh air at a little table outside before they made their way back to the apartment. For the first time in months, Kara felt somewhat alright, enjoying Lena’s quiet company, the dependable solidity of her presence, the knowledge that she’d understand. They didn’t have to talk about things but Kara knew she’d understand and that was enough.

     

                They walked back home and the cleaning continued. His guitar he’d never learnt how to play was packed into its case, his camping gear he broke out maybe five times a year but would never put in storage, his free weights that they had to stack off to one side, too heavy for cardboard boxes. In the bathroom, Kara tossed aftershave and unused razors, hair wax and men’s lotions with ridiculous names into a trash bag that Lena held, the sounds of Bon Jovi still playing from the living room. She tossed his favourite mug and cleared out the bland cereals he’d liked, now stale, and tossed the protein powder and shakers. She kept his computer in the study but tossed his little figurines and comic books into the donation pile.

     

                “Are you sure you don’t want to keep any of this?” Lena hedged as she shadowed Kara from room to room with a box and a trash bag.

     

                “Will you keep any of her things?”

     

                “I- we didn’t really keep anything personal.”

     

                “Ah, minimalists.”

     

                Lena gave her a thin smile, sitting on the edge of the bed as they went into the bedroom. “I’m an architect , an architect who specialises in mid-century modern and corporate minimalist bullshit. Clutter is against my nature.”

     

                “What did your wife do for a living?”

     

                “Ah, tech developer. Family business. What about your husband?”

     

                Kara pulled one of his sweaters off a hanger and hesitated, the faint smell of detergent and his aftershave clinging to it. It brought a lump to her throat and she struggled to swallow for a minute, facing the row of his clothes.

     

                “He was in tech too. A start-up,” she rasped, folding the sweater in her hands and then setting it in a box. “You know, I thought he was such an asshole when we first met. Cocky, arrogant, a total frat boy. And then he made me laugh and he didn’t seem so bad.”

     

                Lena didn’t reply and Kara turned to drag a pair of jeans off a hanger and fold them into the box too. Glancing up at Lena, she smiled thinly.

     

                “How’d you meet your wife?”

     

                “Oh, um, we were at boarding school together. We were friends for years and eventually … she managed to make me love her. I’ll never forgive her for that.”

     

                There was a cold anger to Lena’s brittle words as she clenched her teeth and looked away. Her pain was palpable and Kara had the bizarre urge to wrap her arms around her and hold her tightly. She didn’t, but it was what she’d wanted someone to do to her for months now, just hold her together for a moment, let her feel the touch of someone else, someone who cared. The last time someone had held her like that had been at the funeral.

     

                “What’s that saying? Better to have loved and lost than never loved at all?”

     

                “Bullshit,” Lena snorted. 

     

                “Yeah,” Kara laughed weakly, her mind occupied by the conversation as she started sorting the clothes with more purpose. His old t-shirts with holes in the collar, his college sweatshirts he would never let Kara throw away and his socks with holes in them went into the trash bag while his suits and polished shoes and jackets all went into boxes with his shorts and winter coat and shirts. 

     

                Face crumpling with a bewildered look, Kara cast Lena a quick look, nudging her glasses up her nose. “Everyone keeps telling me that I’ll get over it and that it’s not the end of the world.
