But … if that’s true, why does it feel like the end of the world? I mean … the only relief I get is when I sleep, but … I can’t even do that because all I do is dream him back to life. And when I’m not sleeping, I’m- I’m not sad, I’m not angry, I’m not lonely, I’m just- I’m nothing. All the time, I just feel so empty. ”

     

                A furrow formed between Lena’s eyebrows as she drew her heavy eyebrows together, toying with the rings on her left hand as her cheeks dimpled with her grimace. “Sometimes … I feel so sad that I think it must be genetic. That’s all I ever am. I think I was born sad and the shit happened to me and now I’ve got to spend the rest of my life just … living with it.”

     

                “It’s harder in the beginning,” Kara murmured, sinking onto the mattress beside Lena to take a break. She left a foot between them and looked at her. “It gets better though; it comes in waves.”

     

                Lena let out a heavy sigh, resigned and suffused with her grief. “It’s constant.”

    Chapter 4

                After clearing out the apartment with Lena, it still took Kara another few weeks before she could bring herself to move back in. He’d been dead almost five months when she packed her bags at Alex and Kelly’s apartment on Friday night and emerged after a sleepless night with a duffel bag slung over one shoulder, looking pale and impassive as her sister and almost sister-in-law looked up from their breakfast.

     

                “I’m moving back home,” Kara murmured, monotonous as she hovered uncertainly.

     

                “I- oh, um …” Kelly haltingly replied, glancing at Alex.

     

                “Are you sure you’re ready for that?” Alex slowly asked.

     

                Kara didn’t imagine anyone ever got to the point where they were ready to start moving on from a dead partner, and she would’ve preferred to move to a new apartment if she could’ve afforded the rent on her measly salary, but she couldn’t stay at her sister’s anymore. It wasn’t just the constant nagging and encouragement, the eagerness to help her get back into her life, the impatience when she refused; Alex and Kelly had their own life that didn’t include Kara, and she didn’t want to intrude any longer. But it was mostly for her own peace of mind, to wallow without interruption.

     

                “Yeah. I’ve sorted all of his stuff out already,” Kara replied, a fraction louder and bolder as a muscle jumped in her jaw, teeth grit against the regret, the resentment of having to do that.

     

                “Oh. When was this?”

     

                “A few weeks ago.”

     

                “Why didn’t you tell us?” Alex asked, her brow furrowing as she turned in her seat, looking concerned, a little stricken that Kara had been so evasive as if it had been a secret. “We could’ve helped.”

     

                Kara gestured dismissively, “I wanted to do it alone. Besides, one of the women in grief group helped me out.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                “Stop saying oh,” Kara wearily told her with a sigh.

     

                Holding a hand up defensively, Alex raised her eyebrows a fraction. “I’m just surprised, that's all.”

     

                “Can I borrow your car?” Kara asked, her shoulders slumped and a certain weariness about her that made her sister pause.

     

                Setting her knife and fork down, Alex climbed to her feet, abandoning her eggs. “I’ll drive you.”

     

                “Thanks.”

     

                They didn’t say much as Kara towed her bag downstairs, Alex awkwardly carrying a suitcase after her, climbing into the car and closing her eyes. She could feel Alex’s desire to grill her about the abrupt decision to move back into her apartment, about Lena and why she’d helped her clean everything else out instead of the sister who’d been there through the early days of her grief as a new widow. Kara was glad she kept her questions to herself though and closed her eyes to the early morning traffic.

     

                When she arrived outside, she insisted Alex let her get her bags upstairs herself, assuring her that she’d be fine before her sister finally reluctantly relented, leaving her on the sidewalk with her belongings as she stared at the narrow door leading up to the apartment. It took her five minutes to muster up the energy to open the door and a few more minutes of struggling to lug the suitcase up with the duffel bag. And then she spent twenty minutes crying as she stepped over the threshold of her empty house, devoid of all of Mike’s belongings.

     

                Afterwards, Kara felt slightly better for getting it off her chest and walked to a coffee shop that had opened up in her absence and was blissfully unattached to any memories of him. Her eyes were bloodshot and painful to look at as the barista stared at her with shock, and she ducked her head down, pointing at a bagel in the display cabinet as she tried to compose herself.

     

                Sitting in a back corner, facing the wall, she drank her coffee and ate her bagel and stayed out as long as she could to avoid going back to her apartment. She walked in the park, along the sea wall, in and out of various bookstores and boutiques and ate dinner alone as the day dragged on. Eventually, it was late and she was tired though, and Kara made her way back to the place that used to feel like home and now only felt empty.

     

                The late summer was still hot and the air in her apartment was thick with the chill of the AC as it tried to combat the muggy warmth of the evening. It made it hard to sleep, or it might have been the familiarity of her own mattress, and the unfamiliarity of it being empty beside her. She missed sleeping next to someone, in the most innocent way, just listening to him breathe, the irritation when he snored, elbowing him awake as he mumbled his annoyance at being disturbed. He was always so hot, kicking off the blankets while Kara was cold. They could never sleep well beside each other - now she didn’t sleep well at all.

     

                Sunday was undoubtedly going to drag and Kara combated that with two Ambien, sleeping through the warm afternoon after going grocery shopping for five hours in the morning. Even with a stocked fridge, she didn’t eat anything but plain toast before swallowing the pills and thinking of work tomorrow with relief.

     

                But even with work, it was still a long week and she eagerly volunteered to work late and showed up surprisingly early every day. Kara beat James and William into the clinic every morning for those three days, looking tired despite her copious amounts of sleep aided by pills. They didn’t comment on her early arrivals, or about leaving her to lock up alone and ride the bus home late. James seemed determined to let her do whatever she wanted, and at least she was making a somewhat decent effort to show up now.

     

                Thursday was much the same and Kara was almost looking forward to group after work - or rather, she was looking forward to seeing Lena. Although they barely knew each other, she considered her somewhat like a friend after Lena had helped her clean out her apartment, and it was easier to be around her. Lena didn’t expect anything, didn’t care about her attendance at work or whether she slept all day and did her laundry. It wasn’t even like they even really talked at group, but there was a kindred pain within them that made Kara feel relieved and understood just sitting beside her on a plastic chair for a dull hour.

     

                Lena arrived last again, sweeping in and giving Kara a small smile as she picked up the tea and the glazed donut on a napkin waiting for her on the chair next to Kara. She looked as polished and together as always, as starkly out of place as Kara was scruffily in place with her stained scrubs and worn running shoes, bowed with grief that seemed to age her, like everyone else in the room.

     

                She spent the whole hour wanting to tell Lena that she’d moved back into her apartment on the weekend, restless and distracted, barely offering up any of her thoughts or feelings when it was her turn to speak. Nibbling at her donut and taking small sips of tea, she barely listened to anyone else, which she guiltily thought was selfish even as she continued to tune it all out. Kara was just waiting for it to be over, waiting to go home again and put another week of being a widow behind her.

     

                After she stacked hers and Lena’s chairs, she walked towards the door, where Lena waited for her. They left together, and despite her early thought of how composed Lena was, effortlessly beautiful with her ironed clothes and perfect hair and makeup even in the face of grief, when she looked at Kara as they crossed the parking lot, there was a wary look in her green eyes. It was wariness built from pain, from silent suffering, and Kara was tempted to ask her what was wrong.

     

                “Are you busy?” Lena blurted out as she stopped at her car door, jingling the keys. 

     

                “Now?” Kara asked, her brow creasing faintly.

     

                Humming in agreement, Lena arched an eyebrow slightly in an expectant look, but it was softened by the tense look of panic on her face, in her eyes, as if she was terrified at the thought of something. Kara had been planning on doing nothing but going home and perhaps pretending to watch TV for a few hours before pretending to sleep or maybe drugging herself so she did sleep. 

     

                “No, not really.”

     

                Opening and closing her mouth, uncomfortable as she struggled through her response, Lena clutched her keys in a tight, white-knuckled fist, eyes on the roof of her car. “Do you want to go for a drink?”

     

                Blinking in surprise, Kara’s eyebrows rose towards her hairline. “Right now?”

     

                “Yes, right now. I just … I need to get drunk and I don’t have any friends so … I don’t know, maybe you’ve had a shitty day too.”

     

                Letting out a strained laugh, Kara’s eyes crinkled at the corners, making the faint lines deepen. “Every day’s a shitty day these days.”

     

                “Tell me about it,” Lena said with a wry smile.

     

                There was a moment of silence, weighted with expectation, and Kara realised that Lena was waiting for her to answer her proposition. Blinking again, she shook her head slightly and a thin smile crossed her face.

     

                “I- yeah, I, uh, I could use a drink.”

     

                “Great,” Lena replied, the word breathless with relief as her shoulders drooped. Her face crumpled a moment later and she gave Kara a sheepish look. “Know any bars around here? I don’t fancy going anywhere … decent.”

     

                Cocking her head to the side, Kara smiled again, “how do you feel about dives?”

     

                Wrinkling her nose slightly, Lena’s mouth thinned but she shrugged indifferently. “As long as there’s alcohol, I’m not really in the mood to be picky.”

     

                She pocketed her car keys and Kara led them off in the direction of Al’s. It wasn’t too far and she knew none of her friends would be there on a Thursday night, which meant she could escape their happiness at her showing up. She wasn’t showing up for herself anyway, just for Lena, although Kara did need a drink. 

     

                Neither of them spoke as they walked, Lena’s heels clicking on the grimy sidewalk as she followed Kara’s lead. The thought of her inside the dingy bar with its sticky floor and rowdy regulars was almost laughable but it was the only place Kara could think of that didn’t involve effort. 

     

                If Lena was sceptical at the alleyway Kara led her down a few blocks over, she didn’t show it. A cat nosing around the dustbins bolted at the sight of them and Kara sidestepped a puddle and trash before opening the screeching back door of the bar and leading them into the dim interior. Music pounded through the place and the crack of pool balls scattering across a worn table cut through the sound.

     

                Kara steered her to a booth with cracked seats and made her way to the bar, greeting the surprised bartender and ordering two pints of beer and carrying them over to the table.

     

                “So … you come here often?” Lena asked.

     

                Kara wrinkled her nose as she took a sip of her beer and Lena frowned as she laughed. “That sounded like a bad pickup line.”

     

                “If I didn’t know better,” Kara said with a rueful smile, glancing around the place. “Yeah. Every week before. The rest still come on Fridays - they try and convince me to go but … well, I don’t have it in me for karaoke night anymore.”

     

                “What was your song?”

     

                “I Want It That Way.”

     

                Lena groaned and drank her beer, wincing at the sourness of it and gingerly setting her glass back down as she eyed it. “I shouldn’t be surprised.”

     

                “You really shouldn’t,” Kara agreed with a small smile. “What’s yours?”

     

                “Mine? Oh. No. I don't do karaoke.”

     

                “Come on, you must’ve.”

     

                Giving her a thin smile, Lena shook her head. “You and I have definitely existed in different social circles.”

     

                “Be honest; is this the seediest place you’ve ever been to?”

     

                “Without a doubt. Even the college bars I went to were better.”

     

                Kara let out a quick laugh and drank some more of her beer before bracing her hands on the sticky table with almost immediate regret. “You need a shot. That’ll help you forget.”

     

                Lena winced and looked down. “Just what I need.”

     

                Kara ordered two tequila shots and Al poured them swiftly - not in shot glasses but small tumblers, overfilling them as he kindly tried to dull her grief. Carrying them back to the booth, Kara set one down in front of Lena and swilled her own around before raising the glass and smiling wryly.

     

                “Cheers.”

     

                They clinked glasses and knocked their drinks back. Lena winced and coughed as she set hers back down. 

     

                “That is not tequila.”

     

                “It’s cheap tequila. Sorry. I’m too broke for the nicer places.”

     

                Lena’s lips twitched with faint amusement and she took another sip of beer, her expression a dead giveaway of her thoughts on the alcohol. Still, she ordered the next round and two more tequilas, reclaiming her seat and knocking back the glass. 

     

                They reached a lull in the conversation and after another round of bad tequila, Lena let out a heavy sigh, resigned and grim. Reaching for one of the shelled peanuts in the small bowl on the table, Lena cracked it and slowly peeled the nut, the moment weighted with the anticipation of what was bothering her. Leaning against the back of the booth, Kara watched her and took periodic sips of her beer.

     

                “Today’s my anniversary,” Lena eventually whispered, a glassy look in her eyes from the drink that still didn’t quite mask the pain.

     

                She didn’t cry though, her voice level and quiet and her face stiff as she methodically cracked peanuts that she didn’t eat. Kara’s eyes stung just by hearing her admission of why today was so bad, but Lena didn’t. Her eyes were dry and distant and she blinked slowly as she looked up, meeting her eyes.

     

                Kara took a moment to reply, her voice rasping around the lump in her throat. “How many years?”

     

                “Six.”

     

                “I’m sorry.”

     

                Giving her a wan smile, Lena gave her a pleading look. “Please don’t say that. You of all people must know how … frustrating it is to hear people apologise for … nothing . It wasn't anyone’s fault. No one failed her, no one made it … happen. It just … it is the way it is.”

     

                Wrinkling her nose, Kara made a vague sound of agreement. “Yeah, you’re right. Really what they mean is ‘I’m uncomfortable and I don’t know how to make you feel better’ but … if I wanted to feel better, I wouldn’t be going to a complete stranger for it, would I?”

     

                Lena gave her a wry smile and softly elbowed Kara. “I might.”

     

                “Yeah, you would.”

     

                A hoarse laugh escaped Lena and she scattered bits of shell on the table, wiping her hands on the thighs of her pants as she leaned back. Kara opened and closed her mouth, watching her closely, her chest aching.

     

                “You’re allowed to cry, you know.”

     

                Grimacing, Lena picked her glass up and then sighed softly. “I did that this morning. After I got back from- from visiting her. I’ve never been … the most expressive person.”

     

                “Oh. Well … that’s okay too.”

     

                “Is it? I’ve always thought I was rather emotionally stunted. I’ve never really been that good with other people.”

     

                Kara narrowed her eyes, leaning in as she gave her a scrutinising look before she smiled and pulled back, pointing at Lena. “You should get a dog.”

     

                “I already have a dog.”

     

                Eyebrows rising, Kara cocked her head to the side. “Really?”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “You don’t strike me as a dog person. A cat, maybe. I like cats.”

     

                “Why should I get a dog if I don’t strike you as a dog person?”

     

                Shaking her head, Kara sipped her drink and set it back down a little heavy-handed. “That doesn’t matter; what dog do you have?”

     

                “A King Charles Cavalier. His name is Aristotle.”

     

                Kara let out a loud laugh. “That doesn’t surprise me.”

     

                Arching an eyebrow, Lena gave her a bemused smile. “What does that mean?”

     

                “You have to be rich, pretentious or educated to name your dog Aristotle.”

     

                Choking on a laugh, Lena gave her an expectant look. “And which one am I?”

     

                “Rich and educated. I don’t know you well enough to comment on your pretentiousness.”

     

                “But apparently well enough to know my financial status and my college grades.”

     

                “You own your own architecture firm and you have a nice car; an easy deduction to make.”

     

                Deliberating for a moment, Lena conceded to her point and knocked back her tequila. It was awful. Cheap and hard to get down as her face pinched with disgust, setting the shot glass back down and gesturing for the bartender to fetch them two more, while she nursed her sickly beer.

     

                “This really is awful,” Lena commented, gingerly turning the pint as she eyed the amber beer, the foam head reduced to a thin scum on top of it.

     

                Heaving a sigh, Kara dipped her chin in agreement. “Yeah.”

     

                They clinked their shots once they arrived and Kara hissed slightly as it burned, her stomach warm and a pleasant numbness radiating through her as her senses dulled. Picking up her sweating glass of beer, Lena drained the rest of it and made a disgusted face, setting it back down heavy-handedly before sucking her cheeks in as her brow furrowed. It was a thoughtful look and she turned on the cracked stool to give Kara a long, searching stare before she spoke.

     

                “Do you want to meet my dog?”

     

                “What, now?” Kara asked, blinking owlishly on the sidewalk, her vision swimming slightly as her stomach knotted, pleasantly warm and drunk.

     

                “We can have some wine - good wine. I just- I don’t want to go to bed yet. Not until it’s tomorrow.”

     

                “Okay.”

     

                They decided on dinner before catching a cab to Lena’s, queuing in Big Belly Burger and carrying the greasy bag outside to hail a ride. Kara held the bag and angled it for Lena to steal fries as they went across town, reminding Kara about her previous thoughts about why Lena would ever bother with a grief group at a shitty community centre. She almost asked but didn’t, just watched the other woman eat without enjoyment from the other side of the cab.

     

                Lena lived in a penthouse on the east side, the foyer marble and holding the grandeur of early decades as they rode the elevator upstairs. The building was a century old and everything was antiquated in a luxurious way - chandeliers in the foyer, velvet lounges and frescoes and uniformed doormen and security guards. She let them into the sprawling apartment and flicked a light switch.

     

                The apartment was almost as Kara had imagined it, but a little more dated. It could have been Parisian with its crown moulding and herringbone wooden floors, but the furniture was sleek and modern - tan leather armchairs and glass and brass fixtures with splashes of deep greens and navies and minimalist paintings. It was all expensive, of course, and had been extensively renovated and redesigned, undoubtedly by Lena’s own staff.

     

                A small dog greeted them, ears flopping and tail wagging as Kara knelt to give him a scratch beneath the chin. He was calm and sweet and Kara smiled as she looked up at Lena.

     

                “He’s so sweet. How old?”

     

                “Seven.”

     

                Told to make herself at home, Kara shed her jacket and dropped her backpack at the foot of a cream sofa. She kicked off her shoes and eyed her stained scrubs - a kitten had peed all over her and she was sure she still smelled faintly of dog vomit as well - and grimaced as she stood, looking around with interest. Of course, she’d known Lena was rich to some extent but the apartment was too big and understatedly luxurious for it to be anything other than disgustingly expensive.

     

                She could hear Lena in the adjacent kitchen, and probably could have seen her if she peeked through the open archway leading deeper into the open space, and Kara waited for her to return. It was a moment later, carrying two glasses of wine and standing inches shorter without her heels on. Her coat had been shed as well and there was something more wearied and vulnerable about her in her own home. Perhaps it was just the fact that she fitted in there, rich and immaculate and coldly beautiful.

     

                “I moved back in,” Kara blurted out, standing before the sleek fireplace, the dim glow warm as it kept the darkness of the open apartment at bay. “To my apartment.”

     

                “Oh,” Lena said with mild surprise, carrying over two glasses of wine and palming one off to Kara. “How is it?”

     

                She collapsed onto a cream sofa, careless about spilling red wine over the expensive fabric - she didn’t - and looked at Kara with genuine interest, as if she didn’t know the answer to it herself, after living in the house she’d shared with her wife.

     

                Kara swallowed thickly as she walked over to the sofa and sat at the opposite end, one leg tucked beneath her. “I’ve never lived alone before.”

     

                “Never?”

     

                Shaking her head, Kara gave her a thin smile. “I went from living at home to living with a new family to college, to him , to my sister’s place. It’s … too quiet.”

     

                “You should consider a dog.”

     

                “Mm,” Kara distractedly hummed before fixing Lena with a tentative look of curiosity. “Don’t you hate the quiet here?”

     

                Giving her a wry smile, Lena blinked slowly. “I do, but Andrea and I … we’ve always been busy with our own businesses. It wasn’t uncommon for one of us to get home past midnight, for us to be gone at six in the morning. If I was home, she was probably out; if I was out, she was home. I think most people would’ve found a relationship like ours unsatisfying, but … it worked for us. We loved our jobs and we worked around them. Weekends in Joshua Tree or Napa. We’d go to Argentina every year to visit her father, Vermont for skiing. Otherwise, we mostly … missed each other.”

     

                Looking down at her wine glass, Kara was silent for a moment before confessing. “Mike was needy. I mean, he spent time with his friends and I did with mine, but they kind of became our friends and he wanted us to do everything together. Sometimes it felt like we were living on top of each other, it was so suffocating. And now … I miss him. I miss being angry at him.”

     

                Lena let out a soft laugh, “yeah. I never imagined I’d miss that, but I do too. At the time, I would’ve given anything for her to change the way she was, to- to stop leaving her shit everywhere. God, I’ve always hated mess and she just- she used to leave her shit everywhere and never remember where she left it. It drove me insane but now … I wish she’d ask me where her keys were.”

     

                “I used to think about leaving him,” Kara quietly admitted, taking a sip of wine as her cheeks flushed. Lena arched an eyebrow and her embarrassment deepened. “I know, you must think it’s awful to say, but I did. Sometimes I’d just wonder what I was doing with my life, wasting my time with someone so … average. But he was good and dependable and … I guess I actually had a life then, so … sorry, I don’t mean to dump all of my problems on you.”

     

                She gave Lena an apologetic smile and cringed at how loose her lips had become after a few drinks, a part of her aching to get everything off her chest. It was freeing in a way to have someone who was a stranger to Kara’s life before Mike had died, who wasn’t connected to him in any way and didn’t have any preconceived ideas about who she was or how she should feel.

     

                “Don’t apologise. Everyone’s got shit; it’s actually a relief to think about someone else’s for a change. Mine is … a bit unbearable these days. I feel empty without her. We got lucky; we both loved each other the same.”

     

                “I loved him too,” Kara said as if needing to explain herself, to defend her marriage.

     

                “I know,” Lena said with a small smile.

     

                Swallowing, Kara tapped a finger against the side of her wine glass, feeling overcome with a sudden heaviness in her chest. “It’s just hard to love someone who’s gone. Losing him took so much away from me. It’s like he took a piece of me with him and now I just- I feel so empty and broken. I feel like a- like a …”

                

                “A hole where nothing grows,” Lena rasped.

     

                Kara looked up, sadness filling her blue eyes as her face went slack with relief. It was the relief of being understood and she nodded as she ran a hand over her tired face.

     

                “Every day I try and fill that hole in a little bit more but … today it feels unbearably fucking deep. But … I don’t actually hate being sad because it’s the only feeling I can still feel, so I’m good with it,” Lena said, her voice brittle. 

     

                “The worst feeling for me is when I get so sad, I can’t even cry anymore,” Kara mumbled, rubbing at her tired eyes. “I just feel … tired.”

     

                “That’s the thing they don’t tell you about grief,” Lena agreed, her voice hitching slightly. “Every morning we wake up and have to face the same loss that left us so tired the night before. And it never. Fucking. Ends .”

    Chapter 5

                They started going out together more, Kara’s social life burgeoning to nights filled with drinks at dive bars, the occasional nicer joint, and the sofa at either her place or Lena’s. It was comforting to have someone else who understood without any loyalty to the other people in Kara’s life - she couldn’t tell her friends anything without it spreading like fire through the group - and they latched onto each other like two people lost at sea, struggling to stay afloat.

     

                Her initial assumption that Lena masked her grief well was swept away as they got to know each other better. There were telltale signs, the cracks in her facade that Kara learned to identify. Lena’s eyes were windows to the pain inside, bright with hurt while the rest of her was carved from marble. But even then, there was the tremor in her hands that only a drink could stifle, the slight downturn to her mouth as her sadness prevailed against lighter feelings.

     

                They wore their grief the same way, both of them feeling so unmotivated, that tight, heavy feeling in their chests that was almost like emptiness but couldn’t be described as that with the pit of grief waiting to swallow them up. Kara didn’t know Lena all that well but there was this awful thing connecting them that in a few short weeks it felt as if she was the only person who could understand what she was going through. Even the dozen people who gathered at grief group every week felt outside of it all, unable to touch on the loss of these two young widows who’d lost their chance at love so early on.

     

                On Thursday evening, Kara met Lena outside her work, the sleek building with a floor dedicated to her architecture firm near the top glowing amber in the dark as she craned her neck up to study it, and she felt restless with the need for a drink. Lena emerged a short while later to drive them to grief group, and Kara greeted her with a small smile as they fell into step beside each other on the sidewalk. Before them, the streetlights cast a warm glow over the concrete, glinting off cards as they walked towards Lena’s. 

     

                Sliding into the passenger seat, Kara sank into the leather and closed her eyes as she let the motion of the car jostle her, both of them quiet as the radio played. They parked at the Y and walked inside together, Lena making the tea while Kara plucked two glazed donuts from the box before they sat side by side on the plastic chairs. 

     

                Kara found that she no longer resented the monotony of attending the sessions, her initial contempt for the farce of therapy, used as a shield to pretend like she was making an effort to help herself, fading into an anticipated block of time where she could sit and not feel so alone with the person next to her. To say that Lena wasn’t the cause of her sudden willingness to attend each week and pretend it was working would have been a lie.

     

                “It just has a habit of washing over me in waves,” Kara rasped once it was her turn, leaning forward with her elbows on her knees as she cupped her tea between her hands, feeling the fading warmth. “I get back up and it just- it hits me. All over again. I guess I’m just wondering when it’s supposed to get better, because … I feel like I’ve hit a wall and I can’t get around it.”

     

                “Grief isn’t a straight road,” Thomas said, his placid tone almost preaching as he nodded, making eye contact with everyone in attendance. "Sometimes walls are there so we can lean on them and rest."

     

                “I don’t need to rest,” Kara murmured, her brow puckering. “I need to stop … feeling this way.”

     

                “Grief is something you grow around, not get around. There’s no removing the wall, no making it smaller. Over time, you’ll become bigger than how you feel right now, but you’ll take it with you. Think of it as … the way the ocean drags garbage into itself, makes it part of itself. But that’s not the whole of it, is it? It’s still the ocean. The grief is just a part of who you are, not the sum of who you are.”

     

                Lena shifted on her seat, leaning back with her elbow propped up on the back of the chair, heeled foot dangling as she crossed her legs. She cleared her throat softly and her face was unreadable as her eyes pierced their counsellor, her voice soft as she spoke, not unkindly but with a pointed curiosity.

     

                “What good are you to us, then?” she asked, cocking her head to the side. “If you’re not going to help us get better, then why are we here?”

     

                Thomas smiled softly, cupping his chin in his hand. “That’s a good question, Lena,” he started, “thank you for opening up the circle. Kara, if it’s alright with you, I’d just like to touch on this …”

     

                He trailed off, raising his eyebrows slightly, and Kara gestured for him to go ahead, grateful to retreat back into herself and let the attention shift elsewhere. Clearing his throat, he straightened up in his seat and looked at each of them in turn.

     

                “As I mentioned the ocean, I’ll use a similar example; I’m here to teach you all how to swim. Your grief is a thing that is weighing you down, making it hard to wade through life, perhaps even drowning you. The purpose of coming together, of talking about our shared experiences, is to find a platform for us to swim to, to take a pause and catch our breath before the tide pulls us under.”

     

                A gentle nudge drew Kara’s attention away from what he was saying as she glanced sideways at Lena, whose red lips were twitching at the corners. Arching an eyebrow in a sardonic manner, Lena half-rolled her eyes and Kara felt her face spasm with a ripple of surprised amusement. Pressing her mouth into a flat line, she shifted on her seat and took a sip of tea, avoiding looking at Lena as the urge to laugh built in her chest.

     

                Afterwards, sitting in Lena’s car, Kara let out a snort of laughter as Lena chuckled, shaking her head as she started the engine. “What a load of shit,” Lena scoffed. “Walls are there so we can lean on them and rest? What is that?”

     

                “Honestly, what are we doing?” Kara laughed, rubbing her forehead. “That’s an hour of my life I’ll never get back.”

     

                “Should we stop going?” Lena asked, her voice low and furtive as if they were discussing treason.

     

                Raising her eyebrows, Kara smiled wanly. “I don’t know, should we?”

     

                Leaning forward as she craned her neck to check for traffic, Lena eased them out and wrinkled her nose, shrugging. “I don’t know. I feel like it adds no benefit to my life, but … it doesn’t add any negatives either. Gives me a reason to not spend all my time at work.”

     

                “Am I not a benefit?” Kara lightly teased her.

     

                Fixing her with a piercing look that struck right down to Kara’s core, Lena hummed, her gaze appraising. “You’re a side effect to the cause. I feel like you’d still drink and take Aristotle for a walk with me even if I stopped going.”

     

                “You sound confident.”

     

                “No, I just- it seems like … you need the company as much as I do. I mean, I know you have friends , and a family, but … it’s not the same, is it? They’re all …”

     

                “Normal?” Kara supplied.

     

                Giving her an easy smile, masking the pain, Lena made a left. “Something like that. Where are we going tonight? Bar? Apartment? Club?”

     

                “Club?” Kara choked on a laugh.

     

                “Being a thirty-three-year-old widow out clubbing with the youths is the only thing sadder than being a plain old widow,” Lena said with a crooked grin.

     

                Shaking her head, Kara fought back a smile, leaning back against the headrest. “I feel … a little off today,” she murmured. “Tired of it all, you know?”

     

                “You want to call it a night?”

     

                “No. I could use a drink. Let’s go to yours; your alcohol is better.”

     

                Lena’s sharp laugh filled the interior of the car and she raised her eyebrows. “Using me for my expensive taste, huh?”

     

                “And your dog. I should get my own, really, but yours will do.”

     

                “He’ll be pleased to hear it.”

     

                Basking in the ease of their banter, Kara settled in for the drive back to Lena’s place, the conversation between them somewhat bitter and wry as they spoke of their grief in vague terms and laughed at the ridiculous things that had come up in the grief group over the last few months. It felt like she’d been going for an eternity, had known Lena for a long while, but Mike had only been dead for eight months.

     

                Inside Lena’s home, Kara settled on the sofa with Aristotle as the dog licked her chin and sniffed at her work scrubs, picking up the scent of other dogs, as well as the cats and rabbits, birds and sugar gliders and tortoises she’d cared for that day. Lena moved around in the kitchen as Kara cooed over the dog, waiting for her to return.

     

                “Wine or something stronger?” Lena’s voice drifted back to her.

     

                “Um … stronger.”

     

                “Okay.”

     

                When she returned, it was with a bottle of top-shelf vodka and two tumblers, setting them down on the coffee table with a smattering of takeout pamphlets. Waving a hand to them, Lena turned her attention to the vodka and uncapped the bottle, sloshing a very generous amount into each glass.

     

                “You pick dinner.”

     

                “Thanks,” Kara murmured as she accepted the full glass, shifting precariously on the sofa as she tried not to disturb the dog or spill the liquor. 

     

                She rifled through the scattered pamphlets and picked up one for a nearby Chinese place, eyes scanning over the menu as Lena settled down. “Long day?”

     

                Glancing up to watch as her friend - were they friends? - took a sip of vodka, her expression remaining cool and aloof as if she was drinking water, Kara blinked and frowned slightly. “Um … no, not really. Just a lot of vaccinations and worming and x-rays. A lot of being pissed on too - sorry for the smell.”

     

                Lena snorted, setting her glass down. “Yeah, that warrants something stronger.”

     

                “If I needed a stiff drink each time that happened, I’d be a permanent drunk,” Kara distractedly murmured before tossing the pamphlet back onto the coffee table and raising her eyebrows. “Big Belly Burger?”

     

                “Sure. I’ll order delivery. Same as last time?”

     

                “It’s my turn to get it.”

     

                “Don’t be silly; it’s my treat.”

     

                “You supplied the alcohol.”

     

                “And I’ll supply the tears too if you give me a few drinks. Consider it an apology in advance,” Lena said with a thin smile.

     

                They bickered back and forth while Lena was on her phone, until she’d already placed the order on UberEats and flashed the screen at Kara. Sitting back and folding her arms over her chest, lips pursed, Kara narrowed her eyes.

     

                “You didn’t ask if I wanted-”

     

                “An extra pickle on the side. Yes, I ordered you one.”

     

                Surprise flashed through Kara and she let out a shaky laugh, the idea of being known by Lena so strange. They’d only really started spending more time together over the last couple of months, their weekly drive home and one night of drinks at Lena’s place turning into regular Thursday night drinks, and then the occasional Saturday, or Tuesday or Wednesday, walking Aristotle on the weekend and meeting to sit in a park or a salad bar on their lunch breaks.

     

                It seemed strange that they spent so much time together, seeking solace in each other’s company where other people wouldn’t do. Alex was sceptical about the whole thing, asking Kara to bring Lena to drinks at Al’s so they could meet her new friend, trying to integrate Kara back into the friend group by inviting Lena along too. So far, Kara had objected, feeling too raw to spend more time with her friends than she had to, their laughter and jokes seeming too loud, too much for her when they all got together, the gap where he’d been seeming glaringly obvious. Lena couldn’t fill it.

     

                Taking a large sip of vodka, Kara choked and then managed another one, her face screwing up with disgust as it burned. By the time she was on the second glass, halfway through her cheeseburger and feeling more vulnerable, the vodka wasn’t so bad.

     

                “She was my life,” Lena said, sounding confused and surprised at how she’d wound up here without her.

     

                Kara didn’t have a response to that, no comforting words that wouldn’t have sounded hollow or overused. She knew how it felt though, to build everything around someone else and then have them leave in the worst possible way, irrevocably changing everything . It wasn’t even that Mike had been such a monopolising force in Kara’s life, that he’d taken up all of her time and energy, only that he was there in every part of her life and it was painful to see the losses everywhere.

     

                “No one ever talks about her,” Lena whispered, her sadness so gut-wrenching that it stole Kara’s breath away. “My mom never even acknowledged her as my wife, so when she- it was like I didn’t even lose anyone. My grief seemed fictional. I had no one to cry with. My mom … she didn’t care; I lost her that day and I had no one. ”

     

                Thinking back to the hospital, Mike’s face bloody and broken, looking down at his hands, scratched and bloody from where he’d scraped against rocks - the hands that had made scrambled eggs for her on Sundays, had held her close and slipped a ring onto her left hand. She’d been there with Alex and Kelly, their friends in the waiting room, Eliza flying in from Midvale. Kara had been surrounded by people who’d loved them both, and for the first time, she felt that perhaps she’d been a little ungrateful towards the support that had enveloped her and held her aloft in those first couple of months.

     

                “Do you ever wonder when it’ll be okay again?” Lena asked after a moment.

     

                “They say the first year is the hardest,” Kara rasped, a hollow look in her eyes. “The first birthday. The first time I was sick and- and he wasn’t there to look after me. The first time I caught myself having fun. Knowing my sister wants to get married but feels so guilty about it, knowing that I don’t have someone to spend my life with anymore. The first time I visited his grave and saw the writing on it and it all felt real. I haven’t been back there since. Right now I’m just waiting for the day where those painful firsts are replaced with … better feelings and memories, but … I’ve still got four months to go.”

     

                Lena looked like she was about to cry and her shaky breath got caught in her throat, forcing her to swallow thickly. “Do you blame him?”

     

                Letting out a strained laugh, Kara sniffed and took a bite of her cheeseburger. “I shouldn’t. I know it was an accident - at least they think so - but … I do. I would forgive him for a- a whole list of things, just not dying.”

     

                Swallowing another mouthful of vodka, Kara forced down a few fries and then chased them down with another sip. “And everyone keeps telling me it’s not the end of the world, as if that’s supposed to make me feel better, but that’s only because it’s not them.”

     

                With a pained smile, Lena hummed, the sound rasping at the back of her throat as alcohol and pent-up emotions made her gravelly. “Everyone keeps asking me how I’m doing so well and going on about how strong I am,” she scoffed. “I feel like I’m suffocating and they think I’m … fine because I’m not bawling my eyes out every minute I’m awake.”

     

                “What was she like?”

     

                “Do you want to see a photo?” Lena asked.

     

                Nodding, Kara finished off her burger and crumpled the greaseproof paper in her fist before picking up her drink and cradling it in her lap as Lena took a seat beside her. Opening up a photo on her phone, Lena held it out for Kara to see. They were both dressed in ivory, Lena in a linen suit and Andrea in a fitted satin dress, holding flowers. It was a wedding photo and they were both smiling widely, only a few years younger but filled with so much light that it was easy to see the way it had been driven out of Lena now.

     

                “She was beautiful,” Kara murmured, taking in the dark hair, pale blue eyes, the pretty lines of her face. 

     

                “Mm,” Lena hummed, the sound frayed. “She was kind too, in a hard sort of way. Would always call you out on your bullshit and, God was she argumentative. Neither of us liked being wrong. But she was a good person, would do anything for someone she cared about, and felt things so deeply sometimes that it felt like I couldn’t reach her when she’d go to those places. I think … I’ve always been a bit … repressed about that sort of thing. Growing up … things were just swept aside, but with her , she felt everything.”

     

                “She sounds lovely.”

     

                “She would have loved you,” Lena whispered so softly that Kara wondered if she was supposed to hear her.

     

                Raising her glass to her lips, she drank the vodka and it hit her stomach like a match, heat blossoming inside her as it burned away her grief. Lowering the glass again, she looked into it and was surprised to find it empty again. 

     

                Lena lifted the bottle of vodka, her hand shaking with the effort of holding it aloft, and refilled Kara’s glass for her, blinking owlishly in the dim light of her empty home. Taking another sip, the burn of it almost pleasant as it traced down her throat, numbing her as it took the edge off her grief and made her emotions more volatile. 

     

                “What were you like as a kid?” Kara asked, narrowing her eyes a fraction as she jerked her chin to Lena.

     

                “What was I like? Pretty similar to the person I am now; unhappy around other people, cold, a little unloved.”

     

                “You’re not cold.”

     

                Leaning her head back against the sofa, Lena raised her eyebrows. “You think so?”

     

                “I can only speak from what I know, but yeah, I think so. You just seem like a realist to me, and that makes me feel a little less crazy.”

     

                Lena gave her a crooked smile and it made Kara’s chest ache, wondering how lonely she must be to think this statement from someone who’d only known her a few months was something to smile about, in the midst of so much heartbreak. Returning it with a pang of sadness cutting through her, Kara drained her glass again and let Lena refill it.

     

                Somewhere along the way, they’d lost track of how much vodka they’d drank, finishing off the bottle as they blasted a Backstreet Boys album from hidden speakers, and it was past midnight when Kara fell asleep on the sofa. The half-empty bottle of beer she’d been nursing in the crook of her elbow had shifted in the night and a wet stain seeped into her scrubs, the sour taste in the air, and she was oblivious to Lena stumbling off, vomiting in the ensuite toilet and returning with a blanket to drape over Kara.

     

                Waking early to sharp sunlight suffusing the apartment, Kara shielded her dry eyes as she hissed. She felt too hot, her oily skin clammy and cheeks flushed from too much to drink. A nasty hangover rocked her, her teeth furry as she ran her tongue over them, tasting the acidic remains of vodka and beer. 

     

                Shoving the blanket off herself, she staggered to her feet, the beer bottle clanging loudly to the ground as the dregs swilled around inside, and cursed as she stooped down to right it. Folding the blanket over the back of the sofa, Kara shuffled through the apartment and found Lena sitting at the sleek kitchen table, a wide window offering a park view as morning light filtered in, pooling butter yellow on the table as Lena rotated a coffee cup in her hands.

     

                “Morning,” she hoarsely greeted Kara, looking up, the sunlight bleaching her of any colour.

     

                “Um … I’m going to go,” Kara croaked, blinking as she tried to manage her unruly hair, feeling dishevelled and deflated, a shameful resemblance of an adult with none of the composure.

     

                “Coffee first?” Lena offered.

     

                Holding a hand up in rejection, Kara looked queasy at the thought. “No, thanks. I, uh, I think I need to go home and sleep it off.”

     

                Nodding, her face impassive, Lena rolled her coffee cup between her palms and hesitated, her eyes canvassing the room as Kara blinked and leaned down to pat the dog rubbing up against her legs. “Right. Um, I’ll see you later then.”

     

                Giving her a grey smile as her stomach twisted nauseously, Kara nodded. “See you later. Have a good day.”

     

                Snorting as her expression softened with amusement, Lena raised her eyebrows as she smiled ruefully. “Yeah, I’ll try.”

     

                Gathering her things, Kara made her way outside and flagged down a cab, sprawling limply in the back of it as she asked the driver to turn the AC on high. The cold rush of air was mercifully sweet but the lurching motion of the car forced her to ask the driver to pull over five blocks before her home, yanking the door open to vomit in the gutter. He cursed her and complained before kicking her out, Kara tossing a few bills into the back before slamming the door shut and stepping into her own vomit, feeling at a new low.

     

                Walking the remainder of the way home, stopping at a 7-Eleven for Gatorade, Kara let herself into her apartment and collapsed onto the sofa, letting her bag clatter to the floor as she twisted off the bottle cap and took a swig. It was sweet and sickly but she forced it down as she sent James a text telling him she wouldn’t be in today. She left out the part where she was hungover.

     

                Finishing off the drink, she stripped out of yesterday’s scrubs, the smell of wet dog, cat piss and sour beer mingling in a rank odour, and walked through the apartment to the bathroom. Sitting on the tiled floor, the chill seeping into her, Kara ran the water cold and stayed sprawled there for twenty minutes as she cooled down, trying to get the roiling in her stomach to settle.

     

                Afterwards, she laid on her bed for an hour in her towel, her hair air drying into a tangled mess as her skin took on a greyish pallor. The thought of painkillers for the brutal headache ended up rousing her, and as she chased them down with water, her phone started to ring. It was Alex and she momentarily considered ignoring it but caved and answered.

     

                “Hello?”

     

                “Oh, jeez, you’re hungover, really?”

     

                “No,” Kara lied.

     

                “Bullshit. James said you’re not at work; I wanted to check in on you.”

     

                Kara swallowed and took another gulp of water. “I’m fine. I don’t need a babysitter; I’m thirty-three not three.”

     

                Alex’s short sigh came through and Kara’s stomach twisted with vague embarrassment as she set the cup down on the counter. “Let’s get breakfast,” Alex suggested, keeping her true thoughts to herself. “I’ll meet you at Noonan’s in an hour.”

     

                “I’m actually not feeling up to anything right now, so-”

     

                “Well, if you’re not hungover, what’s the issue?”

     

                Pausing, Kara grit her teeth and shook her head. “Alright, fine. See you there.”

     

                She heard her sister’s snort on the other end and hung up before making her way into the bedroom and fishing out anything clean, pausing as she contemplated laundry but eventually decided against it. If she felt like it tomorrow, she’d put a load on then, but she decidedly did not want to do laundry while hungover.

     

                Dressing and pulling on a coat, despite how warm she felt, Kara grabbed her bag and slung it over her shoulder before locking up and watching the bus pass her by. She waited for the next one, exhaust fumes assaulting her as the passing cars kicked up a breeze, and rode down to Noonan’s, where Alex was already sitting at a table with some horrible green juice set before her. She looked slightly flushed and had her gym bag with her, fresh from a workout.

     

                “Morning,” Kara greeted her, dropping down to her chair.

     

                “You look awful.”

     

                “Late night with a friend.”

     

                “Lena?” Alex guessed.

     

                Shrugging noncommittally, Kara pretended to browse the menu, as if she didn’t have favourites already, before ordering the waffles and a black coffee, which wasn’t her usual but was necessary as she hoped the strong bitterness of it would take the edge off.  They talked as they ate, about work, about Kelly, about whether Kara was going to go out for Nia’s birthday next weekend, if she’d watched the latest season of Killing Eve . It felt normal, as it always was between the two sisters, but there was that underlying unease of Alex’s helpless disapproval and Kara’s reluctance to open up.

     

                In the end, they paid the bill and decided to walk for a while, heading away from the city and out to the waterfront of the harbour, trees shading the path with little parks and overpasses wedged alongside frozen yogurt shops and Subway. The day had cooled and the wind off the water was a relief as Kara breathed shallowly, her eyes glancing over cyclists and families, people sprawled on the grass or kayaking in the shallows where the harbour gave way to a sliver of beach.

     

                She was listening to Alex complain about how she had to stop by the store on the way home, Kelly wanting chilli for dinner, as they walked along the waterfront, the brisk wind ruffling their hair as they buried their hands into their coat pockets. After a moment, Kara squinted at the murky waters of the harbour and her mouth flattened with hesitation.

     

                “Make the chilli.”

     

                “What?” Alex murmured, looking over at her.

     

                “I said you should make the chilli,” Kara said a bit louder, meeting her sister’s gaze. “It’ll take you five minutes to go to the store.”

     

                Gesturing exasperatedly with a hand, Alex grimaced, “but then I have to make the chilli and I’m on call tonight.”

     

                “So make the chilli.”

     

                Brown eyes giving her an appraising look, Alex’s face furrowed. “That’s a lot of aggression for chilli.”

     

                Pressing a hand to her forehead, Kara closed her eyes as they walked for a moment. Her hangover was eating away at her, the wind a soothing balm that wasn’t quite enough to cut through the stifling heat of her layers. Regretting how much she’d had to drink and feeling very prickly as her sister walked alongside her, still dressed from her morning workout, Kara’s mouth turned down at the corners.

     

                “It’s not about the chilli.”

     

                “What the fuck are you talking about?” Alex asked with a sigh.

     

                “Just- it’s one meal . Cook your fiancée dinner and stop whining about it.”

     

                “You don’t even like chilli!” Alex objected as she spluttered, appropriately chastened and bristling against the rebuke.

     

                “It’s not about the chilli!” Kara snapped, her ashen cheeks flushed now as her eyes burned bright. 

     

                They’d come to a stop on the wide path cutting along the harbour, people skating past or walking dogs, a few glances thrown their way as those without headphones on heard their raised voices and hurried past. Clenching her teeth, Kara swallowed thickly, the sour taste of alcohol still lingering at the back of her throat, even though she’d brushed her teeth twice once she’d gotten home.

     

                “It’s about going out of your way to do something for someone you love because at any moment they could be taken away from you with no warning. Make the fucking chilli.”

     

                “Not everything is about-” Alex cut off and clamped her mouth shut, a flush of anger on her face before she stiffened.

     

                A thin smile graced Kara’s lips and she cocked her head to the side, raising her eyebrows. “No, go on, say it. Not everything is about me? Or were you going to say about him?”

     

                With a cutting sigh, Alex pinched the bridge of her nose as she hung her head. “Him,” she admitted, her voice hard. “It’s like you’ve forgotten how to exist outside of him, outside of what happened. You used to be your own person but where is she? What is it? Is it- is it the guilt?”

     

                “Guilt?” Kara choked out, shock flashing across her face.

     

                “Come on, Kara. I remember all the times you cried over him, all the times you fought and the times you told me you’d considered leaving him. Look, I know you loved him, but he was never the best thing in your life. You can- you can start over - when you’re ready, you can start over.”

     

                “Yeah, well, that’s easy to say. The worst thing to happen to you is your fiancée left you and you replaced her with someone else. And Kelly is by far the better choice, so how hard can it really be for you to start over when you have the person you’re going to spend the rest of your life with, hm? You don’t have to … figure out how to exist in a world without her,” Kara replied, her words sharp and a little callous in her annoyance as she started walking off.

     

                Alex grabbed her arm and tugged her around, her mouth turning down at the corners as her eyebrows furrowed with a look of irritation. “This isn't a pissing contest.”

     

                “Well, if it was, I’d win anyway,” Kara petulantly replied.

     

                “Fuck you,” Alex snapped, “you don’t get to walk around acting as if you’re the only person in the world who’s ever lost someone. I get it and I wasn’t half as bratty as you’re acting, and I was a child at the time. Grow the fuck up, Kara. Get some proper help, sort your shit out and stop walking around all uptight about other people being happy and content with their lot just because you feel stuck.”

     

                “Don’t you think I know that things would feel a lot better if I could just loosen up? If I could get past this suffocating feeling? This is the only way I’ve been able to hold myself together so far, so don’t criticise me for doing what I can to not fall apart.”

     

                “I’m not criticising you,” Alex exclaimed, “I want to help you, but you just shut everyone out and go … drinking with your new friend. Who’s that helping, huh?”

     

                “Me,” Kara bitingly replied, pointing at her chest. “It helps me, and it helps her, and as far as I’m concerned, we’re the only ones that matter because we’re the only ones living through a nightmare.”

     

                Alex scoffed, a muscle twitching in her jaw. “And you’re doing a fantastic job of dragging everyone else into it as well.”

     

                Waving a hand dismissively at her, Kara started storming off, her queasiness growing as she strongly considered doubling over the edge of the sea wall and vomiting into the grey water. Behind her, Alex was rooted to the spot for a moment, regret already welling up as her anger cooled.

     

                “Kara, don’t-”

     

                “Enjoy your chilli,” she interrupted, her back to her sister as she walked off, already plucking her phone out of her pocket and texting Lena; How about that coffee?

    Chapter 6

                She didn’t speak to Alex for a week, and even then it was a biting phone call that lapsed into another week of silence when Kara hung up on her. It was just a relief that she was back in her own apartment, so she wouldn’t have had to deal with the uncomfortable living situation if she’d still been holed up in her sister’s spare room, but really it just made Kara feel more alone. If it wasn’t for Lena, she thought it might have consumed her.

     

                Instead, Kara wallowed in her frustration with her sister and tried not to miss her too much as she went to work and went to group and went for walks with Lena and Aristotle and all the motions of ordinary life. She was grocery shopping after work one night, pushing a cart as she grabbed anything that even remotely caught her attention - Cheetos, a jar of pickles, a can of almost fluorescent orange cheese - when her phone started ringing.

     

                “Hey,” she wearily greeted Alex, leaning her forearms on the cart as she hunched over.

     

                “Hey. How’re you?”

     

                “Good. You?”

     

                “Yeah. What’re you doing?”

     

                “Grocery shopping,” Kara sighed, straightening up and reaching for a container of instant noodles, settling on ramen for dinner. 

     

                She tossed it into the growing pile in the cart and continued down the cramped aisle, one wheel rattling, the linoleum checkerboard floor squeaking and the strip lights overhead flickering. Making a left at the end of the aisle, Kara stood before the selection of ice cream.

     

                “Are you coming to drinks on Friday?”

     

                “Maybe. I haven’t decided yet.”

     

                “Kara-”

     

                “I might have plans.”

     

                Kara was lying, or bluffing at the very least, as she jerked open a door and let out a cold gust from the freezer. She shivered in her coat and scrubs, reaching for a tub of Ben & Jerry’s cookie dough and adding it to the cart. The door slammed shut as Alex sighed.

     

                “Let me guess, with Lena?”

     

                “What about it?”

     

                “Look …” Alex started and then trailed off, sighing. “Why don’t you just invite her? We miss you so … just bring her as well. I’d like to meet her.”

     

                Snorting, Kara hesitated, her lips pressed together as she listened to the distant beep of items being scanned at the checkout. “Yeah, maybe.”

     

                “Will you at least come over for dinner tomorrow? I’m making fajitas.”

     

                Closing her eyes, she paused for a moment and then swallowed. Blinking rapidly as she opened her eyes, Kara’s shoulders wilted slightly and she started pushing the cart. “Sure.”

     

                “Six o’clock.”

     

                “Alright.”

     

                Six o’clock the following night, she was still on her way to Alex’s, a cheap bottle of wine grasped in her hand and an audiobook chattering in her ears as she wove through foot traffic and buskers. Work had been busy; a tooth removal on an old border collie, a hysterectomy on an excitable puppy, a day of microchipping all manner of pets as part of their 30% off deal for the next week. She hadn’t had time to change, the lingering smell of wet dog and antiseptic clinging to her clothes as her feet pounded the gum-splattered sidewalk.

     

                Arriving at her sister’s place, ten minutes later than intended, she rang the buzzer and Alex let her upstairs. The place smelled of simmering chicken and bell peppers and spices and they quickly moved past the awkwardness of things, talking about work and how was group and had Kara watched that new show on Netflix? She sipped her cheap wine and ended up drinking half of the bottle herself and rode the bus home later that night, her eyelids heavy and her body pleasantly numb.

     

                It was Thursday the next day and she woke up feeling flushed and groggy, her head pounding a little and the back of her t-shirt damp with sweat. She was late for work, her alarm blaring painfully loud in the stifling warmth of her bedroom, the heater stuttering out gusts of warm air that made her feel sick. Turning off her phone alarm and the heater, she staggered out of bed and took a cold shower, her skin pimpling from the cold as she shivered, her fingernails turning a pale shade of lavender.

     

                Dressing quickly and lacing up her running shoes, she grabbed her coat and her bag and her half-flat phone and just managed to catch the next bus passing her house. She didn’t have time to stop off for a coffee so she made one for herself in the small kitchen at the back of the clinic, stirring sugars into her mug as James and William arrived, the three of them discussing their schedules for the day and drinks the following night, asking whether Kara was going to go.

     

                She stayed back late, until it was time to go to group, and crossed the parking lot of the Y and ducked into the shabby gym. The echoing sounds of shouting from the courts and splashing in the pool greeted her as she passed through the lobby and over to the small meeting room. The chairs were already set up in a circle and she started the process of making two teas and collecting two donuts from the box.

     

                Taking her usual seat with her back to the door, she waited as the room slowly started to fill, seats claimed by regular faces and a couple of new ones. Lena’s donut waited for her on the seat and her tea by the chair legs, yet Lena was nowhere to be found. 

     

                Pulling her phone out, Kara sent her a quick text, her brow furrowed with mild concern and a little dismay. She chewed on her bottom lip as her fingers typed out another message, and then another, hoping the incessant buzzing wasn’t irritating Lena - wherever she was.

     

    [Kara]: hey, just checking to see if you’re coming tonight

     

    [Kara]: I’ve saved you a seat and a donut just in case

     

    [Kara]: psa: the donut might be missing a few bites if you don’t hurry up

     

                She tucked her phone into the pocket of her denim jacket and glanced down at the donut set safely down on a napkin on the chair beside her. A moment later Thomas brought the group into session and Kara glanced over her shoulder at the closed doors, disappointment settling in her stomach. 

     

                The hour passed in a dragging blur and afterwards, Kara couldn’t recall a thing. She didn’t even remember speaking, although she must have when it was her turn. One moment she was staring blankly at the circle of blurred faces and then she was dumping the wasted donut in the trash with the cold cup of tea. Wiping her hands on the thighs of her scrubs, she walked outside, the night black and uninviting as sirens wailed and traffic blared and the city beckoned like an unwelcoming malaise of neon lights. 

     

                Hitching her bag higher on her shoulder, she crossed the parking lot, her running shoes scuffing bits of gravel and broken glass from smashed beer bottles, making for the bus stop. Standing on the side of the road, she waited until the bus finally arrived at a hissing halt, the doors opening to admit her as she paid the fare and took a seat in an empty row near the back.

     

                Swaying side to side as they rode in relative silence, the darkness of the bus drawing her awareness away from herself, Kara almost missed her stop, the back door catching her arm and then hissing open as she thanked the driver and stepped outside. Letting herself into her apartment, she shed her scrubs and put on her pyjamas, fishing out leftovers from the fridge and turning the TV onto an old soap opera as she ate. Once she was done, she took some pills and went to bed.

     

                She was on the bus to work the next morning when her phone started ringing, disrupting the meditative podcast she was trying out. Glancing down at the screen in her lap, Kara saw Lena’s name and straightened. Quietly disturbing the man next to her, she climbed to her feet and shouldered her bag, ringing the bell for the next stop. 

     

                Pulling the earphone jack out of her phone, she balled the wires up in her hand and answered the call, stepping out into the early morning pedestrian traffic as she walked the rest of the way to work. “Hello?”

     

                “Hey. Sorry I didn’t text you back.”

     

                “That’s okay,” Kara lightly replied, “I was just … worried about you.”

     

                Lena let out a short laugh, “I’m alright. Just … a long day.”

     

                “Well, if you want to talk about it, you know I’m here.”

     

                “Are you offering to be my wall?” Lena teased her.

     

                Snorting, Kara’s mouth twitched slightly at the corners. “Maybe I am. If you needed one.”

     

                Lena was silent for a moment. “You got home alright?”

     

                “Me? Yeah, fine. I’ve been catching buses a long time, you know.”

     

                “I know, I just- I didn’t have time to text so … I hope you enjoyed my donut though.”

     

                “It softened the disappointment a little,” Kara joked. “Hey, I actually was going to ask you last night; my sister’s making me go out for drinks with some friends tonight. Did you want to come?”

     

                “Me? Oh, um-”

     

                “You don’t have to. Don’t feel pressured or anything. I just … sort of tried to use you to get out of it because I was still pissed at her, and then she said to invite you too, so …”

     

                Letting out a scoff of laughter, Lena trailed off in a soft hum, considering it. “What’s your plan if I say no?”

     

                “I don’t know,” Kara laughed, “convince you to do something else with me so I can get out of it.”

     

                “And what if I say no to that?”

     

                “I guess I’ll have to go.”

     

                “Do you want to go?”

     

                Humming, Kara shrugged to herself. “I probably should.”

     

                “Okay, I’ll meet you there at six. Just let me know where it is.”

     

                “It’s just Al’s.”

     

                “That dive we went to?”

     

                “Yeah.”

     

                “Alright. Six o’clock.”

     

                They said their goodbyes and hung up then and Kara smiled slightly to herself. Stopping off for coffee, she listened to her podcast as she walked the rest of the way, sipping the sickly sweet latte and following the breathing instructions as she followed along. Her mind was too busy for it though, wandering instead of focusing on the meditative mantras that were supposed to help. It was one of many self-help books she’d tried listening to over the last nine months, and none of them really helped but it was gratifying to think she was trying. That was a recent development, at least.

     

                Work passed by slowly and Kara zoned out while looking at x-rays, autonomously gave puppies and kittens their vaccinations without having to think about what she was doing, and updated charts with only a slither of her attention on the computer as her fingers flew across the keyboard. She only had one surgery that day, putting a little cast on a parrot’s half-bitten off talon when the x-rays showed the damage was too severe to stitch it back together and she’d had to remove it entirely. She was tired and distracted when she left work, changing in the small bathroom and shoving her clothes in her backpack before leaving with James and William.

     

                They got an Uber to Al’s and she tried to remain invested in the conversation as the car drove them across town. Stepping into the dive bar, which was mostly empty at that time of the evening, she insisted on getting the first round and ordered three beers, carrying them over to the table they’d snagged and taking a sip. Alex showed up next with Kelly, both of them having worked the night before and slept all morning, now looking refreshed and ready to drink. 

     

                Lena was next and Kara’s demeanour immediately brightened at the sight of her. She’d been half-convinced that she wasn’t going to show up, and she looked remarkably out of place in her tailored pants and silk shirt, her maroon woollen overcoat cutting a striking figure as she crossed the room. Kara slid from her stool to meet her and noticed how tired she looked though, a dim quality to her piercing green eyes.

     

                “You made it,” Kara softly greeted her.

     

                “Mm, didn’t want to deny you your platform to rest on,” Lena quipped.

     

                Kara let out a sudden laugh, a wry grin twisting her lips as she turned and gestured to the table. Alex was looking at her like she’d sprouted a second head, bewildered surprise quickly smoothing out into polite interest as her eyes drifted to Lena.

     

                “This is Alex. Alex, Lena.”

                

                She made the rest of the introductions and then suggested another round, catching sight of Nia and Querl slipping in and making a bee-line for the table. Accompanying Lena to the bar, Kara rattled off the list of everyone’s preferred drinks and bickered with Lena for a few minutes about who was paying, before Lena slapped down her credit card and Kara helped her carry them all back to the table. She introduced the latecomers and sat beside Lena, who was quiet but observant for a few minutes before answering a few questions flung at her.

     

                “What do you do?” Kelly politely asked.

     

                “I’m an architect.”

     

                “She’s being modest,” Kara snorted, raising her bottle to her lips and pausing, raising her eyebrows. “She owns her own firm.”

     

                Lena glanced sideways at her and arched an eyebrow in a questioning manner. Shrugging slightly, Kara smiled lopsidedly and leaned in, their heads ducked in together, a clash of blonde and dark brunette as she lowered her voice.

     

                “Don’t sell yourself short.”

     

                “I don’t,” Lena murmured, “it just sounds a bit cocky.”

                

                Kara let out a huff of laughter and shook her head, “that’s why I said it for you.”

     

                “Well, yeah, but now it just sounds like you’re bragging about having a new rich friend,” Lena dryly replied, grinning thinly as she raised her glass of wine.

     

                “You’re the only new thing to happen to me in months; let me brag a little about how well I’m adjusting to finding new things and moving on.”            

     

                “Oh, yeah, you’re just killing it at that.”

     

                “Mm, who knew I was so well-suited to being a widow,” Kara said, rolling her eyes.

     

                She let out a quiet laugh as she tipped her bottle back and caught Alex and James eyeing her with wary confusion. Swallowing, Kara set her drink down and leaned forward slightly, her brow furrowing.

     

                “What?”

     

                “Nothing,” Kelly quickly assured her, cutting in before her fiancee or brother could speak. “Um … so, you two met at grief group?”

     

                “Yeah.”

     

                “How’s it going?”

     

                Sharing a sidelong glance with Lena, they both snorted and made a few vague sounds of amusement before Kara grimaced. “Yeah, it’s great. We have so much fun.”

     

                “Alright,” Alex softly interjected with a flicker of annoyance in her eyes, “let’s get another round. Karaoke starts up soon and someone has a lot to make up for.”

     

                Allowing her sister to steer the conversation to a topic that was more comfortable for everyone else, Kara smiled faintly and rolled her eyes, leaning her forearms on the edge of the table and rolling the bottle of beer between her palms.

                

                “I’ve missed our duets,” James said, clapping a hand on Kara’s shoulder before he gathered up some of the empty bottles and prompted Kara to finish hers, taking it with him to the bar so he could place the next round.

     

                Wiping her damp palms on her thighs, Kara leaned into Lena, “do you karaoke?”

     

                “Uh, no, definitely not.”

     

                “Come on,” Kara goaded her, “I need my wall to lean on.”

     

                “I’m a wall for resting ,” Lena loftily replied before letting out a soft laugh, narrowing her eyes as she looked at Kara. “I can’t imagine you getting up there to sing.”

     

                “She’s really good,” Nia supplied.

     

                Straightening up, Lena turned to Nia with a look of mild surprise on her face. “Is she?”

     

                “You don’t need to sound that surprised,” Kara scoffed, pressing a hand to her heart.

     

                Alex returned from helping James with the drinks and set a bottle of beer in front of Kara and a glass of Moscato beside Lena’s half-finished one. Wrapping her arms around her sister’s shoulders, Alex hugged her and pressed their cheeks together.

     

                “I’m glad you came; I’ve missed you.”

     

                Reaching up, Kara gave her hand an affectionate pat, leaning back as she smiled slightly. “Yeah.”

     

                “I’m sorry too.”

     

                “It’s fine. Don’t even worry about it.”

     

                “I worry about you.”

     

                “Well don’t,” Kara said with a tense laugh, breaking Alex’s grasp on her and reaching for her beer. She twisted on her stool and clinked her bottle against Alex’s. “Cheers. Save me a song.”

     

                Lena eyed the exchange with open curiosity and gave Kara a small smile at the questioning look on her face when their eyes met. “I don’t have a sister. It’s interesting.”

     

                “You have a brother, right?”

     

                “Yeah. Nine years older than me. It’s different to this,” she said, gesturing to Kara and then Alex. “I don’t think I’d even consider going to a bar with him. It’s nice though; she clearly cares about you.”

     

                Giving her an exasperated look, Kara’s blue eyes shone with amusement. “That’s not always a good thing.”

     

                “Sure it is.”

     

                Wrinkling her nose, Kara hesitated as she deliberated for a moment and let some of her annoyance bleed out of her. “Yeah, you’re probably right. I don’t know where I’d be without her.”
