                Lena gave her arm a reassuring squeeze and they broke out of their little bubble as Winn arrived, late and already a little tipsy with his wife in tow. He’d been Kara’s friend first and then somehow became Mike’s, and now she rarely saw him. But then, she rarely saw anyone these days. Sure, she went to work now and saw more of James and William than she used to, and she still saw Alex and Kelly more regularly, but those were out of necessity, as a part of her ordinary routine of life. Now, Kara spent all of her time with Lena - or a good portion of it, where she chose to go and do something instead of lapsing back into her life of relative nothingness.

     

                They’d known each other roughly four months, yet Kara felt like it had been longer with everything that had changed. The shell of the person she’d been still existed some days, and on the weekends when there was nothing to occupy her free time, but she’d also filled some of the gaps with Lena. Their walks with Aristotle, their nights after grief group, their occasional dinners and breakfasts and coffee breaks. They added some much-needed spontaneity to Kara’s monotonous life, breaking her free from the rut she’d been in as she wrestled with her grief.

     

                It was still something she was struggling through but Kara was trying and she wished that the people she knew  who cared about her would appreciate that a little more. She was there, drinking her beer and promising to karaoke when that was one of the last things on her mind, but she was still there, and that had to count for something . 

     

                Taking another sip of her drink, she tried to tune in to the conversation and was conscious of Lena sitting beside her, their arms brushing occasionally, Kara turning to rope Lena into the conversation. For all her cool indifference, Lena was rather approachable, which Kara chalked up to her having to deal with investors and clients and all manner of people as the owner of her own firm. But she fancied that she knew her well enough to notice that her easy smiles didn’t reach her eyes, were too easily charming to put people at ease, that her slightly haughty manner of speaking wasn’t the soft, murmuring tone she’d come to associate with Lena. It was amusing and a little baffling.

     

                One by one, they got up on stage to sing, taking it in turns while Kara and Lena sat side by side and watched, their drinks going down easily as their edges blurred pleasantly, taking the sting out of the pit of grief for a moment. But then Kara was goaded into it, and she’d had a few drinks so she caved easily, joining Alex on the small stage and singing one of their usual songs. Kara didn’t have her usual enthusiasm for it, nine months past the last time she’d found herself up there, and she was relieved when the song ended and she’d fulfilled her promise to sing.

     

                It wasn’t even midnight when Lena tried to bow out quietly, murmuring to Kara over the noise of the music. Seizing her chance to leave as well, Kara quickly climbed off her stool and picked up her backpack, scanning the crowd for Alex as she told Lena to wait a moment. Spotting her sister at the bar with James, Kara wound her way over to them.

     

                “I’m going to head off,” Kara said as she placed a hand on Alex’s arm to get her attention.

     

                Her sister turned away from her conversation with James and nodded, pulling her into a hug and rubbing her back. “I’m glad you came tonight. They’ve all missed you.”

     

                “Yeah,” Kara sighed, hugging her back.

     

                Over her shoulder, Alex looked at Lena and a flicker of doubt filled her eyes as she turned her face into Kara’s, her voice stern as she spoke just loud enough for her to hear.

                

                “Be careful with her,” Alex warned her.

     

                Kara pulled back and frowned slightly, “what?”

     

                “She’s beautiful.”

     

                Understanding made Kara stiffen as she pulled the rest of the way free from her sister’s parting embrace. “Her wife’s dead.”

     

                Alex gave her a grim look of exasperation and cupped Kara’s cheek. “Plenty of people have ones that are alive and still make the wrong choice.”

     

                Scoffing, Kara shook her head, ignoring her, and kissed her cheek before pulling away. She fell into step beside Lena and they left through the front door, the cool night air caressing clammy cheeks as they looked around.

     

                “Feel like walking?” Lena asked.

     

                Nodding, Kara buried her hands in her pockets and felt disgruntlement thread through her at Alex’s warning. Was it so hard to believe that maybe they were helping each other through something incredibly difficult? It didn’t have to be anything more than that. They were both too deep in their grief and confused adjusting to life for it to mean anything more than that. And sure, Kara could agree with Alex that Lena was beautiful, but that was irrelevant.

     

                “Your friends are nice.”

     

                “Mm.”

     

                “And your sister …”

     

                Kara’s laugh was strained and she shook her head, smiling crookedly. “Ignore her. She’s just …”

     

                “Ah, so she doesn’t like me,” Lena surmised with amusement.

     

                Closing her eyes, Kara exhaled through her nose as her lips twitched. Glancing sideways at Lena, she shrugged slightly. “No, it’s not that. She, uh, she’s just … worried about me. We spend so much time together and-”

     

                “And what?” Lena pressed when she trailed off.

     

                Sighing, Kara gestured off-handedly and then shoved her hand back into her pocket, a slightly annoyed look on her face as she continued. “She thinks you’re beautiful.”

     

                “Oh. Well, that’s flattering, I guess. It could’ve been worse.”

     

                Pressing her mouth into a flat line, Kara fought back a laugh and raked a hand through her hair. “Are you hungry?”

     

                Shrugging half-heartedly, Lena arched an eyebrow as her lips twitched coyly. “Big Belly Burger?”

     

                “You read my mind.”

     

                They crossed the street at the next set of lights and followed the neon sign to the fast food joint, squinting at the backlit menus plastered on the wall above the counter. Kara already knew what she was going to get though; she got the same thing every time, and even though they’d only eaten it twice together, Lena remembered. She remembered and placed it for her and paid before Kara could even work her purse free from her backpack.

     

                She carried their tray over to a sticky table and set it down, letting Lena take the vinyl bench while she dragged a plastic chair in. Quickly doling out the food, Lena stabbed a straw into her drink and sighed heavily. 

     

                “You alright?” Kara quietly asked.

     

                Lena’s answering smile wavered as she kept her eyes downcast on her burger and fries. She had to work to clear her throat and reply. “Yeah,” she rasped. “Just … a busy few days.”

     

                “Mm, I missed you at group.”

                

                “Yeah?” Lena said with a huff of laughter, her face crumpling as she smiled at the absurdity of it. “Did I miss any enlightening information?”

     

                “I don’t know. I couldn’t concentrate. Not without my platform for support.”

     

                “Ah, well, I’ll save you from drowning next week.”

     

                Kara slowly unwrapped her burger and watched Lena closely, taking in the dark circles beneath her eyes, the glazed look, the weariness as her shoulders slumped and her facade cracked ever so slightly.

     

                “You sure you’re okay?”

     

                “Fine,” Lena murmured, taking a bite of her own burger and sighing. Her eyes flitted around the space and she frowned, her cheek dimpling with deep thought. “You know, I’ve never been in a place like this.”

                

                “No? I guess you probably eat at fancier places. Takeout is the backbone of my diet. Used to be diners but … well, I don’t go to them anymore.”

     

                Raising her eyebrows in a politely inquisitive look, Lena cocked her head to the side. “Is it to do with him?”

     

                “Yeah. We, uh, we met in college and he took a lot of later classes so, on our first date, we went out for breakfast at a diner. We were both seeing other people for a few weeks but then things got serious, but in a good way, you know? He was a very predictable person and I used to have a lot of time for myself because I knew when he was at the gym, when he was watching sports with the guys, and what nights he went out drinking. I had a lot of space for other things like pilates and spin class with Kelly and dinner with Alex and movies with Querl.”

     

                A v formed between Kara’s eyebrows as she set her drink down and wiped the water from the perspiring cup on the thighs of her jeans. There was a distant look in her eyes and she pressed her lips into a flat line, hesitating before she looked up.

     

                “Then he was gone and … I used to sleep a lot. I’d wake up and go to the bodega on the corner at the corner of Alex’s place and get two cups of coffee and go back to her spare room and watch Jeopardy while I waited for the Ambien to kick in and I’d fall asleep again. I didn’t really eat much because I slept so much; they got really worried about me, but … the truth is, towards the end he took up so much of my time that I was constantly doing things for him or together, and then I was left with so much time for myself . I didn’t know how to fill it.”

     

                “It’s weird, how much space a person can take up in your life,” Lena mused aloud, staring at the dirty grout of the tiled floor.

     

                “Do you feel like that too?” Kara hesitantly asked, a hopeful edge to her question, as if she needed to know she wasn’t alone.

     

                Lena pursed her lips slightly and shrugged. “Sometimes. I mean … I’m not really sure that I have so much time for myself, but, uh, I don’t really know how to be a person anymore. That’s what it feels like anyway. I don’t know. I guess the painful part was losing myself in the process of losing her. I loved her so much that I kind of … forgot how to be myself without her.”

     

                Kara cocked her head to the side, holding her greasy cheeseburger in her hands as she stared at her for a long moment, her gaze searching, appraising. Lena gave her a thin smile, arching an eyebrow.

     

                “What?”

     

                Shrugging, Kara looked down, swapping her burger for the fries and taking a few. “Nothing. Well, I’m just surprised. You don’t really … talk about your feelings. Or show them.”

     

                Lena let out a quick laugh, half-raising her Coke to her lips and hesitating. “You know, you have this view of me as this person who has this … secret emotional side. I’m not hiding it; I’m just not very emotional. I don’t talk about it because … there’s nothing to talk about.”

     

                Humming dubiously, Kara narrowed her eyes slightly. “I don’t think someone can be unemotional. That’s like saying you don’t have any thoughts. Or opinions. Everyone has them.”

     

                “You wear your heart on your sleeve,” Lena noted, “just because I don’t, it doesn’t mean I’m hiding something. Maybe my life just isn’t as … emotionally intense as yours.”

     

                “I don’t buy it. You just want other people to think you’re more resilient than you actually are. But you’re not really, are you?”

     

                Hesitating, looking annoyed, Lena took a slow sip, a stiffness to her jaw as a muscle twitched. “No, I’m resilient. I’ve bounced back from it, so I’m resilient, right? Everything died there for a while. I’ve never been a particularly warm person but everything in me was so cold. And now … I don’t know how to explain how I feel. She knew. She always knew. Without me even having to put it into words.”

     

                Kara looked at her and felt like she was seeing herself, the raw pain making Lena’s face taut, the way it crumpled ever so slightly whenever she talked, the bright look of grief in her eyes, trying to keep the rest at bay. There was the glazed look of too much to drink, of too much confusion and emptiness, like a little lost child trying to navigate through the world without the guidance of someone else. She was her sad reflection.

     

                “I haven't felt like myself in months,” Lena shrugged, twirling a fry between her fingers as her mouth turned down at the corners. “I've reached a point where I can't sleep, I can't focus, I don't want to eat. I'm just so … tired . I'm not depressed, I don’t think. Just exhausted. It feels like I'm alone and lost and I don't know how to fix it at this point. Maybe it's just something that will pass, eventually. I don’t know. I just … want to talk about what happened without it hurting . There has to be a way to talk about her without reopening the wounds, without all this pain. I thought … the grief group would help, but … it doesn’t. Everyone else’s losses … it’s different for me. I can’t explain it because … I don’t think anyone else would understand.”

     

                She let out a scoffing sound of contempt and dropped the fry back down onto the greaseproof paper, licking salt off her fingers and leaning back. Kara watched in silence, finishing off her fries and waiting as the silence hung heavily over them and their little booth in the harsh fluorescent-lit corner of the fast food joint.

     

                “You know, it’s very selfish but … I wanted to go first. I’m mad I didn’t go first. I always wanted to so that I didn’t have to feel heartbroken over it. It’s selfish, I know, but … she was supposed to miss me,” Lena heatedly continued, her cheeks flushed with anger, with the unfairness of it all.

     

                “I don’t think it’s selfish,” Kara murmured in reply. “I think that’s a very normal, human experience. But only to anyone that’s lost someone they love like that. We all go through it eventually, we all understand that in the end, we were just unfortunate to get to it a little … early.”

     

                “Do you think it would be easier if we’d had more time with them?”

     

                Kara cocked her head to the side and hummed as she considered the question. Letting out a weary sigh, she gave Lena a pained smile. “Honestly … I think it would’ve been easier for me because I don’t think- eventually, I think that he and I- if we’d gone out separate ways and decades later he’d gone … yeah, I think it would’ve been easier. But I don’t know if it’s easier or harder if you still love them and they go. Yeah, you got more time, but … that’s more time to love them, to miss them, right? When you’re young … I think everyone expects you to just move on.”

     

                “Yeah,” Lena heavily sighed. “I don’t know …”

     

                “Healing’s weird,” Kara blurted out, wrinkling her nose. “Some days I’m okay, I’m- I’m doing fine … other days it’s like it’s fresh. I think people don’t realise that there’s no definitive time frame to get over it, to get better. And … fuck , I’m trying to keep going, to move on, knowing that it’ll be okay one day, but … then I feel like shit because should I be okay that my husband is dead? Even if I know that it was already falling apart, don’t I owe it to him-”

     

                “You don’t owe people anything,” Lena murmured, her voice firm. “You should do things because you want to.”

     

                “I do want to get past this. It’s been … nine months, and I think I’m doing better, but … I don’t know. At what point is it morally okay to move on? One year per year you were together? How do people just move on after six months? Bring home someone new and act as if it was a breakup, and not that the person they loved died.”

     

                “I think it just depends on when you meet someone and it feels right,” Lena replied, her brow furrowed with deep thought.

     

                Kara’s cheek dimpled as she frowned and took a sip of her drink. Setting it down, she leaned back, her eyelids heavy and a bone-deep weariness filling her as she gave a rasping reply. “How do you know if it feels right?”

     

                “I don’t know,” Lena whispered, her eyes burning into Kara. “I don’t think I’ve felt it yet. Maybe I never will.”

    Chapter 7

                The first anniversary of Mike’s death came around quickly and Kara was struck by how different her life was, yet how little had changed at the same time. She no longer felt stuck in that rut of grief, although she still grieved in her own way, and there were the small steps she’d made to move on with her life, emptying their apartment of his things, moving back in, befriending Lena and slowly reintegrating herself back into her friend group. 

     

                A year later, she still felt like a shadow of the person she’d been before, but that wasn’t necessarily a bad thing; there had been a lot of things Kara hadn’t liked about her life with her husband and a year without him had proven to be a big adjustment. Sleeping alone, cooking for one, cleaning up after one, and making plans around her schedule. Not all of it was entirely bad, and yet with that thought came the guilt of feeling that way about losing him. Surely it was wrong of her to feel like she could breathe a little more these days, that she had less to keep track of and more time for herself. Perhaps part of grieving a spouse was learning how to be selfish again, to put herself first where she’d had to put their marriage first on so many occasions before. 

     

                The morning of the anniversary, she woke late to Alex knocking on her door. Her sister had brought coffee and breakfast burritos and a bouquet from her and Kelly, setting them in water as Kara ate the food. She felt pleasantly numb for the most part, the milestone of the date sitting heavily in her stomach but an almost emptiness to her as she tried to push past it. It was just another day without him; a year didn’t mean anything, it was just some arbitrary date to mark the passage of time. Why should one year mean more than three hundred and twelve days? A hundred and forty-two days? 

     

                “Do you want me to come with you?” Alex asked after Kara told her she was planning on visiting his grave.

     

                “No, I think I’ll go by myself,” Kara murmured, chewing thoughtfully around a mouthful of eggs.

     

                “Are you sure?”

     

                “Yes, I’m sure. It’s fine. I won’t stay long anyway.”

     

                Nodding in acceptance of her sister’s wishes, Alex stayed as long as she could, until she had to go to work. With the promise that Kara would be just fine, she kissed her sister’s cheek and left her to her miserable day. Eliza called after that, and there was a trickle of incoming texts from her friends as the day wore on. 

     

                Dressing, Kara grabbed her things and walked to the nearest florist, picking out a bouquet that seemed appropriate and then waiting at the bus stop. She listened to one of the self-help books about grief that Lena had recommended and rode out to the cemetery, the day already warm enough to make her shirt stick to her back once she’d disembarked from the air-conditioned bus, sneakers on the hot sidewalk as the back of her neck was warmed by the sun. The flowers she’d bought wouldn’t last long.

     

                Winding through the neat rows of headstones, the shorn grass crunching beneath her feet, Kara tried to remember her way to Mike’s grave. She couldn’t bring herself to visit all that often, and the rows looked much the same, some newer, some older, some with flowers, a lot without. Eventually finding herself before it, she placed the flowers down before the headstone and squinted against the harsh sunlight as she crossed her arms over her chest and clamped her jaw tightly shut.

     

                Her eyes smarted after a while, and Kara told herself it was just the glare of the sun reflecting off the polished surface. Blowing the air out of her lungs, she swallowed thickly, her throat itching and dry, and wiped her nose on the sleeve of her shirt. Lingering a while, she eventually made herself go, hating the discomfort of standing there in the sun, her loneliness more prominent than ever. Patting the headstone, she cleared her throat and then turned, feeling something akin to relief wash through her as she briskly went back the way she’d come.

     

                When she made it back to her apartment, a bouquet was waiting in front of the door, undisturbed but wilting in the warmth. Picking it up, she worked her key into the lock and shouldered her way into the stairwell as she plucked the note free. Shutting herself into the dimness of the stairwell, Kara plodded upstairs and then worked her apartment key into the lock of her front door, stepping into the sunlight and squinting down at the writing of the florist.

     

    Thinking of you today

     

    - Lena

     

                It made her throat close up and she set the bouquet down on the small dining table and stepped back, surveying them. Lilies, roses, carnations, chrysanthemums. It was a beautiful bouquet in soft shades of white, pink and yellow. Kara stood there staring at it for a long time, thinking about how she’d never received so many flowers from Mike until he’d died. 

     

                Letting out a weary sigh, she eventually turned away from the flowers and went to fetch a glass of water, cracking open the window above the sink to let in the slight breeze. A headache pulsed behind her eyes and her fingers worried at her forehead as she sipped her tepid water and dwelled in her heavy thoughts. It might have been odd that she hadn’t cried yet, that she’d managed to get out of bed so easily, but Kara had spent months stuck in her grief. The difficult part was behind her, so the anniversary didn’t hit her as heavily as she’d anticipated. 

     

                The day was already half over and Kara felt a little lost with herself. She had little appetite and didn’t feel like returning any texts, folding her legs beneath her on the sofa and playing the news on the TV to fill the still silence of the apartment. 

     

                Dusk crept in hours later, and she’d barely moved at all, save to drink some more water and turn her phone off when it buzzed against the coffee table. Limp and unmotivated, Kara eventually roused herself, blue light filtering in through the windows, and she shoved her feet into her shoes and donned a hooded sweatshirt to go and fetch dinner, mostly for the sake of routine. Picking up a cheap bottle of red wine along the way, she brought her dinner of sushi and ice cream back to the sofa and made her way through the three of them, alternating between sips of wine and mouthfuls of food. 

     

                The wine did nothing except make her feel drunk, sitting heavily in her stomach and only further adding to the numbness inside, and Kara tried her hardest to make herself cry. She felt like she owed it to him to shed some tears on the anniversary of all days. It was so easy any other time, catching her off guard at unlikely times, and now abandoning her when she felt like she had the most right to cry. Scrolling through text threads and listening to voicemails, she was dry-eyed and annoyed and ended up slipping two sleeping pills between her lips, even though she knew she shouldn’t mix them with wine.

     

                Waking late again, her mind foggy and her tongue thick in her mouth, the sour taste of wine caught at the back, Kara sat up on the sofa and bumped her glasses as she rubbed her face. She’d fallen asleep in an uncomfortable position, her back stiff and aching, and her glasses were crooked as she straightened. Her phone was still on the coffee table and she reached for it, texting James that she wouldn’t be in. Kara didn’t need to give any further explanation but she felt guilty that her friend would think she was inconsolable at home. Really, she was just empty.

     

                Milling about the apartment all day and trying to be productive, Kara washed her hair for group tomorrow and stripped the sheets off her bed and did a few loads of laundry. The apartment was clean and tidy and she felt a little better, shaking off the guilt and sadness of the day before as life went on, one year slipping into the next day. 

     

                Missing work the next day, Kara went grocery shopping and then bought a coffee at the bodega with too many sugars in it before going to the park. Sprawled in the grass with shafts of sunlight dappling her cheeks and nose, she enjoyed the warmth of the day and sipped her thick coffee and waited until it was late enough to start getting ready for group. There were a few texts from Lena she hadn’t responded to and Kara thought about her friend as she got ready, braiding her hair out of her face, making the effort to iron the wrinkles out of her jeans and a linen shirt. 

     

                Catching the bus, she listened to her music, sitting just behind the back doors and swaying with the rattling motion as her eyes went glassy, unfocused on the sight beyond the window as blue dusk escorted her to the Y. The evening had taken on a chill edge and she hugged her coat tighter around herself as she walked from the bus stop to the car park, kicking cigarette butts and empty Coke cans, breathing in the smell of gasoline and dust and impending rain sweeping in from the harbour. 

     

                She was early and helped set out the chairs, making small talk with some of the other regulars she’d grown familiar with. Kara wouldn’t have said she was friends with any of them - not like she was with Lena - but after the better part of a year spent crying and spilling her guts to the same group of people, there was a sense of camaraderie in it. 

     

                By the time she’d finished arranging the last few chairs in the circle, Lena had arrived. Kara was wiping her palms on the seat of her jeans as she straightened up when she caught sight of her, a small smile softening her face. They both made for the coffee station on the trestle table, from opposite ends of the room and met in front of the steaming urn. Lena grabbed two paper cups and set them down, fetching the tea bags while Kara picked up a carton of milk.

     

                “Hi, how’re you?” Lena gently asked, her green eyes genuine and solemn.

     

                Shrugging, Kara gave her a tight-lipped smile. “I’m alright. Thanks for the flowers.”

     

                Nodding in response, Lena plucked two napkins from the stack and selected donuts for them, carrying one in each hand as she studied Kara. Steeping the tea for a minute, Kara added milk and followed Lena to their chairs. 

     

                She set her cup down beside her and then took a donut from Lena before passing over her tea as others started to trickle in and make their drinks. Sitting close together, tuning out the rest of the group, Kara looked at Lena and raised her eyebrows slightly.

     

                “How’re you?”

     

                “Managing,” Lena gravely replied, nodding.

     

                Humming as she took a bite of her donut, Kara felt a sense of peace in the comfort of her company. They said little and sat in companionable silence as the room slowly got itself settled, the circle filling and the hissing of the urn as it reheated the water lingering beneath the low noise of conversation.

     

                Thomas launched into his usual welcoming spiel, asking a new older man to introduce himself to the group, and Kara was relieved that she was far from the newest there now. She recalled those daunting first few weeks, being freshly widowed and the newest member, barely able to string a sentence together amidst the sea of overwhelming emotions. Now it had been almost a year since she’d started attending, and while she still didn’t think it was helping much, it had been a constant, and wasn’t that really all she’d wanted from it? Something to latch onto to help the weeks go by.

     

                One by one, they started to go around the group and have their moment to speak to the circle, describing their grief, their loneliness, the new miscommunications opening up with living family members, and the rifts growing between friends. It was all familiar to Kara and she listened quietly, sipping her tea as it cooled and finishing off her donut, and then the rest of Lena’s slipped onto her thigh for her. Eventually, it was her turn.

     

                “Kara?”

     

                Chewing on her lip, she jostled a leg and let her eyes crawl around the room for something to capture her attention. Unfortunately, the Y was lacking in any decor aside from a growing water stain that had grown over the months she’d been attending, some leak in the ceiling feeding the rippling patch as it radiated outwards. 

     

                “It was a year the other day,” she started, her voice rasping. “I thought … I expected it to feel much worse, but … it didn’t.”

     

                “How did it feel?”

     

                She shrugged helplessly, silent for a moment as she found the words. “It felt like any other day. If I didn’t know the date, if people hadn’t reached out, it would have felt exactly the same as any other day. I went to- to visit his grave - the first time in a while. I don’t like going there. Um … so, it felt kind of … pointless being there. I thought maybe it would hurt more but it was actually a relief when I left. I don’t know if that’s normal.”

     

                “Feeling the whole spectrum is a part of the process too,” Thomas told her, his earnest sympathy making her feel patronised. “Grief doesn’t always express itself in a way that makes sense to us. No matter how long it’s been.”

     

                Feeling her eyes well up then, her throat constricting as the urge to cry slammed into her, Kara’s voice came out strangled and wavering. “But I- I thought I- it-”

     

                Tears spilt down her cheeks and she felt the mortifying betrayal of a red flush fill her face. Ducking her head down, she pressed her lips into a hard line and tried to stifle the building pressure in her chest. Shooting to her feet, her paper cup with the dregs of tea in hand, she turned and stalked towards the closed door, the hinges shrieking in protest as she let herself out into the hallway and then out into the cool evening.

     

                Inside the room, Lena sat there for a moment as everyone exchanged glances and sat in uncomfortable silence. Reaching down for her bag, she cleared her throat and then climbed to her feet in her precarious heels. The sound of them was muffled by the cheap commercial carpet as she followed after her friend.

     

                Kara was to the left of the doors, tears running down her face as she restlessly paced, fiddling with her fingers and her knuckles and the wedding and engagement rings she hadn’t managed to stop wearing yet. Her breaths were coming quickly and shallow, a light-headed feeling of panic creeping in as it all crashed down on her, delayed.

     

                At the sound of heels scuffing on the asphalt, she whirled around, stricken and pale, and stopped her pacing. Lena’s expression softened with understanding and Kara angrily swiped at her cheeks as she looked down, sniffing.

     

                “I’m fine. I, uh-”

     

                “It’s okay,” Lena murmured.

     

                She reached into her bag and procured a packet of tissues, handing one over to Kara and then wrapping her in a tight hug. It surprised them both and Kara couldn’t remember the last time she’d been held. Not hugged , but cradled in someone’s arms, comforted by it. Letting out a ragged sob, Kara squeezed her eyes shut and buried her face in Lena’s shoulder for a moment. She felt like she should have been too embarrassed to be so vulnerable around someone she’d known for a little over half a year, but Kara couldn’t bring herself to care.

     

                “Come on. I’ll drive you home,” Lena murmured, giving Kara a one-armed squeeze.

     

                Dropping her arm, Lena started towards her car and Kara followed after her, wiping her cheeks and nose with the tissue as she tried to swallow the hitching sobs. Her chest felt tight and she could feel the headache beginning behind her raw eyes as she sniffed and quietly sobbed all the way back to the sleek car. The lights flashed as Lena unlocked it and Kara slid into the passenger seat, her body sagging against the leather.

     

                Neither of them spoke for a long while as Kara tried to regain her composure, and Lena didn’t make her feel ashamed of it or like she was being a nuisance as she cried in the front seat of her car. Drawing in a deep, shuddering breath, Kara exhaled sharply and closed her eyes.

     

                “Sorry. You didn’t even get your turn.”

     

                “I should be thanking you for the distraction,” Lena wryly replied.

     

                Opening her eyes a crack, Kara looked at her, taking in the droll smile, and gave her a small smile in return. Wiping the heels of her palms over her cheeks, she let out a defeated sigh.

     

                “I’m sorry.”

     

                “Don’t apologise.”

     

                “I don’t even know why I’m crying.”

     

                “You’re grieving.”

     

                Confusion clouded Kara’s face as she rubbed her palms over her thighs. “I didn’t even cry the other day. On the anniversary. Isn’t that weird?”

     

                She looked at Lena with anxious expectancy, and Lena shrugged, gripping the steering wheel as she looked out the windscreen.

     

                “No. I don’t think so. Maybe I’m just a lot more emotionally detached than other people but … there is no right way to feel about it. Just because someone bawls their eyes out every day for ten years doesn’t mean they’re grieving more than you because you didn’t.”

     

                “I just- I’m so … confused,” Kara admitted. “My life has changed so much over the last year and not all of it has been bad. My husband is dead and a lot of the time lately I’ve just- all I’ve felt is how easy it’s been. And that’s not- I miss him, but … it’s all just so- I don’t know. He used to leave his shit everywhere. He could be so … inconsiderate at times. So selfish. He’d get mad at me if I wanted us to do something and he had plans with his friends already. Said I never gave him any space. I felt like his maid sometimes; he’d give me a wrinkled shirt and ask me to iron it for him because he didn’t have the time, he’d always ask what was for dinner and never offered to cook, even though I’m a shit cook, and he used to place his dishes in the sink instead of washing them. I let it pile up once, just to see what he’d do. He didn’t have a clean cup for his coffee so he went to Starbucks instead.”

     

                She let out a confused laugh, shaking her head as her forehead pinched. Dashing the cuff of her shirt across her eyes, Kara sniffed and then drew in a shaky breath. 

     

                “God, he was such an asshole. I forgot why I loved him a lot of the time. We’d go days without talking, days being passive-aggressive until it would come to a head. He was always sweet after. Never used to buy me flowers though - even after a bad fight, even on anniversaries.”

     

                Falling silent, she chewed on the inside of her lip and wallowed in her regret. 

     

                “What did you like about him?” Lena asked after a moment. “You’ve told me what you hated. What did you love?”

     

                Kara pressed her lips together as her tear-stained face crumpled thoughtfully. It took her a moment before she started to speak and found it hard to stop. 

     

                “He used to make pancakes every Saturday. His mom and dad did it for him and it was like his own little ritual. Even if I didn’t want pancakes or I wanted to stay in bed, there was a stack of pancakes waiting for me every Saturday. He used to duet on karaoke nights with me - show tunes, Britney, Backstreet Boys, whatever I wanted - and he enjoyed it. He loved getting up on that little stage in that shitty bar, especially when he got to sing Bon Jovi. We spent so many nights there together. He used to send me a lot of voicemails because he was always at the gym or driving or … whatever, so he’d just ramble on about anything and I listen to them when I’m lonely now. My friends and I used to have regular game nights and he was so competitive; if we were having a particular game night, he’d spend the week before it studying so we could win. I remember one time it was Trivial Pursuit so he tried to cheat and memorise all of the answers on the cards. We still lost. He always let me have the last dumpling when we had Chinese.”

     

                “That’s nice,” Lena murmured, a pained smile on her face.

     

                She reached out and picked up Kara’s cold hand, squeezing her fingers tightly. Kara’s mouth thinned in an attempt at a smile and she clumsily squeezed Lena’s hand back. 

     

                They lapsed into silence, the darkness beyond the windscreen making them feel like the only two people in the world. The sounds outside were muffled and Kara would’ve liked to sit there in that bubble of peace for hours.

     

                “Do you want to come to Metropolis with me?” Lena suddenly asked.

     

                Kara turned in her seat and raised her eyebrows, “Metropolis? When?”

     

                Shrugging nonchalantly, Lena pursed her lips, a brooding look on her face. “On Friday.”

     

                “This Friday? Like … tomorrow?”

     

                “Sure. Why not?”

     

                “I- uh-”

     

                “Can you get work off? You won’t have to worry about flights and accommodation.”

     

                Kara frowned, her mouth pulling down at the corners as she sank into her seat in the front of the car. “Why Metropolis?”

     

                “I’m from there. Not that I particularly like it there, but I’m visiting a friend.”

     

                “Oh. Oh, no, that’s okay. I wouldn’t want to intrude.”

     

                Giving her a wan smile, Lena shrugged again. “She works. And has a kid. I’ll be by myself most of the time so … want to come? It’s only for a week.”

     

                Torn for a moment, Kara hummed dubiously and tried to work out the logistics of getting work off at such late notice, of trying to manage her finances, wondering if she could afford the payments on the apartment as well as the luxury of a trip across the country. She didn’t want to let Lena pay for it, and Mike had never had life insurance so she was paying the mortgage alone, but truthfully, Kara needed a break. She wouldn’t even need to tell anyone; she’d gone silent so often that her friends had gotten used to her avoiding calls and texts and work.

     

                “Um …”

     

                “Look, I don’t know about you, but I really need a break from it all. I feel like it’s eating me alive and I just need some … space, some distance. I don’t care how much of an asshole it makes me to leave for a week but I just- I can’t. I need a break.”

     

                She was so firm, so insistent and mildly distraught, that Kara’s mouth opened and closed soundlessly for a moment.

     

                “Okay.”

     

                Turning to look at her, Lena frowned, cocking her head to the side and raking her hair out of her face. “Really?”

     

                “Sure. I’ll come with you.”

     

                “Oh. Okay. Good. Um, I’ll send you more details; it’s a red-eye flight, leaves at ten and we’ll get there at five east coast time. I can pick you up at eight if that works for you.”

     

                “Sounds good,” Kara rasped, nodding with a little more determination now, a stubborn set to her jaw as she grasped at the distraction.

     

                They sat there for a while longer, mostly in silence as they listened to passing traffic, occasionally talking in murmurs until Kara felt utterly drained. Lena let out a soft sigh of resignation and pressed her foot on the brake, turning the key in the ignition to start the engine.

     

                “Come on, let’s get you home.”

     

                Kara didn’t mention how she could’ve used a stiff drink, the burn of cheap tequila to warm her, the sourness of beer not nearly adequate against the inner turmoil. She didn’t mention how badly she didn’t want to go home to her empty apartment, where she was insufficiently haunted by her dead husband to the point that the guilt outweighed the grief she felt. The thought of home conjured up when mentioned wasn’t even the apartment she’d shared with Mike; it was Alex and Kelly’s place, the house she’d moved into when she’d been adopted, the place she’d grown up, hell, even Lena’s sofa, which had seen more than a few nights from her, despite the guest room always offered up after too much to drink. Home was anywhere but home and she felt she was grieving poorly.

     

                The car inched through the city traffic though and came to an idling stop outside the front door of her place and Kara sat heavily in the front seat for a moment. She seriously considered asking Lena to come upstairs and drink with her, but in the end, she let her go and bypassed the dwindling liquor cabinet for bed. Kara had work the next day and a last-minute flight in the night - she’d see Lena then and thank herself for the lack of a hangover.

     

                At work, she didn’t mention her impromptu trip to Metropolis, just getting through the day vaccinating cats and giving a mastiff an ultrasound before operating on a little bunny who’d eaten a sock. It was all rote and Kara felt her mind scattering with distraction as she went through the motions, smoothing soft fur and stroking damp noses as she gently murmured to the creatures brought before her, their hearts beating quickly with fear as she tried to calm them down and do her examinations.

     

                Washing her hands in the kitchen later that evening, her coffee mug spilling suds on the draining board, Kara made a vague outline of her plans for the weekend as James finished off his coffee and William grabbed his things from the battered set of lockers. James asked if she would be going for drinks tomorrow, which had been a more regular occurrence these days, usually with Lena in tow, but Kara made the excuse that she was going to dinner with Mike’s mom, the sting of guilt not quite strong enough to make her feel bad about saying it.

     

                Making her escape and wishing them a good weekend, she briskly walked to the bus stop and restlessly waited, the nimbus glows of headlights and neon signs and muffled sirens keeping her company through the mild evening. Rattling along at the front of the bus as a child fussed and conversation washed over her, Kara felt herself lulled to weariness as she trundled back to her apartment. She’d made a half-hearted attempt to pack the night before, a few shirts and a skirt spilling from the small carry-on, and she shed her scrubs and showered before changing into jeans and a quarter-zip sweatshirt before kneeling beside the case.

     

                In short order, she had a few outfits and her toiletries packed and was methodically making the rounds to each window, checking the latches and closing the blinds. Lena texted her soon after to say she was downstairs and Kara lugged the small case down with her, stepping out into the dark and making for the car illegally parked out front, waiting. Lena popped the trunk and she stowed her luggage before climbing into the passenger seat.

     

                “Hi.”

     

                “Hi,” Lena murmured, “how’re you feeling today?”

     

                Kara sighed and waved a hand dismissively, “ready to be in Metropolis.”

     

                Quietly chuckling, Lena indicated into traffic and pulled out. “You and me both.”

     

                “Bad day?”

     

                Blowing the air out of her cheeks, Lena shook her head, a troubled look on her face. “Just a lot on my plate.”

     

                “Well, we’ll both be free from it all for a week starting from now.”

     

                Giving her a droll smile, Lena changed the radio station and sank into her seat, merging onto the highway towards the airport as they chatted about their day. The sounds of planes taking off and landing filled the night as they passed through the parking metre, the arm rising to admit them, and Lena found an empty spot, yanking up the handbrake and turning off the engine.

     

                Fetching their bags, Kara handed Lena her expensive black duffel bag and wheeled her own case behind her as they made their way indoors. People milled about in the queue at the check-in booth and Kara made to join them until Lena kept walking, bypassing the line for economy and stopping at the one for business and first class, which was empty. Walking up to the counter, Lena presented the tickets to the clerk and they checked their small bags before moving off to security, passing through the detectors and collecting their shoes and phones.

     

                “First class?” Kara sceptically asked once they were through to the departures lounge.

     

                “It was … a last trip planned for my wife and I. Only, she can’t use the ticket so …”

     

                “Oh. Um … I’m sorry.”

     

                Giving her a thin smile, Lena’s eyes darted around. “Don’t be. At least it’s not wasted. Coffee or something stronger?”

     

                Choking on a laugh, Kara’s eyes followed Lena’s gaze to the bar. “Stronger.”

     

                Insisting on buying their drinks, Kara forked out the cash for the inflated prices of airport bar liquor and they sat side by side on barstools, a glass of red wine for her and scotch for Lena. Dour and tired, they said little as they drank and then Lena got the next round before they left for their gate. Queuing to board the plane, Kara felt a prickle of eager excitement at the prospect of sitting in first class and boarded ahead of Lena before pausing at the two seats they were escorted to.

     

                “Oh, uh, you take the window,” Kara quickly insisted, stepping aside.

     

                Lena seemed to pale slightly and quickly shook her head. “No, no, you take it. I’m terrible with flying.”

     

                Surprised, Kara slipped into the spacious row and took her seat, peering out at the lights of the airport. Buckling herself in, Kara was a little restless and watched the other first-class passengers get settled in before she glanced over at Lena, who was stiff with pinched lips.

     

                “God, are you alright? You really hate it that much?”

     

                “I took two Xanax before picking you up,” Lena admitted. “Probably shouldn’t have mixed it with the scotch, but I’ve never liked planes much. I’m fine. I just- this is the first time I’ve flown … without her.”

     

                Audibly swallowing, Lena clenched her hands into white-knuckled fists. Blinking, Kara hesitated and then reached out to take her hand, hoping to offer some small comfort. Closed eyes opening with surprise, Lena met her gaze and seemed to let go of some of the tension held in her shoulders as she squeezed Kara’s hand in return.

     

                They sat that way all through take-off, Kara’s fingers turning numb with the strength of Lena’s grip as they rose from the runway, stomachs swooping and a moment of weightless fear. Even once the plane levelled and they fell into the rhythmic lull of the flight, Lena still didn’t let go and Kara sipped the tepid champagne given to her in her left hand and stared at the unending blackness beyond the porthole window. 

     

                At some point, she slipped into the space between awake and sleep, her head drowsily dropping onto Lena’s shoulder. She didn’t mean to fall asleep and usually found it hard to on flights, her slightly taller frame awkwardly fitting in the narrow rows of coach, but in the spacious seat of first class, she couldn’t help herself. It wasn’t until they hit a bout of turbulence flying over Gotham that Kara woke, startling upright, bleary-eyed and confused for a moment.

     

                With the creased look of sleep still on her face, Kara looked to her right and saw a shoulder before her eyes travelled up to meet jade green. Blinking, she straightened even further and angled her body away from Lena’s personal space, tearing her hand free from Lena’s tight grip, which had persisted even into sleep.

     

                “Oh. Sorry,” Kara mumbled, feeling vaguely embarrassed for falling asleep on her shoulder.

     

                “It’s okay,” Lena murmured, knotting her fingers in the wool of her tapered pants.

     

                Rubbing her eyes, Kara cleared her throat and shifted, touching the screen to check their trip progress and then launching into a murmured conversation with Lena as she attempted to distract her. They ended up putting on a new release movie and sharing an earbud each, Kara creeping back into Lena’s space to share the armrest and see her TV screen better.

     

                The rest of the flight passed by quickly, the early hours of the morning brightening the sky to grey beyond the small window as they descended through the cloud cover of Metropolis. She gripped Lena’s hand tightly as they landed, nodding encouragingly as they bounced along the tarmac and came to a quick stop before idling around to their gate. At the dying whir of their engines, Lena went slack and Kara fought back a smile as she watched her with curiosity.

     

                Disembarking first, they were quick to collect their bags and head out to the waiting car, another oddity that Kara was surprised by, expecting a moderately lengthy wait at the taxi rank with everyone else. Instead, they were bundled into the cool interior of the back of the car and set off through the city with nothing but the quiet purr of the engine and muffled traffic behind the tinted windows to break the comfortable silence. Kara swayed along in a stupor, dishevelled and still tired, despite her nap.

     

                The hotel Lena had booked was in the city centre and oozed a casual wealth that made Kara doubt for a second, hesitating on the threshold as the doorman patiently waited for her to enter the lobby. Hurrying to catch up to Lena, who was making for the front desk to check them in, Kara looked around at the marble and ceiling fresco as her wheels scraped the floor, filling the hushed space with the sound.

     

                It was still predawn and the lobby was silent and empty, aside from the staff, and Kara was stifling a lawn as she watched Lena sign the paperwork and collect the keycard. A bellhop had come to collect their luggage in the meantime and they made for the elevator, Lena pushing the button for one of the top-floor executive suites while Kara made a few hesitant comments on the luxury of it all.

     

                Whether she was just tired or it was normal, Lena didn’t really respond and swept into the spacious hotel room without little interest in the decor. Shedding her coat and kicking off her heels, Lena made for the heavy blackout curtains and yanked them shut over the lightening window.

     

                “I changed the reservation so we could have a king each,” she said, gesturing to the bed.

     

                Kara’s mouth opened and closed for a moment as she hovered uncertainly. “Um … okay, thanks. Did- did you want a specific bed?”

     

                Giving her a mildly exasperated look, Lena arched an eyebrow. Nodding in silent acceptance of Lena’s unspoken answer, Kara hitched her case onto the bed end rummaged through for pilled sweatpants and a college T-shirt. 

     

                “Mind if I use the bathroom?” 

     

                “Help yourself.”

     

                She shut herself into the space, which was almost bigger than her apartment, and stared at the double vanity and the free-standing tub, the rainfall showerhead and underheated flooring. It was perhaps the nicest place she’d ever been in and Kara was still trying to process how two nights ago she’d been crying in Lena’s car, and now she was on the other side of the country with her in a luxury hotel. Kara hadn’t even told Alex and felt a little blindsided by the spontaneity of it all. It wasn’t something she was exactly known for.

     

                Trying to be quick so she didn’t hog the bathroom, Kara showered and changed into her sweatpants before applying a moisturiser to her face and brushing her teeth. That was the extent of her routine and she stepped back into the spacious suite to find Lena flicking through channels on the TV. She looked up at Kara’s arrival and raised the remote.

     

                “They have HBO. I don’t know if you watch anything on there but I’ve been watching Succession. It’s good.”

     

                “Oh, um, yeah I use my sister’s account. She gets my Netflix. Good show though.”

     

                Nodding, Lena climbed to her feet and gathered her things, slipping into the bathroom as Kara packed away her dirty clothes and sank onto the bed. The mattress was soft and she was tired, the effort to stay awake out of politeness as she listened to the sound of running water behind the closed door was almost too much for her. She was beneath the blankets and blinking sluggishly, her face free of her glasses and a softer look of youth about her as Lena stepped out and surveyed her.

     

                “Comfortable?”

     

                Kara let out a small laugh, her cheeks turning pink. “Are we sleeping? Or are we going anywhere? I have to say, I’m not as good at all-nighters as I was when I was twenty. I’m getting old.”

     

                “Old,” Lena scoffed, smiling slightly. “Go to sleep. Sam’s working until tonight anyway; I’m meeting her for dinner if you wanted to join.”

     

                “Can I?”

     

                “Well, I didn’t drag you across the country with me to leave you in the hotel room the whole time.”

     

                Shuffling beneath the blankets, Kara hummed with satisfaction and smiled. “I wouldn’t mind it; this place is nicer than my apartment.”

     

                “Go to sleep,” Lena repeated, a little softer this time.

     

                Kara watched her get ready for bed from the safety of her own and found herself drifting off to sleep the moment Lena turned off the lights. She was already too far gone to respond to the murmured goodnight from her friend and slept soundly until past lunchtime, her stomach rumbling and an air of confusion around her when she finally woke.

     

                Brushing her hair out of her face, Kara squinted and fumbled for her glasses before her eyes landed on Lena. Legs crossed at the ankle, dressed in pressed clothes with headphones on, she was typing away at her laptop. It wasn’t until Kara sat fully upright that Lena looked over at her, pulling her headphones down.

     

                “Hey.”

     

                “Are you working?”

     

                “I run my own company,” Lena reminded her, “I have clients to handhold; my architects do the heavy lifting.”

     

                “Hm. You know, you’ve never shown me any of your work before.”

     

                “You’ve seen my house. That was my work.”

     

                “But other buildings.”

     

                Lena bit her lip, hesitating. “You know Obsidian North?”

     

                “Of course.”

     

                “That one was mine. A personal gift, in a sense.”

     

                “I heard their CEO got sick a while ago. Had to step down.”

     

                Lena didn’t respond, and Kara didn’t catch the tightening of her mouth at the corners in the dimness of the lamplit room. Shifting, Lena cleared her throat and closed her laptop, removing the headphones completely.

     

                “Lunch? We can get room service.”

     

                Caving to the mention of food, even though she could’ve slept another twelve hours and eaten Big Belly Burger, a cheaper alternative to the exorbitant prices she knew room service would have, Kara ordered a chicken burger from the menu. Lena picked at her falafel pita as they watched an episode of Succession together on the TV, sitting at the small table set off to one side.

     

                Kara felt a little uncertain, travelling with someone she’d known all of seven months, give or take, but Lena had the uncanny ability to seem perfectly at ease in any situation. Even if that situation happened to be a spontaneous holiday with a newly widowed friend met at an unhelpful grief group. Whatever reservations Kara had about going, they quickly disappeared.

     

                After lunch, Kara showered again and dressed in jeans and a plaid shirt and they went to a coffee shop that Lena liked, sipping oat milk lattes as they walked through the mid-afternoon warmth of Metropolis. It was still hours before they had to meet Sam for dinner, so they stopped at bookstores and bakeries, buying butter croissants and buying a book for each other as they rattled off a few authors they liked, filing the information away. On the way back to the hotel, Kara suggested they stop at a bodega and bought a few Coronas and cheap bottles of wine for the hotel room, Lena dubiously eyeing the labels in the fluorescent lights. 

     

                Back at the hotel, they got changed for dinner, and it wasn’t until they were at the closest subway station, buying tickets for the next train that she remembered. Her husband was dead and she was enjoying herself on the other side of the country with another woman. Throat closing up, she forced herself to swallow, squeezing a thanks out as Lena handed her a ticket, and managed not to trip over her uncooperative feet as she followed her down to the platform.

     

                “Are you okay?” Lena perceptively asked as Kara stared blankly at the subway tiles, trash blowing past and announcements coming over the intercom sounding tinny and distant.

     

                “Fine,” Kara croaked.

     

                “No, you’re not. You’re thinking about him.”

     

                Closing her eyes, Kara swallowed. “Yeah, I am.”

     

                “What’re you thinking?”

     

                She shook her head, a breath forced out of her lungs. “Nothing. I just- I remembered he’s dead. That’s all.”

     

                “It gets quieter and smaller but it always comes rushing back in at the worst moments, doesn’t it?”

     

                Choking on a laugh, Kara’s lips twisted wryly. “I was starting to feel like I could finally … breathe a little. Why do we have to suffer so much? They died once , but we have to keep living every day, constantly reminded of it. Do I just … carry it around with me for the rest of my life now? Is that how you feel?”

     

                “I think there are different kinds of grief,” Lena murmured. “There’s the kind you carry around with you and the kind that makes you stuck.”

     

                “Which one are you?”

     

                Their train arrived then, a gust of wind rushing down the tunnel as the tracks screeched, and Lena buried her hands in the pockets of her trench coat, grave and beautiful. She didn’t respond as they boarded, graffiti and trash and the smell of urine and weed filling the cart, opting to stand at the end of the carriage, holding the overhead bar as the train lurched into motion a moment later. Kara wasn’t going to pursue it, wondering if it was too personal, but Lena let out a weary sigh a few minutes later.

     

                “Stuck. I … think about her every minute of every day. I work so much to avoid being alone in our house. I still cry myself to sleep at least twice a week.”

     

                “Do you?” Kara asked, surprised.

     

                Lena had seemed so stoic through it all, and that wasn’t to say she hadn’t loved her wife deeply, but Kara had always marvelled at her ability to seem so level and steady amidst the sea of grief. She would never have thought Lena still cried herself to sleep, over halfway through the first year of widowhood. 

     

                “I do. Sometimes in the middle of it, I think I’ll never be able to stop. Then I just … I get tired and it shuts off, and it’s for the best because I think the sadness would kill me if I let it stay.”

     

                Mouth thinning with the same sinking feeling of dismay, Kara stared out the window as they rattled along a track overlooking the harbour. The train car was relatively quiet and the blue dusk outside was soothing. Their stop was three later and they stepped out into a warm evening with a cool breeze sweeping in off the coast, cutting through the smell of pollution and trash.

     

                They met Sam in an austere upscale restaurant in one of the other neighbourhoods, sitting on the waterfront as lights reflected off the inky darkness of the water. Kara’s first impression of her was gentle kindness and exuding warmth and shook her hand with genuine delight to meet Lena’s friend. They got a bottle of wine and ordered dinner and Kara was content to remain outside of the conversation as the two friends caught up.

     

                “So … you two met at that grief group thing? Is that right?”

     

                “Yes,” Lena murmured, turning her wine glass by the thin stem. “You know we did.”

     

                “I’m just checking,” Sam said with mild defence, showing her palms. “You’re so tight-lipped about it. I’m still surprised you went to start with, not to mention you still going. It’s good.”

     

                Kara wrinkled her nose and quietly scoffed. “You wouldn’t think that if you went. If it wasn’t for Lena, I wouldn’t be going anymore, that’s for sure.”

     

                “You don’t find it useful for processing your emotions?”

     

                Lena made a sound of amusement at the back of her throat as she swallowed a sip of wine, head tipped back to expose her throat as her arm ran behind Kara, along the booth seat.

     

                “I don’t think anything gets processed in that room. It’s just a place for sad, pathetic people to feel like they’re helping themselves while doing absolutely nothing to seek out genuine help. Present company included.”

     

                “Has she always been this cynical?” Kara asked.

     

                Sam pursed her lips and hummed, “in the eight years that I’ve known her … yes. Although, Andrea had the habit of tempering her moods.”

     

                Clicking her tongue, Lena shifted, arm drawing back as she reached for the bottle of wine and refilled her glass and then the other two. “She tempered my moods but hers were worse than mine.”

     

                “Well, given the circumstances-“

     

                “I’m aware of the circumstances,” Lena curtly responded, a brittle edge to her tone.

     

                Kara drummed her fingers on the table and let out a strained laugh. “I think that’s enough about dead spouses for dinner table conversation, don’t you? What do you do for work, Sam?”

     

                Dinner was a nice affair, the conversation flowing so easily that it was a welcome reprieve from Kara’s ordinary life. Lena had brought a distraction to her through their meeting, something new that wasn’t tied to her own life, and by extension of her, Kara found that this was the first dinner she’d had that was completely free of any reminders of Mike. Of course, they’d touched on their grief, but neither of them had known him, and it didn’t cast a pall over the evening.

     

                After more than a few glasses of wine, Sam had to get home and pay her daughter’s sitter, which left Kara and Lena out near the water with a few more hours of idle time before bed. They ended up at an uptown bar, sitting on the cracked leather seats of a booth, a broken jukebox leading them to listen to the old school rock music over the speakers instead as peanut shells crunched beneath their shoes. They had margaritas, the salt rim making Kara cringe at the first sip, and she barely remembered getting back to the hotel.

     

                Tumbling into bed, the last thing she was aware of was moonlight slanting through the parted curtains, her body leaden and her eyes slit to reveal the fuzzy outline of Lena walking back and forth in the open space at the ends of their beds. She was just as hurt as Kara, lost in the same way, both of them broken and trying to patch up the cracks, and Kara was too drunk to make sense of it all as she watched Lena pace instead of sleeping.

     

                Their days in Metropolis passed by quickly and Kara felt somewhat reborn by being there. There was an ease in her chest she hadn’t felt in years, feeling rested and stronger, the reprieve from a life filled with afternoons spent playing velcro tennis in Sam’s backyard with her daughter, Ruby, drinking rum at a bar after oysters and taking naps in the park as the sun warmed her skin, listening to live music on an outdoor patio with a jug of sangria. The business of their social schedule kept her from thinking much about her normal life and Kara sent James a text feigning sick and avoided any subsequent calls from friends and family as she drank and ate and forgot to be a widow for a few days. 

     

                She woke in the morning on Thursday with a dry mouth and a headache, but a strange moment of clarity. Lena was already awake and dressed, tired circles beneath her bare face and a cup of coffee from the hotel kettle and complimentary sachets fighting off her exhaustion and a mild hangover. Sitting up slowly, Kara dug the heels of her palms into her eyes and sat there for a moment before flipping back the covers. That day marked the first time she could remember waking up without the expectation that he’d be beside her.

     

                Relief knifed through her and Kara frowned as she raked a hand through her scraggly blonde hair before reaching for her glasses. Sliding them onto her face, she met Lena’s questioning graze and gave her a wan smile, the weight of disappointment oddly absent, along with the sound of the coffee maker going, a loud conversation waking her from the kitchen.

     

                “You okay?”

     

                “Yeah, yeah,” Kara quickly replied, although there was an odd note in her voice. Frowning at the carpeted floor, she brooded for a moment before meeting Lena’s eyes and letting out a scoffing laugh at her raised eyebrow. “I just- I … I didn’t expect him to be next to me this morning. I think that’s the first time I didn’t expect that.”

     

                “Oh,” Lena murmured, closing her laptop.

     

                She rose to her feet and crossed the space between their beds, sitting beside Kara and hesitantly patting her knee. Their eyes met and Kara gave her a fleeting smile.

     

                “Is that good or bad?”

     

                “How would it feel if you woke up without expecting her to be there?”

     

                Blinking in surprise, Lena considered it for a moment. “For me … I think it would make me sad.”

     

                “It makes me feel relieved. Like maybe it does get easier - a hell of a lot easier.”

     

                “Come on, let’s get breakfast,” Lena suggested, “everything’s easier after a good meal, including talking.”

     

                Kara couldn’t argue with that logic and went to get ready, grabbing her things and then following Lena out of their suite. They rode the elevator down to the lobby and Lena suggested a place, which Kara was all too willing to agree to, given her lack of knowledge about the city. Watching Lena navigate the familiar streets, Kara found herself thinking how Lena looked so much like she belonged there, more than she did in National City.

     

                Seated in a booth at a cafe that advertised artisanal pastries and organic coffee beans, Kara sipped her dirty chai and gave Lena a scrutinising look. “Why’d you move to National City?”

     

                Lena hesitated, setting her cup of black coffee down and clearing her throat. “I needed the distance from my family. I’ve never had a good relationship with them, and they didn’t take too kindly to my wife either, so … it was just better to put myself on the opposite coast and put all of my energy into good things; my wife, my business, my mental health. Didn’t really work out how I’d planned.”

     

                “Do you miss being here? Sam-”

     

                “Sam used to live in National City - used to work for me, actually - but she has her own reasons for moving to Metropolis. Even if it means I have no friends anymore. Well, one friend.”

     

                Kara let out a quick laugh, rolling her eyes. “It’s lonely, isn’t it? Grief.”

     

                “Yes,” Lena quietly agreed.

     

                “Even with all the people I still have, the people I love, it’s- some of them have lost family so you’d think that would make it easier. But I still feel like I’m the only person in the world who’s ever felt this way. Maybe grief has made me too self-centred. Or maybe I’ve just lost one too many people now.”

     

                “I guess it’s easier for me. I find it hard to- I- Sam’s my friend, my best friend, but … I find it hard to love people. Andrea was the only one and, I don’t know, that was- that was frightening enough, learning how to be vulnerable with her. I know I’ll never be able to let myself go through that again.”

     

                “It must have been hard, knowing what was coming.”

     

                Lena made a gravelly sound of agreement at the back of her throat. “I know how sudden it was can’t have been easy for you-”

     

                “No, no, I completely agree that waiting and watching would’ve been harder. Was it cancer?”

     

                “I- no, not cancer. Um …”

     

                “Sorry, that’s personal,” Kara murmured, “I shouldn’t-”

     

                “It’s fine. I don’t mind, I just- I haven’t had to tell anyone in a while-”

     

                Kara’s phone started to ring and she winced apologetically. Lena gave her a quick smile, cut through with relief as her shoulders slumped and she leaned back. They’d gravitated towards each other across the table and Kara pulled her phone out to silence it as they drew away from each other.

     

                “Sorry, let me just-”

     

                “Answer it,” Lena encouraged.

     

                It was Alex and Kara stared at her sister’s name for a moment before answering. “Hey.”

     

                “Hey, where are you? I’m outside.”

     

                “Oh, um, I had to go out for a bit.”

     

                “Oh. I thought we could get coffee. James said you haven’t been at work all week so … I just wanted to make sure you were okay.”

     

                Letting out a short laugh, Kara rubbed at her eyes. “I’m fine. I, uh, I’m in Metropolis, actually.”

     

                “You’re where?”

     

                “It was a spur-of-the-moment thing.”

     

                “Wha- are you serious? You’ve been dodging my calls all week because you’re on the other side of the country and didn’t tell anyone?”

     

                “We’re only here for a week.”

     

                “We? Who’s we? Lena?”

     

                Hesitating, Kara cleared her throat, her eyes landing on Lena as she bit her lip. “Yes.”

     

                “I- Kara,” her sister said with growing frustration. “What the hell are you playing at?”

     

                “It’s just a trip to get a break. I’ll be back on Saturday. We can get coffee then.”

     

                “Kara-”

     

                “Okay, bye, love you.”

     

                She said it quickly and hung up before things could get out of hand, her sister’s concern manifesting itself in some brash anger that pissed Kara off in turn. Alex seemed even more protective and worried since Mike had died, and a year on it was still just as exhausting to have to explain herself so her friends and family would give her some breathing room.

     

                Shoving her phone into her pocket, Kara sighed and gave Lena a rueful smile. “Sorry about that.”

     

                “Alex?”

     

                “Mhm.”

     

                “You didn’t tell her we were coming?”

     

                Looking vaguely sheepish, Kara shrugged. “I have to explain myself a lot when I decide to do things like I’m some child who can’t make a rational decision for myself anymore. It’s caused more than a few arguments since he died and … I don’t have the energy for that right now. I’d be stuck on the phone for an hour trying to resolve it because … well, I can never end things on bad terms with people. Not knowing if that last thing she’d hear me say was something horrible … it eats away at me to leave on a bad note. It’s stupid-”

     

                “It’s not stupid at all. The most painful goodbyes are the ones we never get to say, so … at least you’ll know you always said it, they always knew how you felt about them.”

     

                “What was it like for you? Losing her?”

     

                Expression crumpling, Lena looked down at her lap for a moment. “I was just … exhausted. In a lot of pain. It was the lowest point of my life so far, that day- I put on one of her sweaters and just drove for hours. I made it to Big Sur, crying my eyes out. The lump in my throat wouldn’t go away and I fell asleep in my car near the sea and slept for eighteen hours. I stopped eating and drank a lot and I’d- I’d visit her every day. As disgusting as it sounds, I couldn’t bring myself to shower at the beginning; I just used to sit around in her clothes until they stopped smelling like her. Sam had to stay for a few weeks to get me back on my feet, but … I haven’t really felt okay until this trip.”

     

                Kara set her hand down on the table, palm upwards, sliding it across to Lena. Glancing down at it, she blinked a few times and let out a hoarse laugh, sniffing as she put her hand in Kara’s. Looking up with a faint sheen in her eyes, she cocked her head to the side.

     

                “What was it like for you?”

     

                It took a moment for Kara to make her voice work past the tightness of her throat. “Yeah, just like that. Except, I didn’t really feel okay until I met you.”

    Chapter 8

                They came back from Metropolis with a little more peace in their hearts and a closeness that was enough to have them spending almost every day together if they were both free. On Tuesday, Kara invited Lena plant shopping to replace some of the withered ones she’d been neglectful towards, and Wednesday she accompanied Lena to the park to walk Aristotle. They both went to group on Thursday and Al’s on Friday for drinks with Kara’s friends, and Lena had to work most of the weekend but they still caught up for cheap tacos and tequila on Saturday. 

     

                Weeks slipped by and there was a companionable comfort between them, their friendship deepening over pizza nights on Kara’s sofa and whisky or scotch or bourbon on Lena’s after every group session. Alex questioned Kara numerous times of the nature of their relationship and Kara didn’t know how to explain it to her; they were friends in a different sense to Kara’s other friends, out of a necessity to fill that void their spouses had left, out of some shared grief that had come into their lives at the same time. It was the same way Alex and Kara had grown closer once they’d shared the bond of losing a parent, understanding parts of each other that had previously been unknown to them until they’d gone through the same thing. 

     

                A few months after their trip Lena confessed it was the one year anniversary since she’d lost her wife and Kara bought her flowers and offered her what empty condolences she could, cold comfort in the face of grief. Kara didn’t see her that day and didn’t get a response until later on that night, past dinnertime, filled with the anxious urge to go to her apartment and check on her. But she gave her space and saw her again the next day, seeing the grief written plainly on her face and offering up a night of wine and reality TV at her place as a distraction.

     

                The next group meeting, they collected their donuts and tea and their seats beside each other and quietly talked about their days as the other members filed in. Over the last year, people had come and gone, but Kara was secretly still glad that Lena was still attending, even though they both knew they were only showing up for each other and didn’t find it very helpful. Their drives home and drinks afterwards were far more honest and therapeutic than spilling their guts to strangers in a circle of a dingy YMCA.

     

                They’d chosen Lena’s apartment that night and when they entered her home Kara was struck by the smell of her perfume, lingering smoky and sweet, a visceral reaction sweeping over her as she paused in the doorway, brow puckering. Slowly removing her jacket, Kara hung it up on the rack and her clouded expression brightened at the scrabbling of claws as the little dog greeted her, tail wagging at hyper-speed, and she crouched down.

     

                “Aristotle! Hello, sweet boy,” she softly exclaimed, scratching him beneath the chin and laughing as he tried to lick her cheek.

     

                Lena watched her and let out a soft laugh, shaking her head, before she shed her coat and continued into her apartment. Rising to her feet, Kara followed after her, the dog jumping up at her for more attention as she cooed and ducked down every few feet until he was satisfied enough to trot after her.

     

                Lena pulled a bottle off a shelf and held it up with raised eyebrows and Kara didn’t bother to read the label as she nodded, letting Lena pour them both doubles in polished glasses.
