It was bourbon, syrupy and golden as they sipped it on the sofa, Aristotle’s head in Kara’s lap as she tried to explain her feelings towards Mike.

     

                “In hindsight, I can see that … he gave me very little and I … I tried to build a whole future out of it,” she said with a strained laugh, old pain resurfacing in her chest as her face furrowed with confusion.

     

                “Why did you stay? I mean …”

     

                “I guess after everything growing up I just thought … it’s better to love someone than no one , isn’t it?”

     

                Wrinkling her nose, Lena gave her a tight smile, her eyelids shuttering as she nodded. “Speaking as someone who didn’t have anyone to love until her … yeah. Yeah, it was a hell of a lot better. But I still stand by my earlier statement that it’s bullshit to think it’s better to have loved and lost than never loved at all. I would’ve been … fine by myself. It was all I’d ever known until her so I would’ve been okay. ”

     

                “I just wish things had been … better. I’m not sure if it’s a blessing or a curse now to have had a marriage on the rocks before he died. It’s just confusing losing someone that I have so many conflicted feelings about. I loved him and maybe I would’ve tried to make it work a while longer but I think I knew even before I married him that he wasn’t the great love of my life, you know? That never seemed important to me after everything with my parents and all of that. I was just happy to have something stable but now I think I would’ve been fine by myself too because I’ve realised a lot about myself since he died and … I don’t know if I’d want to go back to how it was before. Not- I don’t mean I wouldn’t bring him back if I could, just … I probably would’ve left. Eventually.”

     

                “You’re allowed to miss someone without wanting them back, like as your husband, or … be over them or moving on with your life. There’s nothing wrong with that.”

     

                “I know,” Kara wearily replied, a brooding look of confusion on her face as she took a sip of bourbon, letting it warm her through. “It’s just … he was such a big part of my life and I feel like I owe him some retroactive grace at least. He wasn’t perfect but … well, thinking unkindly of him now just seems like a shitty thing to do. I loved him. I loved him but I don’t- I don’t think that was enough.”

     

                “I’m sorry.”

     

                Bewilderment amusement crumpled Kara’s face as she smiled crookedly. “What are you apologising for?”

     

                Lena softly snorted, running a hand over her face. “I just can’t imagine how confusing it must all be for you. On top of an already fucking awful situation. You don’t deserve that.”

     

                “People rarely get what they deserve. And honestly, I don’t pity myself because … there are a lot of people who have it worse. And I think really I’m in the same boat as everyone else who’s lost someone. You and I … I don’t think there’s much difference between how we feel, only how it happened and how our marriage was. At the root of it all, grief is the same for everyone. There are just different levels to it, right?”

     

                “And what level are you at?”

     

                “I don’t know. Not the bottom anymore, I think. At least I’m … processing things now. Or I’ve gotten used to his absence to not expect things, which is almost the same thing. And you?”

     

                Mouth opening, Lena inhaled sharply and then shut her mouth as her brow furrowed. She made a disconcerting sound and then sipped her drink before trying again.

     

                “I guess the same. It just … even though I don’t expect things anymore, sometimes it still catches me. How do you spend a year without living with someone and still expect them to walk through the door or call from the next room?”

     

                Kara hummed in agreement and turned her glass in her fingers as silence descended between them for a moment. Huffing, Lena shook her head and smiled wanly.

     

                “No offence, but God I feel so lonely,” Lena said as she ran a hand over her face.

     

                “I’m not offended,” Kara said with a fleeting smile. “I know better than most that friends can’t fill that hole for long. When you’re alone again … it just comes back.”

     

                Deflating as her shoulders dropped, Lena gave her an aching look of understanding, which quickly turned sheepish with embarrassment as she fiddled with her glass. “I keep opening the window to hear the sounds of the city, so I can pretend that I have people near me. I know … I’ll be alright but I just- I miss the sound of her using the coffee machine in the morning, her speaking Spanish to the dog, her hogging the shower. The house is just empty . It’s so quiet. And I miss being kissed . I know it sounds pathetic but … God, I would kill to just feel wanted again.”

     

                “Yeah,” Kara agreed, heavily sighing. “I’ve been thinking about dating again. Well, Alex keeps suggesting it. Maybe not- not dating , exactly, but … I don’t know, maybe sleeping with someone else will help me get past some of it, you know? At some point … I’m going to have to-”

     

                “You don’t have to do anything,” Lena gently reminded her and Kara gave her an uneven smile.

     

                Raking a hand through her hair, Kara let out a small laugh, “I know. I don’t think I’d be able to. Not with some random person. But then … it’ll just be complicated with anyone I know even half well enough to sleep with.”

     

                “I think about it when I’m lonely, but then I just feel guilty for even thinking about it. Like I’m betraying her, even though she- she’s not coming back. So what am I supposed to do? Be stuck on her forever? Waste my life because she- it’s just … complicated. They don’t tell you how complicated it’s going to be. I wish it was cleaner, like a break up, something that you can get over quick enough if you’re determined. I don’t think sleeping my way through half of National City will have quite the same effect as it does fixing a broken heart.”

     

                They were silent for a moment and then Kara heavily sighed, her glass halfway to her lips before she hesitated, lowering it a fraction. “What are we supposed to do now?”

     

                Shrugging as she smiled bitterly, Lena leaned her head into the back of the sofa and closed her eyes. “I don’t know. Just keep going, I suppose.”

     

                “Can I ask you something personal?”

     

                “Sure.”

     

                “Do you … regret not having kids? Like now . Like … do you think it would’ve been easier to have a kid, someone to make you have your shit together. You know, give you a purpose or something, instead of just being stuck.”

     

                Brow furrowing, Lena considered it for a moment and slowly replied. “No, I don’t regret it. I think I would’ve regretted it more having them, putting them through all of this. And I’m glad that I didn’t have other people relying on me because it’s given me the space to fall apart without anyone expecting anything from me. I guess … my purpose is my company. If I didn’t have that to focus all of my attention on … it’d be a lot harder.”

     

                Making a small sound of understanding, Kara nodded, “I guess that’s true. Maybe if I had more responsibility at work, I’d feel a stronger urge to … I don’t know, show up more.” Letting out a hollow laugh, Kara raked a hand through her hair. “Instead, I feel like I’m just existing. I have nothing tying me down and … I think if it wasn’t for my sister I could easily just pack up and leave. But I don’t think moving somewhere else would fix things either.”

     

                “I’d miss you if you left,” Lena confessed.

     

                A soft smile curled Kara’s mouth and she took a sip of her drink. “Yeah?”

     

                “Mm, no one ever tells you how lonely your thirties are when you’re alone. Not that I had much of a social life before but everyone else is focused on getting married and having kids. And I already got married and now I’m just … here. And you might be the only person I know who’s in the same position.”

     

                “Ah, well, I couldn’t leave anyway. You’re stuck with me,” Kara joked with a quick smile. 

     

                “Good.”

     

                They finished their drinks and then had another one before Kara decided it was time to leave. She would’ve been content to sit there all night with Lena, drinking scotch and talking through the long hours of their loneliness, but she didn’t want to outstay her welcome. Gathering up her things, she walked to the door and slipped on her jacket as Lena hovered nearby.

     

                “Goodnight,” Kara said, slinging her bag over her shoulder and turning to give Lena a hug and a kiss on the cheek, only for Lena to be midway through the same motion.

     

                Their kisses landed on the corners of each other’s mouths, not so much a kiss but a clumsy placement of their lips, and they both jerked back, blinking in surprise and nervously laughing. Kara felt her face flush red and Lena mumbled an apology and then Kara left quickly, trying to quell the uneasy warmth in her stomach that verged on horror at the thought of kissing Lena, but shockingly, suddenly verged on the searing, prickling urge to kiss Lena. Not just a slight graze of the corner of her mouth but a proper kiss, the kind of kiss that would have her pressed up against the wall, leave their lips ever so slightly swollen and leave her wanting more.

     

                The thought sprung to mind so suddenly that Kara didn’t know how to react, her mouth opening and closing as she looked down, adjusting the strap of her bag on her shoulder.

     

                “Sorry,” she managed to force out.

     

                Lena gave her a strained smile, “my mistake. Um … you’ll let me know when you’re home?”

     

                “Sure, I’ll text you.”

     

                “Good.”

     

                Nodding, Kara lingered a moment and then cleared her throat, reaching for the door handle. “Have a good night.”

     

                “You too.”

     

                She rode the bus home, confusion keeping her company as her teeth worried at the corner of her bottom lip. It had been accidental but the faintest graze of a kiss haunted Kara for the next couple of days. When she called Lena on Monday and asked if she wanted to meet her at the strip of food trucks on a closed-off road for dinner, they didn’t mention it as they shared nachos, bao buns and churros as they went from vendor to vendor. 

     

                It was a relief that things were normal, that they could talk about their feelings and work and what they were stuck on without any awkwardness of the almost kiss that she didn’t think either of them was ready for. Or maybe she was and that’s why her whole body had reacted in such a way, but it couldn’t be Lena that she felt that way for. Not that she’d even considered thinking about her in any way other than as a friend for emotional support.

     

                They had group on Thursday and Kara invited her to drinks on Friday and things felt normal again but there was an underlying tension in Kara that she wasn’t sure was inside her head or not. She couldn’t be sure if Lena felt it too or not, if she was thinking about nothing too much, if the almost kiss had affected her far more than her friend. One-sided tension would’ve been worse than if it had been mutual because at least then she wouldn’t have felt so weird about it but Kara wasn’t sure, and as the weeks went by she finally allowed herself to relax, to shrug off any expectations of things getting messy between them because of the ramifications of a clumsy accident.

     

                Of course, she let her guard down too soon, let the tension evaporate on her end while not knowing it had eaten Lena up in a similar way. It was weeks before it all came to a head and Kara was surprised by the sudden realisation that she had had a reason to panic, to tread carefully. They’d been out for Friday night drinks again with all of her friends and her sister, one too many tequila slammers after several rounds of beer and karaoke leaving Kara quiet and tired in their booth. 

     

                When Lena whispered she was leaving, Kara leapt at the opportunity to go as well, feeling more subdued than rowdy. She hadn’t even sung by herself and had to be dragged up to the little stage for a group Spice Girls performance with all the girls. Excusing herself as she slipped out of the booth, she kissed Alex’s cheek and said goodnight before following Lena outside.

     

                “We can share the ride,” Kara suggested, “to yours first.”

     

                Lena didn’t object and gave the driver her address as they buckled themselves in, slumping against the seats as they pulled out into traffic. Rubbing her forehead, Kara stared at the starburst headlights and neon signs, her attention fixated on the city as her mind wandered, yet a part of her was aware of Lena’s eyes on her. She didn’t look though, but a furrowed v formed between her eyebrows as she questioned what was going on.

     

                “Here,” Lena whispered to her as they started to pull up in front of her apartment. “For the cab.”

     

                “No, it’s fine,” Kara insisted. 

     

                “No, really, take it.”

     

                Hesitating, Kara pressed her lips into a flat line and unbuckled her seatbelt. “Pay the driver. I’ll see you inside first.”

     

                “You don’t have to do that.”

     

                She was already opening the car door as they came to a halt, ducking out into the night and holding the door for Lena as she followed her out. Hands in the pockets of her coat, Kara escorted her into the lobby and up to her apartment, some odd tension sparking between them in the elevator as they shared sideward glances that left her mouth dry and her expression clouded with confusion.

     

                “Well, goodnight,” Kara murmured as they stopped outside Lena’s apartment.

     

                Nodding, Lena managed to get her door open and stepped inside, holding the handle as she turned.

     

                “Come inside,” Lena whispered, coaxing the door open wider and cocking her head to the side.

     

                “I shouldn’t,” Kara managed to get out, her heart hammering in her chest with the knowledge of what happened next.

     

                She could stop it. She could stop them from making this terrible mistake, which wouldn’t feel terrible right now but would mortify them in the morning. In a few ways, they were all the other one had to lean on, the only ones who understood and whose grief was current enough to feel so similar. If things got out of hand, they could lose that so easily and Kara was uncertain about risking it.

     

                Lena could sense that too, had the same wariness behind the glassy look of too much to drink. “But you could .”

     

                “Yes,” Kara agreed.

     

                They hesitated a moment, staring at each other, the tension palpable and begging for release, until Kara took a slow, measured step over the threshold and Lena stepped aside to let her in. Shutting the door behind her, Kara hung up her coat and kicked off her boots, arranging them neatly by the door. Aristotle was curled up on the sofa and reared his head, tail wagging as he remained curled up, tired and quiet after being woken.

     

                Removing her heels, Lena carelessly tossed them aside and grinned over her shoulder as she walked through the apartment. “Have a drink with me.”

     

                It was more of a demand than a request and Kara nodded, following after her as the world seemed to stretch and pitch, a muffled haze to it all. She’d probably already had enough to drink - too much if she was inside Lena’s apartment right now - but one more couldn’t hurt and one more would bolster her wariness a little.

     

                “Just one.”

     

                Lena didn’t give her any options, just pulled her favourite whisky from the shelf and poured them both doubles. Kara sat beside the dog and smoothed her fingers over his fur and sipped her drink as Lena sat at the opposite end, her green eyes glittering in the dim lighting of the room, watchful and tense.

     

                “Did you have fun?” Kara asked.

     

                “I did. You?”

     

                “Mhm. I’ll probably regret it in the morning. Drinking so much.”

     

                “Probably,” Lena conceded and Kara was sure she wasn’t talking about a hangover.

     

                Taking another sip and rolling it around her mouth, Kara shifted and then cleared her throat. “What are you doing tomorrow?”

     

                Deliberating as she hummed, head tilted to the side and eyes rising to the ceiling, Lena’s mouth thinned. Her eyes lowered to meet Kara’s and she hesitated before responding. “I think … I’m going to be busy tomorrow.”

     

                “Okay.”

     

                She finished her drink off, the taste of it spreading through her, warm and honeyed, and she cleared her throat as she leaned forward, setting the glass on the coffee table. Climbing unsteadily to her feet, Kara nudged her glasses up as she rubbed the bridge of her nose, and then removed them, her vision blurring everything as she safely stowed them in her pocket.

     

                “I should get going then. Let you get some sleep for tomorrow.”

     

                “It’s already tomorrow. No point rushing,” Lena said with a thin smile, cradling her glass.

     

                “Ah, well, even more reason for you to sleep, right?”

     

                “I don’t like sleeping anymore,” Lena confessed before draining her glass and setting it down at the opposite end to Kara’s.

     

                Not knowing how to respond to that, although she knew the line Lena was waiting for, like a play she hadn’t memorised her lines for. Running a hand over her face, Kara decisively moved towards the door, the weighted air between them too unbearable to linger in. They were both in different stages of their grief and any mistakes would no doubt throw the semblance of normalcy they’d cobbled together into disarray. Neither of them needed any added trouble on top of the mountains they were already wading through.

     

                Still, Lena followed after her and Kara had her coat halfway on, still shoeless, and stared at Lena as she shoved her other arm through the sleeve. Hands clasped behind her back, Lena rocked on the heels of her feet, restless as she wrestled with herself until she rocked forward and let the motion carry her a step forward. A step towards Kara, the gap between them shrinking in the hallway.

     

                Shrugging her coat on, blonde hair tucked beneath the collar, Kara’s mouth went dry and she shifted closer to Lena, without even consciously deciding to move. She was a few inches taller than her and could see the blurry mascara on her lashes, the smudge of her mouth with the remainder of her lipstick, and the small scar beneath her eyebrow. Kara could smell her perfume and the whisky on her breath and it was heady enough to make her stomach clench, a sensation she hadn’t felt in a long time that left her unbalanced.

     

                “Say no,” Lena murmured, reaching up to untuck Kara’s hair from the collar of her coat and running her fingers down her sleeve afterwards.

     

                Leaning in slightly, Kara hesitated, the tip of her nose brushing Lena’s cheek as her lips parted. She didn’t kiss her though, just left the answer to her question up to Lena. She didn’t want to say no, no matter how much she would come to regret it, so she gave Lena the chance to say it instead.

     

                But she didn’t. Closing the gap between them with as much caution as Kara, the feeling that they were playing a game of chicken creeping up on them, urging the other one to say no or do it so they could avoid any blame, Lena’s lips brushed against Kara’s in a soft graze. A quiet sound escaped Kara, embarrassing in its blatant neediness as her cheeks flushed red. It was all the incentive Lena needed though, kissing her again with more purpose this time, her hand coming up to cup the back of Kara’s head as she crushed their lips together.

     

                It was clumsy and urgent, like two high schoolers at a house party instead of two widows trying to make headway in moving on, but they were drunk and that was enough cover for them to be careless and messy. Holding her tightly wherever she could, Kara kissed her back with just as much need, somewhat nervous and fumbling, over a year since she’d found herself in this predicament, a decade since it was with a woman.

     

                A prickling heat crept over her and Kara broke it off, her hands finding Lena’s shoulders, her chest rising and falling quickly as she gave her a searching gaze. “Lena-”

     

                “Don’t.”

     

                “Let’s have another drink,” Kara said instead, her voice shaky and hitching as she pressed the back of her hand to her forehead, trying to blink through the haze of alcohol to find a reason why they shouldn’t.

     

                There were plenty of them, but another drink would thicken the fog in her mind and blur her inhibitions. Lena considered her suggestion and nodded before jerking her chin at her in a haughty manner.

     

                “Take your coat off.”

     

                Obliging, Kara shed it and missed the hook, letting it crumple to the floor as she moved in a dream, unsteady on her feet and her eyes trained on Lena’s retreating figure, barely more than a slip of a shadow moving through the dim apartment.

     

                Lena smashed a glass in the kitchen as she fetched new ones for them, her laughter stuttering as she stared at Kara with surprised eyes, sloshing whisky into another one and knocking hers back quickly. Kara drained hers almost as fast and took the bottle from her, adding another two fingers to her glass and filling Lena’s as well, blue eyes watchful and intense, their fingers brushing and that pull in her stomach again that made her sip her whisky slowly before she pulled Lena forward and kissed her hard.

     

                Teeth scraped over her bottom lip and Kara made a sound at the back of her throat, lifting Lena onto the countertop, her hands slipping up the back of her shirt as she untucked it, running over soft, warm skin and the feeling of her ribs and spine underneath. Lena had a hand in her hair, guiding her head to the side so she could kiss a path along Kara’s jaw and down her throat, a gentle bite eliciting a surprised laugh from Kara.

     

                Her mouth was hot on her skin and Kara’s breath hitched as she closed her eyes, drunk and light-headed and swaying in between Lena’s legs bracketing her. She had to brace herself against the edge of the counter, holding herself steady as she fumbled to grasp Lena’s chin in her hand, bringing her mouth back to hers and kissing her deeply. Lena’s hands slid over the soft-washed cotton of Kara’s t-shirt and she pulled up the hem, until it was halfway up Kara’s stomach and she helped it the rest of the way off. 

     

                Getting frustrated with Lena’s buttons, Kara ripped it open and slurred an apology as she stumbled backwards with the force of it, her back hitting the island counter as she blinked rapidly to steady the room. Lena slipped off the counter, staggering as her feet hit the floor, and Kara reached out to balance her, pulling her in, their faces so close she could feel Lena’s breath on her cheek.

     

                Her eyes strayed to the bottle and she leaned past Lena and snagged it, drinking straight from it until she thought she might be sick. Passing it off to Lena, Kara hunched her shoulders, hand pressed to her mouth and then looked up at her. Lena had her lips around the mouth of the bottle, her head thrown back and the pale column of her throat moving as she swallowed. Kara crossed the space between them, one hand cradling Lena’s waist and the other cupping the back of her neck as she kissed a trail down to her exposed collarbones.

     

                Pressing Lena up against the counters again, her hands slid up the bare skin of her thighs, beneath her skirt and Kara paused as Lena took another drink. Stepping back, she turned around and paced a few steps away, tipping her head back and pinching the bridge of her nose as she tried to unscramble her thoughts. And then Lena was behind her, softly kissing her shoulder and mumbling some vague assurance as she reached her arms around Kara and unbuttoned her jeans.

     

                She lost almost the rest of her clothes there, before they somehow wound up in the bedroom, things growing patchy and fuzzy as her mind tried to keep up. They were in Lena’s bed then, Kara sitting on the edge of the bed, Lena struggling her way out of her pencil skirt and the lacy underwear that Kara was too drunk to appreciate. She was bracing herself above Lena, one knee between her legs, Lena holding a fistful of her hair back to stop it from tickling her cheeks as she arched herself up to kiss Kara.

     

                “You’ve done this before?” Lena breathlessly asked, confusion clouding her voice.

     

                “Yeah.”

     

                “You like women?”

     

                “Yes,” Kara replied somewhat impatiently, her fingers digging into Lena’s thighs, a puckered look of annoyance on her face as she tried to understand why Lena was asking her that.

     

                She was too far gone to ask though and knew she wouldn’t remember much in the morning. It was blissful in a way, the relief cutting keenly through her as she kissed and touched and knew wouldn’t remember enough of it to feel too badly about the consequences. 

     

                But in the morning, she remembered enough , blearily blinking herself awake to a sun-filled room that was not her own, expensive sheets covering bare skin and the stale taste of whisky in her mouth. Pushing herself up, skin prickling with sweat and a headache behind her eyes as her hangover made itself known, Kara’s stomach lurched with dread.

     

                Scrambling out of bed, she managed to find her underwear and nothing else, crossing an arm over her chest as she slipped out of the bedroom and paused in the kitchen. Glass sparkled on the floor and her clothes were scattered about as Lena sat stiffly at the table near the window.

     

                At Kara’s sudden appearance, she looked at her and Kara couldn’t see how red her eyes were from crying. She could hear it though, in the scratchiness of her voice when she broke the tense silence.

     

                “Morning.”

     

                “I- morning. We, uh, we … what did we …?”

     

                Lena was silent and Kara searched around for her clothes, pulling on her jeans, finding her t-shirt before her bra and pulling it on, pocketing the latter when she came across it and finding one of her socks. She found her glasses in her other pocket and shoved them on her clammy face, blinking at the dishevelled look of Lena sitting in a robe with a glass of whisky in hand and the telltale splotches of tears on her pale face.

     

                She couldn’t remember much of the night before: too many drinks; a cab ride to Lena’s; more drinks; lips on her throat; bedsheets; limbs. Had there been tears? Kara was seized by panic and her fingers touched the spot where she remembered Lena’s mouth had been, although she thought they must have been in plenty of other places too.

     

                “I, uh, are you … okay?” she awkwardly asked.

     

                Making a noncommittal sound at the back of her throat, Lena raised her glass to her lips and sipped. There was the wide-eyed look of someone who couldn’t believe what they’d done, guilt and regret and horror written on her face. Under different circumstances, Kara would’ve thought it was the look of someone who’d woken up to find they’d had a drunken affair, but instead, she was confronted with the worse alternative of a widow who’d fucked someone else and was feeling the same sickening shame that was creeping up on her now. It almost felt like a betrayal in a way, that she could do that with someone else after losing him.

     

                “I should go,” she managed to say.

     

                Lena didn’t respond, just cupped her forehead in her palm, shoulders hunched, and Kara made her way through the apartment, bypassing Aristotle, who had her other sock, to put her shoes on and grab her coat. Panic made her chest feel tight as she rode the elevator down to the lobby, the cool city air a welcome caress against her flushed skin, and she set a rapid pace as she walked away from Lena’s apartment, far enough away to allow the panic to fully creep in.

     

                She felt awful, alcohol writhing in her stomach, exhaustion leaving her shoulders sagging, guilt making her breaths come quicker. Nausea blossomed in her gut and Kara had to grip the sides of a trash can on the sidewalk, heaving into it as pedestrians made sounds of disgust and cursed her out. Grey-faced and sweating beneath her coat, Kara waved off the concern of an older woman offering a half-drunk bottle of water and waited at the next bus stop for the one that would take her across the city to her apartment.

     

                The duration of the bus ride made her feel queasy and Kara had her fingers knotted in her coat as she fought off wave after wave of dread, guilt, mortification, worry and a dozen other emotions. And she hated to admit it to herself, but not all of them were negative. Beneath the blanketing feeling of wrong , there was a prickle of honesty that reminded her that she’d wanted Lena, even if it had taken her a few extra drinks to take that step. Kara had known what would happen if she stayed, and she’d chosen to despite that. That didn’t make it any less embarrassing for her to wake up to the reality of the aftermath and maybe she’d been rash and hadn’t thought through the consequences, but it was too late for that now.

     

                Back in her apartment, she peeled off her clothes and was sick again in the toilet before having a cold shower and taking some pills before collapsing into bed. She slept until after lunch and woke to the oppressive warmth of her room, which only made her feel worse. Sweaty and flushed, Kara turned on the standing fan, which only served to move around warm air, and then opened as many windows in the apartment as she could before pouring a glass of water and draining it quickly.

     

                Craving something greasy, she went to a nearby diner by herself and ordered bad coffee and scrambled eggs that came in a congealed pile on her plate. Grey-faced and limp, she forced herself to eat and then walked back home, feeling exactly the same as before, and then suddenly even more nauseous as her phone started ringing around the corner of her apartment and Alex’s name flashed on the screen.

     

                “Hello?”

     

                “Hey, where are you?”

     

                Rounding the corner, Kara stopped in the middle of the sidewalk as she caught sight of her sister standing outside her front door, neck craned back as she looked up at the open window. 

     

                “I was just getting something for lunch. I’m- I’m almost home. I can see you.”

     

                Alex looked around and then spotted Kara, who raised a hand in a half-hearted wave. Her sister hung up and Kara let out a weary sigh as she pocketed her phone and walked the rest of the way home. Fishing out her keys, Kara unlocked the door, mumbling a greeting and plodding upstairs to let them into her apartment.

     

                Shedding her coat, she wiped her shiny forehead on the sleeve of her shirt and collapsed onto the sofa. Alex shut the door and looked at her for a moment before letting out a quick laugh.

     

                “You look like shit.”

     

                “Feel like it too,” Kara rasped.

     

                “You didn’t look too far gone when you left.”

     

                “Oh, uh, yeah, I had a couple more after.”

     

                Closing her eyes, head tipped back against the sofa, Kara drew in shallow breaths and used her feet to kick off her shoes. They clattered to the floor and she could hear Alex taking off her jacket, collapsing onto the sofa and putting her feet up on the coffee table.

     

                “Oh my God,” Alex exclaimed, amused and a little condescending as the words rose and fell in pitch. “Is that a hickey? Who have you been screwing?”

     

                Kara’s eyelashes fluttered and her hand leapt to her neck, covering the stretch of skin there as she tried to remember seeing it in the mirror earlier. She hadn’t been paying much attention to her reflection, the waxy sheen to her skin, the dark circles beneath her eyes and the bloodshot look of exhaustion.

     

                Red crept into Kara’s cheeks and she turned her head aside, teeth worrying at her chapped bottom lip. “No one, I-”

     

                “Clearly someone. I thought you were still thinking about it.”

     

                “Well, I didn’t realise I had to keep you so involved in my sex life,” Kara wearily countered.

     

                Rolling her eyes, Alex turned on the sofa, her back braced against the arm and knees bent. She reached out and nudged Kara, who swatted her foot aside, feeling too old for them to be behaving like they were in high school again, intent on annoying each other to death. Tipping her head back again, Kara let out a heavy sigh, her body sagging against the sofa.

     

                “Wait, that wasn’t there last night ,” Alex deduced, and then groaned loudly, “please don’t tell me you screwed Lena.”

     

                “What?” Kara blurted out, “why would you say that?”

     

                “You left with her.”

     

                “Yeah, that doesn’t mean I went home with her, does it?” Kara countered, pointing out the hole in Alex’s assumption, which was a valid point but had definitely not been the case last night. “She’s a- a friend. I wouldn’t want to risk that by doing something stupid.”

     

                Not a lie either. It didn’t mean she hadn’t risked it though and Kara was agitated as she shifted on the sofa, hot and tired and uncomfortable. Rubbing her forehead, she stared at the blank TV and felt her stomach twist itself into knots.

     

                “Probably a smart choice. She’s nice but that’s a whole lot of damage you don’t want to deal with, no matter how much she looks like she should be on the cover of Vogue,” Alex agreed, although Kara already knew well enough about her opinion of her getting involved with another widow. “So … who then?”

     

                “Just some guy on Tinder,” Kara lied, a blatant one this time, slipping out easily without any feelings of guilt.

     

                Kara wondered if it was because she was already riddled with guilt because of Lena, but she didn’t feel bad lying to Alex just this once. It did make her sheepish as Alex so readily believed her, having no reason not to. It was just easier to pretend it had been a stranger she’d never have to see again. 

     

                “Oh. Oh, well that’s … that’s really good!” Alex softly encouraged her, giving her a supportive pat on the knee.

     

                Masking a wince, Kara made a faint sound of agreement at the back of her throat and wondered just how good it was. She didn’t regret it, that much she knew, and she didn’t feel as bad as she’d thought, the guilt of betrayal not nearly large enough to overwhelm her other feelings, but it was more like the old college memories of embarrassment from a one night stand where you really didn’t want to see the other person again. Except it was Lena, and Kara did want to see her again. And therein was the real problem.

     

                “Kelly said that it was one of the biggest hurdles when her fiancée died, but she said afterwards it made a lot of things easier. It’s good that you’re dating.”

     

                “I’m not dating,” Kara said, growing irate as she ran a hand over her face. “It was … stupid. A mistake. I rushed things and … I just think I need more time to process things before I- and it’s fine. I don’t need to date anyone. I think … I think it’ll be good for me to have some time alone. To know what kind of person I am now.”

                

                “Oh. Okay, yeah, that’s good too. Better to take it slow to make sure you’re ready. You wouldn’t want to make a mess of things by rushing in.”

     

                “Yeah,” Kara managed to choke out. “Yeah, I wouldn’t want to do that.”

    Chapter 9

                Kara didn’t see Lena for the next few days and was relieved she didn’t have to dodge any texts or calls, but wondered if maybe she should reach out instead. She called in sick to work twice, even though she couldn’t really afford to, and anxiously paced back and forth in her apartment like a caged lion, existing on leftover pizza and Big Belly Burger as she worried over the horrifying mistake of sleeping with her closest friend. Would it even have been right to call Lena that? Kara had plenty of friends and her close-knit circle as well, but she’d spent the better part of a year ignoring them until Lena had helped coax her back out of her shell after taking the place that Winn and James had previously occupied.

     

                On Thursday, she almost considered bailing on Group, but that felt unnecessarily dramatic so after she finished work for the day she packed up her things and made her way to the Y for her usual routine of tea, glazed donut and a long hour of listening to other people vent their grief and sadness to the room. Usually, it was bearable with Lena beside her, that shared amusement palpable between them as they shunned the purpose but came for the act of doing something.

     

                When Lena wasn’t there on time, her tea and donut that Kara had fetched for her waiting at the seat beside her, Kara’s stomach sank. She’d hoped that they would both be able to coexist in the same place without it being too awful. But then a few minutes after their session had started, the rusty hinges squeaked open and the smell of Lena’s perfume hit her first, a gut punch of familiarity that made Kara fight back a flush as she remembered her face buried into the side of Lena’s neck. 

     

                Picking up her donut, Lena sank onto her seat without a word, her tea cooling on the floor beside her and a steadfast focus on the teary-eyed man currently speaking as Kara cast sideways glances at her. She subconsciously angled her body towards her friend, an anxious curve to her shoulders, but it may as well have been as if she wasn’t there as Lena shifted every so often, trying to stifle her restlessness as she reached down for her paper cup of tea, took a bite of her donut, brushed her hair off her shoulder. Each movement stirred the smell of her perfume, assaulting Kara, whose body tightened as she clutched her cup tight enough to crumple it.

     

                She found it hard to concentrate but eventually, it was her turn and she cleared her throat, feeling self-conscious as all eyes trained on her, including Lena’s. Mouth opening and closing, Kara rubbed the back of her neck and stared at the worn patch of carpet in the middle of the circle, finding it easier to talk to the floor as she scrambled for something to talk about. Group was never helpful but at least she could always be honest there, skirting around the uncomfortable truth to a room full of people she didn’t particularly care about and didn’t feel embarrassed about speaking about her grief to.

     

                “I, uh, my sister has been trying to convince me to get back into dating. I wasn’t really sure it was time yet, even though I know it’s been over a year now but, uh, I was with a friend the other day and … things got out of hand. I think it just made it more complicated because it was someone I knew, and I think … maybe it would’ve been easier if it was a stranger, but also my grief- it’s such a big part of my life that I think I need someone who understands.”

     

                The words felt clumsy and awkward in Kara’s mouth as she tried to articulate how she felt, highly conscious of Lena’s rigid posture in the chair beside her. She didn’t react, didn’t say a word or touch her arm in a fleeting moment of comfort. Kara felt compelled to say more as a moment of heavy silence blanketed the room.

     

                “It’s not like we’re dating or anything but … I’m just worried that it’s- I’ve gotten used to having them around and I guess I’m just scared that they’ll leave. I’ll be left all alone again. I could just … really use a friend.”

     

                “We’re all here to support you,” Thomas said, nodding encouragingly as his gaze swept around the assembled group, trying to coax affirmations out of the other members.

     

                Kara wanted to laugh. There was only one person in the group who she needed support from and it was the one person she’d potentially fucked things up with in the worst possible way. Swallowing the bubble of laughter that rose in her throat, Kara let out a quiet strangled sound and nudged her glasses up her nose.

     

                “Yeah, well, I guess I just didn’t want to lose the support from that person. I think … it’ll be a while before things could go back to normal - if at all - so … I don’t know when I’ll see them again. I think it would just be for the best if we had space because I know it’ll complicate things a lot for them. I guess I’ve just lost a lot of people before and they mean a lot to me so I’d … I’d hate to lose them too.”

     

                She gave up the rest of her time after that, fiddling restlessly as she didn’t give much of a response to Thomas’s coaxing until he eventually moved on. Lena refused the offer to speak that week, sitting silently for the duration of the hour and then rising with everyone else. Normally Kara would’ve hung around to help stack the chairs but she was almost the first one out of there, others lingering behind to socialise and have another cup of coffee.

     

                Cool air hit her face and some of the tightness in her chest lessened and she almost thought she’d gotten away until she heard the click of heels rapidly approaching and knew that she hadn’t quite been quick enough.

     

                “Kara.”

     

                She slowed down at the sound of her name but didn’t turn around, her running shoes crunching gravel and broken glass as she crossed the parking lot. Hitching her bag higher on her shoulder, she swallowed thickly.

     

                “I, uh, I can’t stop,” Kara said, pretending to glance down at her watch, which was unreadable in the dark. “I need to go.”

     

                “Will you just stop a second,” Lena sighed, defeated and faintly pleading. “Let me give you a lift and we can talk a bit.”

     

                “It’s okay, I’ll catch the bus.”

     

                “It doesn’t have to be like this.”

     

                Coming to a final stop, Kara hesitated and then turned around. Her mouth was a grim line and she gripped the straps of her backpack tightly.

     

                “I know, I just- I think we should both take some time to process it. I know it’s- it’s different for you. I think you regret it a lot more than I do, so … I just want to give you some space to sort it all out.”

     

                “Don’t you think talking about it will help?” Lena asked with a short, confused laugh.

     

                Teeth worrying at her bottom lip, Kara cast her gaze aside, unable to look at Lena as she shrugged helplessly. “I don’t know. Maybe, but not yet. I think … you should take some time to think first. I mean … you were crying so … it upset you a lot. And I get it and I’m not trying to be an asshole, I just want you to be okay first before we dredge it all back up.”

     

                “Right,” Lena flatly replied, her expression clouded with annoyance as she gave Kara a flinty stare, her haughtiness unfamiliar and surprising to Kara.

     

                Faltering, the breath escaped Kara and she wilted slightly beneath her sheepish guilt, reaching out to grip Lena’s arm in a fleeting gesture of reassurance. “I’ll see you at the next session.”

     

                There were no mentions of walking Aristotle, dinner after work, or drinks tomorrow night. Nothing. Normally their weeks were filled with each other, enjoying the company of someone who understood without having to be told but Kara’s skittish mention of their next session was a clear message that she wouldn’t see Lena again before then.

     

                Lena didn’t reply as she abruptly turned and walked off to her car, tense and back straight as she yanked open the door and vanished inside, the loud slam a little too pointed for Kara to think it had been accidental. Deflating, Kara watched as the brake lights flared red in the dark as the engine came to life and Lena swiftly drove off. Listening to one of her Podcasts, Kara wearily plodded to the bus stop to find that she’d just missed hers. Everything piled up and she found her eyes stinging with angry tears as she waited in the dark, arms hugged to herself and the thought that life was particularly unfair at the moment.

     

                The bus eventually came and she rode it home with the quiet company of night and the droning tone of the meditation guide in her ears as she slumped in her seat at the back, tucked away in the shadows of darkness as she waited for her stop. Coming home to her empty apartment felt like a kick in the chest and the worst part was that she’d done it to herself. If she wasn’t so anxious about ruining things even more she could’ve gone out for a drink with Lena, pretended that nothing had happened as they drank cheap beer and laughed at their group session.

     

                Taking a can of beer that had been sitting there for more than a year, waiting for the next football game or poker night with the guys, Kara looked down at the label of the can and felt her confused feelings tie themselves into more knots. Running a thumb over the Coors script, her mouth thinned and she let out a weary sigh, cracking open the beer and taking a sip. She’d never really taken to Mike’s preferred beer but anything was better than being stone-cold sober, even a weak lager that tasted sour as she sat in her dark apartment by herself, still in her scrubs and her denim jacket and her worn running shoes that had been pissed on no less than three times that day.

     

                The rest of her week was no better and Kara holed herself up on the weekend again with a bottle of cheap wine and reruns of Golden Girls as she set her phone on silent and was grateful that her apartment door wasn’t accessible unless someone bypassed the door at street level. Alex would be annoyed at her on Monday but then wasn’t everyone already annoyed at her? Kara had a penchant for pissing people off regardless of what she did; too proud, too passive, too stubborn, too loud, too clumsy, too arrogant, too spineless. She’d never felt like she could win with Mike, had always been too much of one thing or another and then contradictory another time but at least having someone be annoyed at her was consistent. She just hated that Lena was one of them.

     

                A part of her hoped she’d receive a phone call sometime during the week, knowing that she was too cowardly to reach out herself, wanting to shirk any blame for what had happened by avoiding the fallout. Only, the fallout came for her whether she avoided it or confronted it, leaving her bored and lonely without the usual company of Lena. She had dinner with Alex and Kelly on Tuesday and drinks with James and William after work on Wednesday and still felt that hollow feeling of loneliness eating away at her even in the midst of her friends.

     

                It was almost a relief for Group on Thursday, the opportunity to see Lena again, to regain some semblance of normalcy. She got there early and helped set out the chairs, claiming her usual spot with her back to the door and then hanging around until it was close enough to their start time to make two cups of tea and claim two glazed donuts. She wondered if Lena would show up this time or if she’d finally had enough, ignored for almost two weeks now and ignored Kara in return.

     

                But she was there, earlier than last week, murmuring a thank you beneath the hum of conversation as everyone settled in or made their coffee. She took a sip of her tea and her green eyes scanned the room while Kara shifted on her chair, licking her lips as she tried to pluck up the courage to speak to her, feeling awkward as the last two weeks cast a pall over their usual ease. It was a self-inflicted awkwardness but she’d thought it would be easier to make the call herself than have Lena leave her hanging high and dry over what had happened.

     

                She didn’t manage to force anything out before Thomas took a seat amidst the circle of grievers and started the session. Kara tried to focus and managed to fumble out some vague explanation of how she was feeling and how the last week had been as she fiddled and tripped over her words and flushed at the feeling of so many eyes on her. It was a relief when she ran out of things to say and Thomas had to move on to someone else, but it was almost even more anxiety-inducing when he turned his attention to Lena.

     

                “Lena? Would you like to go next?”

     

                Curtly nodding, she was silent for a moment, slumping slightly in her chair as she folded her arms over her chest, legs crossed at the knee. Glancing sideways at her, Kara took in the furrowed look of concentration as she picked her words carefully.

     

                “I think this last week has been the loneliest I’ve felt since my wife …”

     

                “Why do you think that is?”

     

                “I guess I just- I was so fixated on her that I had this big hole left behind, and I filled it with someone else. And they weren’t around for the last week, and I knew they wouldn’t be, which was okay, but I guess it made me realise how dependent on them I’d become. But … that’s also made me feel … guilty? The thought of replacing her with someone new …”

     

                “It wouldn’t have to mean replacing,” Thomas said as she trailed off into silence. “You need to remember that no one will ever be able to replace our lost loved ones, but we should be open to accepting new people into our lives and hearts.”

     

                He pressed his hands over his chest, earnest and eager to lecture her on the way to process her grief. Lena resisted the urge to wrinkle her nose at the cheesy sentiment and just nodded instead. Kara’s cheek dimpled as she bit the inside of it, trying to hide her smile as she knew Lena’s thoughts. She knew them almost as well as her own within the walls of the old Y and it made her heart ache - just a little.

     

                “What if other people aren’t so accepting of having me in their life?” Lena asked, her voice small and almost childishly vulnerable.

     

                “Well … our grief can be a large elephant in the room for some people to welcome into their own personal lives but ultimately … the relationships that can withstand that, can help carry the weight of our losses, are the ones that will matter the most.”

     

                “And what if they’re just the ones that wreck us a little bit more? As if a loss wasn’t already enough to bear,” Lena countered, arching an eyebrow, her manner just a little bit haughty and her words pointedly aimed at Kara, even if the rest of the room didn’t know it.

     

                Shifting forward, fingers laced together and elbows propped up on her knees, Kara spoke softly, her voice gravelly. “Sometimes it’s not about them accepting you; you have to accept them too. Maybe they just don’t think you’re ready to move forward without her. Maybe they’re not trying to wreck you but are being gentle, carrying that weight with you until you’re ready to give it up.”

     

                Cocking her head to the side as she deliberated, Lena barely looked at her as she replied. “Maybe. But then maybe they should let me make my own mind up instead of making it for me.”

     

                There was a murmur of agreement from a few people and Kara straightened back up, inhaling deeply and opening her mouth to reply before she let it go. Exhaling softly, she just nodded and let Lena finish her turn. She didn’t have much to say after that but Kara could feel her bristling tension beside her. 

     

                Sitting silently beside each other for the remainder of the session, Kara made a swift exit and carried her trash with her as she barrelled out into the night. Dumping her trash in the can set off to the side of the steps, she paced back and forth, waiting for Lena to appear so she could talk to her. Leaving things to blow over was definitely out of the question with the way things were going, wounded feelings and unsaid things were left to fester and make it worse. Somehow, in just two weeks, it already felt worse than it had been the next morning, as if it had grown into something bigger than necessary.

     

                Kara lingered beside the steps, restless as her throat closed up and she wiped her clammy palms on the thighs of her scrub pants. When Lena wearily shouldered her way through the front door and walked down the steps, heels clicking on the concrete, Kara hurried to her side, anxious and meek.

     

                “Hey.”

     

                Lena arched an eyebrow at her, cool and aloof, “are you talking to me now?”

     

                “I wasn’t not talking to you,” Kara mumbled, fiddling with her fingers.

     

                Glancing sideways at her, the corner of her mouth twitching with a smile, Lena let out a weary sigh. “Yeah, well, you didn’t act like it.”

     

                “I’m sorry.”

     

                “I don’t want you to be sorry.”

     

                “I told you why, though.”

     

                Coming to a stop, Lena scoffed, facing Kara. In her heels, they were the same height, yet Kara felt smaller as she hunched her shoulders slightly, seeming to shrink in on herself as she looked down at the asphalt of the parking lot. 

     

                “That wasn’t a good enough excuse for me,” Lena replied, honest but not bitter. “Don’t you think I should’ve been able to choose if it was too much to be around you? You made me feel lonely again. It was shit.”

     

                Mouth opening and closing as her cheeks reddened, Kara felt that flicker of guilt flare up and shifted awkwardly on her feet. “I just- I wanted you to make sure you still wanted us to be friends.”

     

                “Well, I can’t really afford to lose the only person I have here,” Lena said with a small, strained laugh. “I would’ve told you that if you’d even given me the chance to speak before trying to get away from me as quickly as possible.”

     

                Closing her eyes, Kara swiped the pad of her thumb over her eyelids, humming disconcertingly. “Yeah, maybe. I just … well, I thought you’d say the opposite. And I didn’t want my feelings to get hurt. It, uh, it’s … I don’t know, I just think … I’d be lonely if you said you didn’t want to see me anymore.”

     

                Blowing the air out of her cheeks, head tipped back and hands on her hips, Lena was silent for a moment. Then she looked at Kara and fished her keys out of her coat pocket, jerking her head towards the parked car.

     

                “Come on. I’ll give you a ride.”

     

                Hesitating, Kara followed after her and slipped into the passenger seat, sinking against the cool leather with relief. Shutting the door, she buckled herself in and sat in the darkness of the interior as Lena likewise settled in behind the wheel. They both sat there for a prolonged moment of silence, neither of them moving, and Kara could feel the bottled-up emotions rising up inside her chest, that shaky feeling building, the urge to cry creeping up on her. 

     

                As if sensing all of that, Lena gripped the steering wheel and didn’t look at her as she spoke. “Are you okay?”

     

                Letting out a pent-up breath, Kara curled forward, arms wrapped around herself as she squeezed her eyes shut against the burning feeling pressing behind them. Anger rushed through her on the heels of her guilt and the breath hitched in her throat as she straightened back up, leaning into the seat as she wrestled with her confusing and conflicting emotions.

     

                “I’m sorry,” Kara rasped, “I’m really sorry.”

     

                Tears filled her eyes and she brushed them away with the back of her wrists, staring straight ahead through the windscreen, misery written in the lines of her face as she tried to even out her breathing.

     

                “It’s okay.”

     

                “No, it’s not okay. My husband is dead and your wife is dead and-”

     

                “That’s-”

     

                “I should feel bad. I should feel bad but I don’t.”

     

                “Oh.”

     

                Kara inhaled deeply and then let out a forceful breath, sniffing and wiping the cuff of her denim jacket over her flushed cheeks. “I wish I could say I did, that I felt more than just … a tiny bit of guilt, because then at least we’d both feel the same about it, but I don’t and you do. That’s somehow worse .”

     

                “Why?”

     

                Shrugging, Kara’s mouth twisted as she blinked rapidly, a scowl furrowing her brow. “Because I’m sorry for putting you in a situation that you didn’t want-”

     

                Scoffing, Lena raked a hand through her hair, a muscle twitching in her jaw. “We both knew what would happen if you came inside that night. We were both drunk, we weren’t thinking straight.”

     

                “Yeah,” Kara agreed, her voice cracking. 

     

                “I’m not upset with you that we made a drunken mistake,” Lena murmured, starting the engine as the headlights flooded to life. “Only that you ignored me for two weeks.”

     

                Letting out a bark of surprised laughter, Kara twisted in her seat to stare at Lena. “How can you not be upset that we slept together?”

     

                A ripple of pain and guilt and shame ran across Lena’s face in rapid succession before she managed to smooth it out into her usual mask of indifference, leading Kara to wonder how much she was ordinarily hiding away from her. So much of Lena was calm and collected and a little bit detached from real life, and Kara enjoyed that. Welcomed the reprieve from her festering guilt and grief. 

     

                “It was a mistake,” Lena reiterated. “It won’t happen again so we can both just … move on. Pretend it never happened.”

     

                Nodding as her chin wobbled, fighting off another choked sob, Kara swallowed hard and Lena slowly started the car, engine growling to life and headlights illuminating the parking lot. She pulled out of their bay and crept into traffic without another word, driving Kara home without asking for direction as they sat in tense silence, Kara occasionally sniffing or wiping at her now dry cheeks, while Lena’s knuckles would whiten as she tightened her grip on the wheel.

     

                Kara expected Lena to drop her off, their old routine of some kind of drink down the drain lately, and was surprised when Lena killed the engine and unbuckled her seatbelt. She followed behind Kara as she pulled out her keys and opened the front door to the narrow staircase leading up to her apartment and the two of them went up together.

     

                Opening the apartment door, Kara flipped the light switches and dumped her bag on the floor, shedding her denim jacket as she walked and kicking off her running shoes. Her mess was strewn around the place but she couldn’t bring herself to care, sitting heavily on the sofa and closing her eyes. Lena paused inside and then stooped down to pick up Kara’s bag, setting it safely aside, and then picked up each shoe and the denim jacket and set them near the skirting boards and hung up on a hook before she silently moved through the apartment.

     

                Kara listened to the sound of her movements, to the sound of running water, the grumbling of the coffee machine and the clink of china as Lena moved around the place as if it was her own home. It brought a lump to Kara’s throat, that someone else could be in her home and know which cupboard she kept the mugs in, and how she drank her coffee. When Lena reappeared with two mugs in hand, she handed one off to Kara, who murmured her thanks and took a sip. Perfectly sweet with two sugars and a splash of milk.

     

                Blinking back tears, Kara set down her mug and folded her legs beneath her on the sofa. The silence was broken by the muffled wailing of sirens and traffic beyond the dark windows and Kara felt compelled to say something as Lena made herself comfortable and sipped her own coffee.

     

                “How’s Aristotle?”

     

                “I think he misses you. Your sock is all but ruined.”

     

                Swallowing past the tightening of her throat, Kara licked her lips. “And how are you?”

     

                Lena arched an eyebrow but was otherwise impassive, but she answered honestly, if a little warily. “I miss you too.”

     

                Meeting Lena’s eyes, Kara’s shoulders drooped as her face softened with pleading to understand. “I’m sorry.”

     

                “It’s okay.”

     

                “Did you- did you mean what you said about being lonely?”

     

                Averting her gaze, Lena let out a strained laugh, raking a hand through her silken hair and then taking a sip of coffee. Shrugging nonchalantly, she sighed heavily and returned her gaze to Kara’s face.

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “Oh. I’m-”

     

                “Don’t say you’re sorry again,” Lena wryly ordered her, lips curving with a smile.

     

                Kara’s answering smile was rueful. “But I am. I thought … I thought that maybe I’d be doing you a favour-”

     

                “I know what you thought. Can’t really blame you for that. And … you were right; maybe I do regret it more than you do, but only because of the guilt. Like you’ve said before, every new first without them … it hurts. But now it’s done and I can’t take it back so I have no choice but to … keep pushing forward. I’ll get over it; I can’t be alone forever, can I?”

     

                “You could if you wanted to be. But you’d still have me if you did.”

     

                “Oh, so we’re still friends?” Lena teased, some of the tension bleeding out of them as they fell back into their usual ease.

     

                Wrinkling her nose, Kara laughed and shook her head. “Only if you let me buy you lunch tomorrow and walk your dog for you as an apology.”

     

                “Now that seems more like an apology to Aristotle.”

     

                “Ah, but he won’t be able to enjoy lunch at Noonan’s, will he? I’ll even throw in a few glasses of pinot.”

     

                “Let’s hope you don’t have any surgeries scheduled for the afternoon.”

     

                “I’ll sneak out early and let James do it.”

     

                Snorting, Lena’s eyes narrowed in amusement. “You know, one day he’s going to fire you for too many sick days.”

     

                “He’s my friend; he won’t fire me. Besides, maybe a really good friend would hire me as her personal assistant if I was ever unemployed.”

     

                Laughing, Lena sank down on her seat and picked up the TV remote, switching it on and browsing Netflix as she replied, “I already have one of those.”

     

                “Do you?” Kara asked, surprised.

     

                Eyes glancing sideways, Lena smiled faintly, “of course. It’s a pretty big firm.”

     

                “Oh. Well … maybe I need to show up to work more.”

     

                “It’s fine, I’d fire her for you.”

     

                “That’s nice. Best I could offer you is free vaccines for Aristotle.”

     

                Humming, Lena put on some reality TV show Kara was halfway through, “good to know. I’ll bring him to you for his next round.”

     

                “I’ll even give him a free treat so he doesn’t think I’m an asshole for sticking him with needles.”

     

                “What treat do I get for not thinking you’re an asshole?”

     

                Thinking for a moment, Kara climbed to her feet, “I have a pint of ice cream in the freezer.”

     

                “Perfect.”

     

                And just like that, everything felt normal again and they fell into their familiar routine of nihilistic and pessimistic rants about grief and the world and their jobs and anything else that was bothering them as they put everything else behind them. But still, there was that prickle of tension, that occasional jolt of a hazy memory that gave them a pause, weeks and even months later. No matter how hard they tried to stifle it, it persisted.

    Chapter 10

                It was almost a year and a half since she’d lost Mike when Kara found herself thrown back into the dating pool. After Lena it had made her feel hesitant about attempting to date anyone else, her confusing thoughts and feelings leaving her out of sorts, and it was only out of a desire to get her out of her system, to put the idea of anything between them to bed, that she made the drunken mistake of sleeping with William one night after drinks.

     

                Kara had regretted it immediately, something which shocked her considering she hadn’t felt all that bad about sleeping with Lena, but she’d dressed and caught a cab home and barely spoken to him at work since. It hadn’t made her feel better in the way she’d hoped, now guilty of sleeping with two people and doing potentially irreparable damage, although Lena insisted that their friendship was as normal as ever. It did give Kara the push to try dating again though, the possibility of sleeping with people without being burdened by her feelings and any attachments oddly freeing.

     

                Of course, that wasn’t her main objective but she wasn’t overly confident that she’d find someone she could actually envision as a potential partner. Still, the nights she didn’t spend having dinner with Lena or going to SoulCycle classes together or walking Aristotle were filled with a parade of men and women and a string of bad dates that made Kara cringe and occasionally go home with them if they weren’t that bad. 

     

                Still, after recounting the latest awful one to Lena, who coaxed them out of Kara each time they saw each other, Kara groaned and put her face in her hands. He’d taken her to a bar that some band was playing at, only for it to turn out that he played guitar in the band and left Kara at a table with a drink as they played while he knocked back vodkas in between songs and gave another girl his number while she watched. It had been a relief to have an escape from that one and because the night had been early she’d called Lena to see what she was up to.

     

                “Why do you insist on going on all these dates?” Lena asked, bewildered.

     

                “I’m just … trying to move on. If I go on enough dates, maybe I’ll find someone who I click with, you know?”

     

                “Mhm,” Lena dubiously replied, “except you’re not really dating them, you’re just fucking them, so how do you know if you’re clicking or not?”

     

                Kara opened and closed her mouth, “well … that’s not entirely true.”

     

                “You said you haven’t been on a single second date, and you slept with that English guy from work. Clearly you knew you wouldn’t click with him or it already would have.”

     

                “Okay, well, he was purely for the sex,” Kara admitted. “I had to- … never mind.”

     

                Reaching for her glass, Lena laughed. “No, go on, say it. No judgement from me; I’m living vicariously through you.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Kara gave her a wan smile, sipping her own drink. “I was going to say … I had to get you out of my system.”

     

                Struck speechless for a moment, Lena’s expression was slack with surprise. “Oh. Oh, um … what do you mean by that?”

     

                Choosing her words carefully, Kara set her glass down. “I already told you, I think it meant more to you than it did to me. And I meant that as in … I didn’t feel as guilty as you did and … maybe everything that had gone on between us was making me think that maybe there had been something there. I’ve always had … meaningful sex with people, I guess, like it’s always been emotional and not just physical for me so I kind of got inside my own head about what it meant if I slept with you. This whole dating and casual sex thing has been helping undo that for me as well. Anyway …”

     

                “Oh, um … okay. Well … just so you know, there could have been something there, if we were in a different position. I mean, that’s what I think, but obviously, it’s more complicated than that.”

     

                “I know,” Kara said, wincing at the embarrassment of having a conversation like that at her age. It made her feel like she was back in college, being dumped all over again. “It’s fine, it’s not like I was expecting us to date. We were drunk, so it was a mistake, I just- I’ve never been good at separating my feelings from things. That’s why we needed the space for a couple of weeks.”

     

                Lena’s expression was oddly blank, her eyes scrutinising as she gripped her glass tightly. After a moment, her lips twitched with a fleeting smile and she raked a hand through her hair.

     

                “Right. Anyway, back to dating. What are you using?”

     

                Kara wrinkled her nose, sheepish as she replied. “Tinder.”

     

                Letting out a quick laugh, Lena scrambled up straighter and held her hand out. “Let me look.”

     

                Hesitating, Kara relented with a sigh, handing Lena her phone and scooting closer to her on the sofa. They were shoulder to shoulder, heads ducked together, and Lena hummed at the first guy.

     

                “No.”

     

                The next one was a woman with blonde hair and Lena scoffed, swiping again.

     

                “No.”

     

                The next guy, Lena snorted and shook her head. “Absolutely not.”

     

                “Why not?”

     

                “He's ugly.”

     

                A quick laugh escaped Kara and she drew back slightly. “Are you really going to be shallow about it?”

     

                “It’s Tinder. It’s inherently shallow.”

     

                “What if they have a good personality? God, I should be lucky we never met on here or we would never have matched.”

     

                “Of course we would have,” Lena dismissively replied, continuing to swipe through Kara’s options.

     

                “Really?” Kara sceptically asked.

     

                Looking up, Lena blinked in surprise. “Yes. You’re exactly my type.”

     

                A confused laugh escaped Kara as her brow creased. “I thought you liked brunettes. Your wife-“

     

                “Had the most beautiful baby blue eyes,” Lena interrupted, a smile softening her face. 

     

                She hesitated before reaching out to touch her fingers to Kara’s face, pinpoints of heat from temple to cheek. Kara was still beneath her touch as her heart stumbled and her stomach swooped, aware of how close they were sitting and how much whisky they’d been drinking. Her stomach sank with the realisation that she wanted to kiss Lena, wanted to sleep with her again and remember it this time, no matter how stupid the idea was.

     

                “Lighter than yours,” Lena continued, her thumb brushing Kara’s face. “But just as honest. Just as kind, as comforting. I think that’s why I spoke to you at Group; something about you just reminded me of her. Not anything that’s actually similar but … just a sense that you’d make me feel a little bit more understood, kind of like she used to.”

     

                “Lena,” Kara whispered, a plea and a warning.

     

                Eyes shuttering as a smile spread across her face, Lena made a low sound of amusement at the back of her throat. It was raspy and thick from the whisky and Kara’s stomach jolted as she involuntarily leaned into her touch.

     

                “Don’t,” Lena murmured. “Don’t tell me what I already know.”

     

                “Okay,” Kara whispered.

     

                “I’m going to kiss you now.”

     

                “Okay.”

     

                She was slow to do it, draining the rest of her whisky, leaning forward to set it down on the coffee table and handing Kara her phone back. The anticipation was awful, Kara’s chest feeling tight as she shallowly breathed, a tense stillness to her as Lena seemed to gather herself.

     

                Then she fixed Kara with a look and Kara was too impatient, and last time it had been Lena who made the first move so perhaps this time Kara deserved some of the blame. She shifted to her knees as she moved forward, her hand finding the back of Lena’s head and her lips finding her mouth, fitting together with ease, as if it was rote for them.

     

                Lena let out a small gasp into her mouth and Kara faltered for a moment. Tugging her closer, Lena pushed back against her lips and Kara could taste the whisky and feel the neediness, trying to curb her own slight desperation as she tried to think rationally. When Lena’s fingers moved to the zipper of her dress, all rational thought fled Kara’s mind though and she was off the sofa, Lena rising with her, and in her friend’s bed before she could remember why it was a bad idea to repeat their previous mistake.

     

                Ruled by the overwhelming part of her that wanted to indulge in the moment with Lena, the act of being close to someone who wasn’t a stranger, someone who she was hesitant to admit she had some sort of stronger feelings towards, even if she wasn’t emotionally available to act on it. Instead, Kara split herself in half and divorced herself from her feelings, undressing Lena with the clinical thought that it was purely physical and wouldn’t alter their relationship at all. She told herself that because she knew it was what Lena wanted.

     

                Although, Kara hadn’t thought Lena wanted to sleep with her again, even as a drunken mistake, so perhaps she wasn’t quite so aware of what her friend wanted. She knew what Lena wanted then though and was generous with her attention, taking her time and going slow as she tried to read Lena's emotions in the dark. There were moments where they paused, where one of them stiffened, awkward and closed off before they relaxed back into it, a gentle kiss at the hollow of a throat, the caress down the ridges of a spine, following the curve of a thigh coaxing them away from guilt and grief and shame. 

     

                Afterwards, Kara turned over onto her stomach, her arms folded under her head like a pillow, and she looked at Lena. They were nowhere near as drunk as last time so there was no ease of unconsciousness to slip into and avoid any talking. Lena had pulled a corner of the sheets up over herself and was laying on her side. Sweat prickled over her shoulders, drying in the cool air of the bedroom and Kara felt bound to say something.

     

                “Lena.”

     

                She whispered her name, and she could feel Lena’s body tremble as she tried to fight the tears, shaking with silent sobs. When Kara reached over to touch her arm, feeling Lena shy away from her touch, she felt guilt well up tenfold for making her cry.

     

                Slowly pushing herself up, Kara raked a hand through her dishevelled hair and reached for her glasses on the nightstand. The mattress jostled with her movements and she stilled at the tight grip of a hand on her thigh, fingers digging in. Glancing over her shoulder, Kara’s brow puckered slightly as she took in the pale smudge of Lena’s face in the dark.

     

                “Please don’t go. Please don’t leave me alone.”

     

                Gut-wrenching pity knifed through Kara and she silently removed her glasses and set them back down. Laying down beside her in the dark, Kara stared at the pale expanse of Lena’s shoulders peeking out above the sheets and hesitated. She was torn between trying to comfort her and silence.

     

                In the end the latter won and Kara carefully hitched the sheets up over Lena’s shoulder and turned the other way. She didn’t touch her, didn’t try and hold her and make it feel more intimate than she had any right to. Lena fell asleep first, the hitching breaths evening out into a steady, deep rhythm and Kara lay awake for a while longer until the pleasant hum of whisky lulled her under as well.

     

                She woke the next morning to the smell of coffee and tobacco, emerging from Lena’s room to find her sitting at the table like last time in a bathrobe. A cup of coffee sat before her, a cigarette held between her fingers, half-smoked to the filter. When she turned to meet Kara’s eyes, her own were bloodshot and raw. Letting out a defeated sigh, Kara walked over to her and dropped to a crouch at her side. Reaching up, her throat felt constricted as she touched Lena’s chin.

     

                “You can’t do this to yourself,” Kara murmured.

     

                Flicking ash off the tip of the cigarette, Lena let out a hoarse laugh, averting her gaze. “Don’t feel bad,” Lena told her. “It’s not because of anything you did.”

     

                “It doesn’t feel that way.”

     

                “Kara, look … you already said it; it’s different for me. I can’t reconcile the part of me that feels like I’m betraying my wife with the part of me that just wants to feel a little bit less alone.
