I have a wife, I- I love her, it was supposed to be me and her but it’s not. I was never supposed to love anyone else - love you. Do you know how fucking confusing that is?”

     

                “Yes. Yes, of course I do,” Kara whispered, rigid and pale, feeling a little nauseous at the turn of the conversation, watching Lena come apart at the seams, guilt eating away at her the same way it had worn away at Kara.

     

                “No, you don’t,” Lena sobbed, putting her face in her hands. “It’s different for you. It has been tearing me in half to be with you when she- I don’t want to do this to you. I’ve tried … so hard to not feel this way and it’s- it’s just been pointless because … I can’t. And the worst part is that I- I feel guilty but I don’t , and these days the only thing that’s been able to make it easier is just drinking until I don’t feel like I’m- I’m betraying her every time I’m with you but … I love you and I don’t know how to stop and it makes me feel like shit every time I remember her . And I know she wouldn’t begrudge me this - she’d want me to be happy, and you’re the only thing that makes me happy anymore - but how do I- how do I just … replace her? How do I love you and not think of her? It’s just … shit. ”

     

                She was crying freely now, her angry words hitching and her chest rising and falling quickly as if she couldn’t get it all out fast enough. The confession held a palpable air of relief as well though, as if Lena felt unburdened by getting it off her chest, so many weeks or months - how long had she been internalising it all? - of angst and frustration finally spilling out of her without pause. 

     

                All Kara could do was listen, unable to react to the information that bombarded her. She wondered if she should be insulted by Lena’s stubborn determination to not love her, her desire to only love her wife, but she couldn’t fault her for it. There had been a part of Kara at the beginning that had hated the thought of letting go of Mike, of letting someone else into that part of her heart that had been reserved for him for a decade. It had never felt right for there to be room for two but Kara knew exactly how Lena felt, fighting so hard against the feelings that her mind and body had conjured as she’d been swept along with it like a bystander in her own life.

     

                “It’s okay,” Kara whispered, her voice thick and wavering.

     

                Taking a hesitant step forward, she let momentum do the rest, closing the gap between them quickly. Bundling Lena up in her arms, she held her close and rubbed her back as she rocked her in a soothing manner, her own eyes swimming with tears. Brimming with so much nervous tension, Kara couldn’t even begin to manage her own feelings, the adrenaline from even touching on how she felt leaving her jittery and hollow.

     

                “It’s not okay. None of this is okay. How is it okay that I wake up next to you every morning instead of her? And sometimes I think, just for a second, that it’s her, until I realise. And I don’t know if I’m supposed to feel disappointed or- or glad that I’m just not alone. I just feel … so confused all the time. And it’s not fair to you, because you don’t deserve to be compared to her, to be a replacement-“

     

                “Lena, I- I know I can’t be a replacement,” Kara murmured. “I know that you still love her, and you always will. I know all of that because … that’s how I feel too. I feel just as guilty, just as relieved and sad and confused. I can’t even put into words how it feels, but … I don’t have to with you. I know you understand and that … well, to me, that makes the whole thing more bearable.”

     

                Letting out a breathless sob, Lena drew back and wiped her face on her sleeve, keeping her head lowered as Kara stood inches away from her, her hands cupping Lena’s triceps, keeping her close. Teeth clenched, Lena looked away, the tendons in her neck taut as she wrestled with herself.

     

                “It’s not fair,” Lena ground out.

     

                A huff of laughter escaped Kara and she cupped Lena’s face in her hands, wiping away her tears with the pads of her thumbs and tilting her head so their eyes met. “Things rarely are. All we’ve been doing is- is … making the best of a shit situation. And that’s okay. I’m not … I’m not asking you to replace her or for us to date and the whole … thing. I just- it’s been killing me to keep it inside and … I couldn’t tell you because … I never wanted you to feel bad about it or- or pity me if you didn’t feel the same way. I would hate it if things got awkward between us.”

     

                “I- I tried to tell you in the only way that I- that I could. I … I never wanted to say those words to anyone else, I didn’t want to- but you … every time I drank, I couldn’t help but say too much. I thought … I thought you didn’t- that you were pulling away because I-”

     

                Choking on a laugh, Kara smoothed down Lena’s hair and then cupped the underside of her jaw, an agonised look of amusement on her face as she groaned. Then she kissed her, softly, tenderly, the way she’d always wanted to kiss her, just for the sake of it and not as a precursor to sex. Lena’s eyelids fluttered shut as tears traced down her cheeks and Kara pulled back, wiping away the fresh ones.

     

                “I thought- I thought you were teasing me. Not on purpose, just … we said that we wouldn’t, that we knew what we were doing, so I thought you were … I don’t know, making fun of the situation. Of what Alex and everyone else was worried about. It … it hurt. I didn’t- I didn’t mean to pull away, only … I know how you feel and this isn’t- it’s not what you wanted. I know that and I understand. I’m not … expecting anything, I-”

     

                “But I love you,” Lena murmured, her voice cracking, confusion crumpling her face. “I do want to be with you, I just- I’m having a hard time- you make me happy but … there are things that have happened. It’s not going to be that simple.”

     

                “After the last year and a half … I don’t think anything is simple anymore,” Kara weakly replied.

     

                Surprised laughter shook Lena’s shoulders and she sniffed, letting out a weary huff. “No, it’s really not. I just- we need to talk about things.”

     

                “Of course,” Kara quickly agreed.

     

                Pulling back, she wrung her hands together and then glanced at the half-cooked dinner behind her. Hesitating, Kara’s lips twitched with faint amusement.

     

                “Um … I’m going to make some tea and … you go and put your pyjamas on. I might order takeout as well; what do you feel like?”

     

                Running a hand over her face, Lena shook her head. “I don’t think I have the energy to pick.”

     

                “Right, well … leave it to me,” Kara reassured her, hesitating before reaching out to squeeze her hand. 

     

                She ended up ordering from their favourite ramen place, a comforting food that suited the situation, everything still a little up in the air despite their confessions. Tossing the evidence of her cooking, Kara loaded the dishwasher and had two cups of tea steaming on the counter by the time Lena reemerged, face free from makeup, making her look even paler and younger. 

     

                Shoulders slumping as agonised confusion wrenched her, Kara exhaled softly and opened her arms. “Come here.”

     

                Lena went willingly, allowing Kara to engulf her in a warm hug, holding her tightly for a moment. Kissing the top of her head, Kara let her go and nudged a cup of tea closer. Taking it, Lena set it safely aside and hopped up onto the counters, leaning back as she blew the air out of her lungs and seemed a little more at ease than she had been when she’d gotten home. There was still a visible air of tension about her though, which Kara chalked up to jittery adrenaline lingering from the confrontation.

     

                “I ordered ramen. It should be here soon.”

     

                “Okay, thanks.”

     

                Nodding, Kara picked up her cup and took a sip, standing a safe distance away as she eyed Lena. Her own eyes were raw and bloodshot from her own tears and Kara felt the long day catching up with her, strong emotions draining her of all of her energy. She couldn’t wait to go to bed and a small part of her wondered if that would be on her own, after everything was said and done.

     

                “Um … so, should we talk while we wait?”

     

                Snorting, Lena reached for her own tea and took a sip before clearing her throat. “There are things … that might take a while to come out. It’s difficult to talk about-”

     

                “It’s okay, just take your time. We don’t need to get into the heavy stuff right now, that can wait. Just … maybe get on the same page about things. You’re right; we should’ve spoken about this the minute it all started to get confusing and I’m sorry that we didn’t but … it seems like a good place to start now.”

     

                “When did you start thinking that way?”

     

                Chewing on her lip, Kara closed her eyes, sighing softly. “Honestly? I think … I had an inkling before I moved in. That’s why I was so against it at the start. I thought … it would only be a couple of weeks, and I’d be able to get past it. Then I got … comfortable . It was nice to come home to someone - to you - and … I realised I couldn’t just stamp it down anymore, that maybe it- maybe it was more than I’d originally thought but I didn’t want to tell you that. The thought of losing you … I didn’t want that to happen so I decided to be mature about it. I guess … I haven’t handled it well lately though.”

     

                “Oh. So … about five months?”

     

                Shrugging, Kara closed her eyes and ran a hand through her hair. “Probably longer. I knew I liked you before we even slept together. We wouldn’t have even slept together in the first place if it hadn’t been there, right? I mean … it wasn’t anything meaningful but I knew the potential was there.”

     

                “Yeah, I think- I think I knew that too,” Lena admitted. “Maybe … a part of me selfishly wanted that. I could never admit it though; it hurt too much. I just kept feeling guilty each time we were together so … I couldn’t bear the thought of it meaning something. But … it did. A little bit more each time. I’m sorry I made you feel like you couldn’t tell me.”

     

                “You didn’t. I just- I know things were a lot different in your marriage and you’ve been having a harder time moving on. I didn’t want to stress you out more.”

     

                “You don’t stress me out - except when you’re avoiding me,” Lena pointedly replied, a smile on her lips.

     

                Wrinkling her nose as she ducked her head, toying with the rim of her cup, Kara looked appropriately apologetic. “Sorry. I was trying to draw the line.”

     

                “I know. I get it. I … I don’t know whether I wish it had been drawn or I’m grateful it wasn’t. I think I’m going to spend the rest of my life torn in half.”

     

                “Eliza said at the wedding that … our futures can either have each other in it or not but … it won’t have them in it. It’s the bitter truth but …”

     

                Pain ran across Lena’s face, coupled with guilt and regret and a longing look, and she looked down at her lap, lips pressed into a flat line. “Kara, I- I care about you a lot. I want you in my life. I can admit that now but … I meant it when I said that this isn’t over for me. My grief isn’t going anywhere, it’s never-ending and I just- I don’t want you to waste time on someone who-”

     

                “I wouldn’t be wasting time.”

     

                “You don’t even know what you’re promising to stick around for.”

     

                “I do. I’ve seen you at your lowest-”

     

                “Not yet, you haven’t. I- look, my wife-,” Lena started before cutting off with a huff. “I love my wife and I always will. I know that I’ll never feel happy because of her again and … I’m okay with that, I’ve accepted it and I know … moving on is what’s best for me but I can’t leave her behind. If you could give me some time to-”

     

                “I don’t expect anything from you. Take as much time as you need,” Kara repeated.

     

                Letting out a shaky breath, Lena nodded and rubbed her forehead. Her throat bobbed as she swallowed thickly and she gave Kara a wan smile. “It’s just been so tiring. All of it. I don’t know how to explain …”

     

                “Don’t explain. Just tell me what you want.”

     

                Lips twitching ruefully, Lena looked up through her lashes as she fiddled with her fingers, a doe-eyed look of vulnerability welling in her green eyes. “You. If I can’t have her, I want you.”

     

                Taking Lena’s hand, Kara pressed a kiss to her palm and gave her a grim smile. “I’ll do my part to try and make you happy.”

     

                “You already do,” Lena insisted, before letting out a ragged laugh. Lena dug the heels of her palms into her eyes, perched on the kitchen counters as she hunched forward. “But happiness isn’t supposed to hurt this much.”

     

                “Hey,” Kara murmured, squeezing her knee as she stepped in front of her. “It’s okay. It’s … painful, I know. I’m not expecting the world of you; I just like being with you. You make the world bearable, and I’ll try and do that for you too if you let me.”

     

                “I- just … don’t make any promises yet. Please. There’s a lot to talk about and … I don’t want to hurt you. I care about you a lot, you have to know that, and I just- I don’t think I could bear it if you- if you left but … I’d understand so don’t promise anything. Not until we’re on the same page.”

     

                “Okay,” Kara whispered, holding Lena’s hand firmly and kissing her knuckles. “No promises. But I’d like it if we could just … keep doing what we’re doing.”

     

                “So would I,” Lena murmured, running her thumb over Kara’s fingers. “I’d like that a lot.”

    Chapter 20

    Chapter Notes

                A week passed by in peace, both of them still wary and surprised by the turn of things. Nothing changed, not really, but just that awareness and understanding made even coming home have a certain weight of intimacy to it. Before there had been the casual brushed up against each other, hands touching, waists held as one of the scooted past in the spacious kitchen or wide hallways, now it was more intentional. It didn’t feel like overstepping or blurring the boundaries to come home and greet each other with a quick kiss, to hold hands on their walks with Aristotle or for Kara to sleep beside Lena in her bed every night that week. Nothing changed, but so much did.

     

                As far as weeks went, it was perhaps one of the best ones Kara could remember in a long while, the stress of her feelings for Lena dissipating as everything was out in the open. The unburdened relief of confessing and not being greeted with the sting of rejection made her feel lighter than she had in weeks, or maybe even longer than that. She hadn’t realised the true extent the toll of bottling everything up had taken and it was a period of genuine happiness, even as they tried to muddle through how things would work with their grief.

     

                It almost felt laughable on Thursday night to meet at Group, as usual, and talk about their feelings of missing their partners while sitting beside each other with this new relationship burgeoning between them. It felt strange, it felt as if it should have been harder, but they’d known each other for eighteen months now and it didn’t feel strange at all. In fact, it felt familiar and that in itself was a relief. They didn’t have to change anything because it had been a gradual slope to this point, happening in gradual increments, so nothing really changed at the moment, except for the things they’d tried to always rationalise as infrequent occurrences became more regular. Kara never would have dreamed of waking up beside Lena every day for a week straight before. Now, it was her new normal, and it wasn’t too drastic from the few times a week she’d found herself there before.

     

                Kara hadn’t said a word to her sister or friends, keeping it private and feeling protective of this new and fragile thing, as if letting other people in on the secret would be asking for trouble. As it was, she didn’t have to ask for trouble, it inevitably found her itself. It was just a shame that they’d had barely a week of bliss amidst so much confusion and sadness and guilt before it all fell apart.

     

                She hadn’t even been anticipating it, enjoying another day at work at her new clinic with her slightly arrogant clientele with their dog breeds that cost a minimum of thousands of dollars for their pedigree. It was an upscale clinic and she found her time mostly occupied by anxious nannies or assistants with lap dogs and house cats panicking over some minor ailment or another while the more severe cases offered the opportunity for surgeries that cost a hell of a lot more than James had charged. It was still relatively the same work, just with a different tax bracket associated with it, and Kara enjoyed it just as much as she had before, although she missed the ease that came with a familiar environment and her old friends. 

     

                After work, she drove home with a feeling of warmth in her chest. It felt different somehow, that knowledge that it wasn’t just her overthinking things, that Lena loved her too, that this thing - whatever it was - wasn’t just temporary. They hadn’t discussed the living situation yet but Lena had never wanted her to leave in the first place; now, it seemed almost an unspoken surety that Kara was staying.

     

                Home first, as she often was, Kara showered quickly and then sat on the floor with Aristotle, playing tug of war with him as he happily spent some of his energy, and Kara promised him a walk later. The sound of the door opening greeted them and Kara looked up, pausing.

     

                “Who’s that?” she whispered to the dog, rubbing behind his ears. “Quick, go see mom.”

     

                Climbing to her feet, Kara dusted off her hands, smiling softly as she emerged from the kitchen as Lena was shedding her coat. There was a clouded look on her face, vaguely stressed and worn out, but she smiled tiredly at the sight of Kara.

     

                “Hi.”

     

                “Hey, you. Good day?”

     

                Mouth twisting derisively, Lena shrugged. “Difficult.”

     

                Humming as her mouth thinned, Kara drifted closer as if drawn to her like a magnet. “What happened?”

     

                “Oh, just … a lot going on. How was yours?”

     

                “It was pretty good.”

     

                “Good,” Lena murmured, reaching up to cup Kara’s cheek as the latter leaned in for a kiss. 

     

                Giving her a quick peck, Kara took the bag of Big Belly Burger and the drinks tray from her. Lena took her heels off and picked them up before continuing along the hallway, dropping her keys into the small dish on the console. She went to go and change into something more comfortable while Kara unpacked the bag of food and set their orders in front of their spots. 

     

                Returning a few minutes later, Lena’s fingers trailed along the back of Kara’s shoulders as she rounded the counters. “Don’t wait for me, your burger will get cold.”

     

                “I can wait,” Kara insisted.

     

                Sitting across from Lena, she gave her a small smile, still somewhat smitten by the change in circumstances, even though worry still simmered, as if she didn’t believe it was real or would last. She was right to worry, of course, but at that moment her worry was misplaced as some residual anxiety from losing one too many loved ones. 

     

                They talked about their day as they unwrapped their burgers and dipped fries in ketchup. Lena vaguely skimmed over the various meetings and phone calls while Kara recounted a particularly yappy terrier that had been terrified of getting his shots that morning. She was just finishing showing Lena a video of a litter of kittens scaling the bars of their cage as they both laughed at how adorable they were when they were interrupted.

     

                Lena’s phone started ringing, laughter fading on her face until she was softly smiling, setting down her burger and reaching for her phone. Her expression quickly sobered up and she climbed to her feet, tension in the lines of her shoulders as she put her back to Kara.

     

                “Hello? Russell, hi. Is she alright? Yes, I’m on my way now. I’ll meet you there. The private one, yes.”

     

                Lena had visibly paled during the course of the short phone call and Kara looked perplexed as she took a bite of her extra pickle, eating quietly. At the grave look on Lena’s face, green eyes wide and suddenly youthful with fear and regret, a defeated slump to her shoulders, Kara swallowed her mouthful and lowered her pickle.

     

                “I have to go,” Lena blurted out.

     

                “Is everything okay?”

     

                “No. No, it’s not. Um … can you- can you come with me? We need to talk. It’s- it’s bad timing and I know … we should’ve had this conversation before, I get that, but I need you to come with me now and just- just listen for a second.”

     

                Her voice was laced with urgency now, frantic and oddly strained as she brushed past the table and out to the living room, carrying on to the console, where she snatched up the keys to her Lexus and then dragged a coat off the hook. It was Kara’s coat but Lena was in a rush, with slippers on her feet and her loungewear underneath the coat. 

     

                Mouth opening and closing as she hastily followed after her, abandoning her dinner, a furrowed look of confusion on her face as she shoved her feet into her sneakers, standing on the heels as she didn’t pause to unlace them and get them on properly, Kara grabbed another coat and managed to catch the door before it swung shut as Lena left. Rushing after her, trying to keep her feet half in the shoes as she gripped the coat in hand, Kara felt a sense of panic but she didn’t know what for.

     

                “What’s going on?”

     

                “There’s been an accident.”

     

                “What happened?” Kara asked, worry clouding her eyes. “Lena, what happened? Who’s hurt?”

     

                Jamming her thumb into the elevator button, Lena winced, raking a hand through her hair as Kara scrambled into her coat. Mouth opening and closing, Lena couldn’t speak as she ducked her head in shame, waiting until the doors opened and stepping inside.

     

                Kara trailed in after her, a searching look in her eyes as Lena pressed the button for the basement. The elevator jolted and they started to descend and Kara just stared at her, waiting for her to speak. Clearing her throat, Lena wouldn’t look at her as her chin trembled, eyes filling with tears.

     

                “I- my wife ...”

     

                There was a moment of heavy silence as Kara blinked, confusion furrowing her brow. “What, like … someone vandalised her grave?”

     

                “No, I mean … my wife … is in an ambulance. On her way to the hospital.”

     

                Mouth opening, Kara’s face fell, her stomach tying itself into nauseous knots as a pitiful sound of surprise escaped her. Jerking back, she felt her throat constrict as she stared at Lena speechlessly. Drawing in a shuddering breath, Lena tipped her head back and exhaled sharply.

     

                “I know it sounds bad-”

     

                “You- your wife is … alive?” Kara haltingly asked, her voice gravelly and her face so white it was almost greyish. 

     

                “Yes, but-”

     

                Letting out a choked breath, Kara’s eyes stung fiercely as she tried to process what she was hearing. Her cheeks started reddening with anger and embarrassment, confusion curdling in her stomach. “Tell me this is some sick joke. Tell me you haven’t been lying to me for the last eighteen months.”

     

                “Just … come with me. I’ll explain it all in the car,” Lena softly begged, her words precise in an effort to stop her voice from trembling too much. 

     

                “What, are you- are you separated? I mean … what the fuck,” Kara’s voice steadily rose as she ran her hands through her hair, gritting her teeth as she stared speechlessly at Lena, horror creeping up on her as everything started to fall apart.

     

                Letting out a breathless sob, Lena covered her face. “No, we’re not- we’re not separated. I- she’s sick. She’s in a care home.”

     

                Closing her eyes, Kara covered her eyes with a hand as she thought for a moment, trying to get everything straight in her mind. After a moment, she dropped her hand and shook her head, as if to clear it, blinking rapidly before she glanced up at the floor number they were on and pushed the button for two floors below. They jerked to a stop a moment later and the doors parted.

     

                Rooted to the spot for a moment, Kara didn’t even look at Lena as she stepped out. Turning, she stared down at the floor and waited for the doors to slide shut, cutting them off, but Lena slammed a hand against the gap the doors slid out of, keeping the elevator waiting on that floor.

     

                “Kara, wait-”

     

                “Just go,” she rasped, her voice thick with tears now.

     

                “Please, will you just-”

     

                “There’s no fucking way I’m getting in that car with you so just go. Please.”

     

                Flinching back slightly, a mournful look crumpling her face, Lena nodded and then hesitated. “Can you just- can you wait until I get back? I’d like the chance to explain. You don’t owe it to me, I know, but … maybe if you know the whole story … you’ll understand.”

     

                Kara visibly winced at the familiar line Lena had given her over and over again, about how she didn’t understand why Lena was behaving the way she was, why she did the things she did and couldn’t say the things she wanted to. The air was pushed from her lungs in a forceful exhale, winding Kara as she felt a sharp pain in her chest. Now she really understood why.

     

                “I’m not leaving until you promise-”

     

                “Fine, I’ll wait. Just go; I don’t want to look at you right now.”

     

                Meekly nodding, her cheeks stained with tears and her bottom lip quivering with the threat of more, Lena shrank back into the elevator and jammed her finger into the button to close the doors. The moment they slid shut, Kara let out a ragged sob, clapping a hand to her mouth as she curled her shoulders inwards, eyes squeezed shut, and tried to keep it together.

     

                After a few minutes, once she was sure Lena was in the basement, Kara jammed her thumb into the button for the lobby, aware that she didn’t have a key on her. Luckily, the security guard knew her and escorted her back upstairs to let her into the apartment after an awkward elevator ride where Kara quietly cried the entire time. Aristotle bounded over to greet her and Kara kicked off her half-on sneakers and sank to the floor, burying her face into the dog’s fur as she sobbed.

     

                It took her almost an hour to pick herself up off the floor and Kara was at a loss of what to do. It was overwhelmingly clear that she couldn’t stay there. She would wait, as promised, but she couldn’t even begin to imagine what sort of explanation could make it all okay. There was nothing Lena could say to make up for the fact that she’d misled Kara this entire time. 

     

                In the kitchen, Kara surveyed the mess of their half-eaten dinner and robotically went through the motions of cleaning up. Her movements were stiff and jerky as she tried to wipe her mind of any thoughts, bundling everything up for the trash as she tried scrubbing her mind clear of the rest of her evening. It was futile.

     

                Once she’d finished, Kara retreated to her bedroom and unzipped her backpack before yanking open the drawers. She began the slow process of finding the important necessities to see her through the next few days until she could pack things up properly, carefully folded each item and tucked it into her bag. It was almost meditative and she passed another hour that way, at which time Lena came home.

     

                She heard the front door open first, followed by the jangle of keys and the quiet sound of the door shutting. Freezing, Kara’s heart pounded in her chest and she swallowed the lump in her throat as she slowly resumed packing.

     

                Her door was wide open so she saw the flicker of movement as Lena appeared in the mouth of it, wary and exhausted. She still quietly knocked on the door frame so Kara couldn’t even pretend she didn’t see her. Looking up, there was a moment of prolonged silence, as if neither of them knew who should go first.

     

                “How is she?” Kara hollowly asked.

     

                Mouth turning down at the corners, Lena shrugged as she looked down, fiddling with her fingers, the rings she’d never taken off. “Broken arm.”

     

                Nodding, Kara continued to fold her clothes and pack them into her bag. Standing in the doorway, Lena watched on, brimming with nervous tension as she fought back the urge to burst into tears.

     

                “Look … I know you must have a lot of questions, that- that you’re mad. I just- I never intended for things to go this far.”

     

                “You never intended- you had so much time to tell me,” Kara hotly replied, her voice breaking as devastation cut through her anew. Tears filled her eyes, quickly spilling over as she let out a rough sob. “You had so much time, I-”

     

                Cutting off, Kara angrily wiped the back of her hand across her eyes before fixing her glasses. Sniffing, she let out a shaky breath and continued to pack, her head ducked down.

     

                “I’m sorry.”

     

                “Don’t say you’re sorry. If you were sorry, you wouldn’t have done it. You- you would’ve told me when we first became friends. You would’ve told me when we fucking slept together. Or the other day when you said that you- fuck, I’m an idiot.”

     

                “Don’t say that.”

     

                “Well, how about you’re a fucking liar,” Kara choked out.

     

                Swallowing thickly, ducking her head as her lips twisted with bitter acceptance, Lena nodded. “I deserve that.”

     

                “Is that all you have to say?”

     

                A muscle twitched in Lena’s jaw and she swallowed past her indignation, annoyance flashing in her green eyes as she curtly replied. “No.”

     

                Neither of them spoke for a moment and Lena tipped her head back, inhaling deeply and then letting out a weary sigh. She looked exhausted, not just from the hospital visit but from the emotional toll her worry about the anticipated conversation had on her. Now that it was here, she seemed reluctant to have that conversation, despite begging Kara to stay for it.

     

                “You told me she was dead,” Kara shouted, anger and hurt making her voice rough as she disturbed the silence, startling Lena slightly.

     

                “No, I never said she was dead. Not once.”

     

                Mouth opening and closing, Kara was struck speechless for a moment as she floundered at that small caveat. It was true; Lena always said she’d lost her wife and Kara had made her own assumptions from that. The only information Lena had given her was that her wife had been sick. Kara had filled in the gaps herself, and Lena had been all too happy for her to do that so she didn’t have to explain herself.

     

                “You let me think that she was. This whole time! Co-opting my grief, as if you know how it feels. You’re fucking unbelievable.”

     

                “I do know how it feels,” Lena snapped, her eyes wild with anger as she jabbed a finger at her chest. “My wife is gone. She’s not coming back, same as Mike. How is that any different?”

     

                “It’s different because she’s alive.”

     

                “And I wish she wasn’t,” Lena shouted, drowning out the end of Kara’s sentence.

     

                The ensuing silence was deafening and Lena quietly broke down, burying her face in her hands as her shoulders shook with the effort. Kara was rooted to the spot, her arms hanging limply by her sides with a plaid shirt held in a white-knuckled grip. Her lips parted with surprise but she made no effort to move to comfort her.

     

                Letting out a gut-wrenching sob, Lena drew in a ragged breath, hitching in her chest. “I know that makes me horrible but … I wish she was because she’s not- she’s not coming back and I’m reminded of that every day. I visit her almost every day - before work, after work, on my lunch break. She … about a year after we got married, Andrea was diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer’s. Early early-onset. She’d just turned thirty . Um … it’s extremely rare for people to be diagnosed that young but … it’s not unheard of. There are even people younger than her. But we just thought she had a bad memory until then. We, um, we … we used to make jokes about it, about how she couldn’t find her keys or was terrible with directions unless she had maps open, and … um, then one day … she called me from the grocery store. She didn’t know where she was, couldn’t remember how to get home.”

     

                Tears slid down her cheeks and she angrily wiped them away with the cuffs of her shirt, her grief more palpable than ever as she finally revealed the truth about the circumstances of it. Kara felt sick as she listened, disbelief making it hard for her to breathe as a tight ache in her chest constricted her lungs.

     

                “They say by the time you get a diagnosis, you’re already at the end of the first stage. It’s all rapidly downhill from there. She- she tried to leave me. Didn’t want me to be around for all of it. I wouldn’t let her, of course, but … um, it did get worse. Obviously. She- she started … she started getting, um … confused. Would have a meltdown at work, would forget conversations that we’d had. She started writing little notes so she wouldn’t forget things; what to pick up at the store, if Aristotle had been fed yet, if we- if we’d had a fight. Used to keep them all in her purse so she wouldn’t lose them.”

     

                Lena let out a small laugh, a smile twitching the corners of her lips at a memory. “I used to steal the ones about our fights so she’d forget to be mad at me. It got … worse. She started to forget … who I was sometimes. Sometimes I’d wake in the middle of the night to her freaking out about me in our bed; it would take hours to calm her down. It became … too much. We’d already had the conversation about in-patient care and … she was still herself enough to decide it was time. I put her in there a month before we met. She was thirty-four. And now … she has no fucking clue who I am. I am a stranger to her. She hasn’t recognised me in months. Not once. I wish it would be over so I don’t have to wake up every single day in this fucking hell, watching her disappear, watching her get violent and erratic and forgetting how to do things. Do you know what that’s like for a person like her? All that brilliance just … wasted. She would be mortified if she could see herself. But she’s still my wife, and I love her, so even if it takes another twenty years to kill her - which it eventually will - I will be forced to watch because … I can’t leave her. So, yes, Kara, I know how it feels to grieve for someone; I’m forced to do it every single day and I can’t just move on like you.”

     

                “Yes, because I’m so lucky,” Kara managed to choke out, her anger still smouldering at the revelation.

     

                “You are lucky,” Lena ground out as fresh tears blurred her vision. “Your husband is dead. He’s not coming back. And as shitty as that is, you got closure from that, you get to move on .”

     

                A scathing sound of hollow amusement escaped Kara as she rammed her shirt into her bag, her hands shaking as she gave up on packing and jerked the zipper across, trying to swallow the caustic words on the tip of her tongue that would go beyond the point of return. No matter how heartbroken she was at that moment, she didn’t want to hurt Lena. It was an all-around terrible situation for them both and she knew it beneath all the pain of betrayal; the least Kara could do was not add to the pain out of her own selfish desire to pay it back.

     

                “Well, let’s just hope I’m as lucky moving on from … whatever this is,” Kara gravelly replied, gesturing vaguely between them before slinging her bag over her shoulder.

     

                Scoffing, Lena gave her a rueful look, full of pain and bitterness and a soft plea cutting through it all. “You know what it is.”

     

                “You’re right, I do - it’s a lie,” Kara murmured, ducking her head.

     

                “It’s not and you know that. I know that you’re mad- I- I’m sorry. Can we just- can we sit down and talk about this?”

     

                Head jerking up, Kara stared at her with disbelief, narrowing her eyes slightly. “Sit down and talk about it? Lena, I- no, I don’t want to sit down and talk about it. I stayed to hear you out and now … now I’m done, so … that’s all there is.”

     

                The breath was forced out of Lena’s lungs and her shoulders slumped in weary defeat. Face crumpling, she held out a hand and then let it drop back to her side a moment later, limp and resigned.

     

                “Please,” she croaked. “You’re all I have.”

     

                “No, I’m not,” Kara muttered. “You have your wife. And for her sake, I hope you sort your shit out because … if she could remember, I don’t think she’d like what she’d see.”

     

                Hoisting her bag up on her shoulder, she moved towards Lena and angled her torso so she could bypass her without touching. Regret and bitterness filled her and Kara’s mouth thinned as she swallowed thickly, pausing in the hallway.

     

                “I’ll get the rest of my things tomorrow.”

     

                “You don’t-“

     

                “I’ll leave the keys behind.”

     

                “Kara.”

     

                She carried on, passing through the kitchen and into the living room, Lena following after her, her meek apologetic air of shame sharpening into wounded anger now. How could she have expected any other outcome though?

     

                “Where are you going to go? Huh? You don’t have anywhere to stay.”

     

                Lips twitching ruefully, a sadness so deep she could’ve drowned in it welling in her eyes, Kara choked on a laugh.

     

                “You’re not my girlfriend. It’s not your concern.”

     

                Her words twisted the knife in Lena’s chest a little and she squared her shoulders as she carried on down the hallway.

     

                “Like hell it isn’t,” Lena snapped. “A week ago you told me you loved me. And now that’s it? That’s all I get?”

     

                Reaching the door, Kara sighed heavily, so depleted that she didn’t have the energy to fight. Yanking it open, she glanced back, taking in the slight figure anxiously wringing her hands as she gave Kara a yearning look of desperation. 

     

                “Yes, Lena, that’s generally what happens when somebody lies to you for months.”

     

                And then Kara left, pulling the raft out from under her and leaving Lena to drown in her sea of grief alone. The door slammed shut behind her and she walked to the elevator and rode it down to the lobby, where the security guard watched her leave while trying not to be too obvious about staring at her bulging backpack. 

     

                The rest of the night was a blur as she stepped outside and walked to the bus stop that connected to the line she was looking for. Completely detached from herself and her emotions, Kara let the bus lull her into a stupor as she hollowly stared ahead, unseeing, until she was dimly aware of her stop approaching. 

     

                Jerkily climbing to her feet after pushing the button, Kara hauled her bag after her and climbed off the bus as the doors opened. It was a windy night and she walked the familiar route to the apartment building with a shakiness in her chest as she barely held it together. She knew the minute Alex questioned her, she wouldn’t be able to do it any longer but even shame at being proven wrong couldn’t keep her from going to her sister then. Kara had nowhere else to go.

     

                Ringing the buzzer as she stood outside the building, she hoped Alex was home from the hospital and was greeted by Kelly’s voice a moment later.

     

                “Hello?”

     

                “It’s me. Can I come up?”

     

                The door unlocked a moment later with a hum and Kara let herself into the lobby and made her way up to the apartment. Knocking on the door, she was greeted by her sister-in-law, who was welcoming but bewildered, ushering her inside.

     

                “I was just about to make some spiced tea. Do you want a cup?”

     

                Making a noncommittal sound, Kara dropped her backpack to the floor and sank down onto the sofa. The TV was on and she stared blankly at the screen as Kelly moved around the kitchen, until Kara’s silence made her wary.

     

                “Kara, is everything alright?” Kelly called, her voice lilting and low with caution.

     

                Letting out a forceful breath, Kara felt as if her chest was caving in as her exhale turned into breathless sobs. She couldn’t even form any tears, her eyes raw, but she shook with shallow sobs as she struggled to breathe, each one leaving her quietly gasping as she curled in on herself, clutching at the front of her shirt.

     

                A spoon clattered on the counter and Kelly hurried over to her, dropping to a knee before her as she grabbed her shoulders. 

     

                “Hey, hey, it’s alright. It’s okay. What happened?”

     

                “I think I might need to stay here for a while if that’s okay.”

    Chapter 21

                Lena didn’t sleep at all that night.

     

                Instead, she got a bottle of vodka - the cheap stuff that burnt, that would leave her with a violent hangover in the morning so she could hate herself just that little bit extra - and drank it straight as she sank onto the sofa with an empty glass and a packet of cigarettes. She didn’t bother texting or calling Kara, she just drank quickly with the intention of getting blind drunk as she dissolved into quiet sobs.

     

                Curled up on the sofa, she was sloppy and careless, the uncapped bottle wedged between her thigh and the arm of the sofa as she chain-smoked the cigarettes and let the ash fall into her lap. The vodka worked quickly, the caustic, clinical taste of it scouring her throat as she coughed until her eyes watered - then again that might’ve been fresh tears - and she wallowed in her pit of grief and anger and helplessness. 

     

                So much was wrong that she couldn’t even begin to try and make sense of it all. Anger blinded her to the rest of it, her heart aching as she stewed in the heartbreak of Kara leaving, knowing she’d brought it on herself. How many times had she tried to tell her? Lena couldn’t even begin to count them. She’d never made it past the beginning of referencing her wife, present tense, before getting choked off by her own fear, her own cowardice.

     

                She’d never intended for it to go that far, that deep, had never imagined in a million years she could ever fall for someone else while she was utterly consumed by her love and heartache for her wife. It had felt like a betrayal, like she’d forsaken every wedding vow to Andrea whenever she’d so much as looked at Kara, but it had been the only thing that had kept Lena sane. The toll of a sick wife, one who didn’t even know her, who didn’t even remember there had been a brief period where their world had started and ended with each other, was far greater than Lena could ever have imagined.

     

                And still, she wouldn’t leave. Lena would stay until the very end, until the moment she lost the very last breathing shred of her wife because she loved her. And she loved Kara, in a way that she would never get to explore, never get to fully realise, destroying it before they’d even had the chance, just like she’d promised Kara months ago. She was always the destructive one, the one who had nobody. No one but a wife who couldn’t even remember her anymore.

     

                Bitter and devastated, Lena drank and drank and smoked until the packet was empty and the room was filled with the acrid smell of tobacco. It clung to her hair and her clothes and even the dog didn’t want to be near her, Aristotle curled up on the floor at the opposite end of the sofa as he watched her with sad, dark eyes, almost judgemental in a way.

     

                Brushing ashes from her lap, Lena drew in a shuddering breath and took another sip of vodka as she stared hollow-eyed at the blank TV. The apartment was silent, save for her crying, the thick emptiness of Kara’s absence making it feel inhospitable, but she was too tired to turn it on, didn’t want the loud harshness of reality TV as cold comfort without the woman who’d made it fun for her. 

     

                Lena knew an apology wouldn’t cut it. Not with this. She should’ve been honest from the beginning, had meant to be, except for the shockingly quick speed at which their friendship had started, where Kara had already made her assumptions based on Lena’s reluctant participation at Group. And she could’ve corrected her but there had been that understanding, that kinship in their shared pain for a loss that wasn’t quite the same but felt achingly familiar. That understanding would vanish the moment she confessed to her circumstances, that alien situation that left her feeling like she was the only person in the world going through it. All too quickly, it became too late for her to bring up the truth about Andrea, even if she’d been able to talk about her, force the words out. And Kara didn’t know her in the slightest, there were no expectations and no need for that unbearable pity that came from the people who knew her circumstances, and Lena basked in that feeling of being someone different.

     

                With Kara, she wasn’t the wife of the woman who’d been lost to an unfairly early diagnosis of a horribly degenerative illness, their time together now limited and virtually one-sided. With Kara, Lena was a presumed widow who’d already gone through the worst of it and was fighting her way back to the light. Except Kara had realised recently that wasn’t the case at all for Lena, that Lena was stuck, that Lena had to drink each night to cope, that the stress of her life was handled with cigarettes she hated but had taken up as if carrying the torch of Andrea’s nasty habits in her honour. That was her reality, but it had been nice to pretend for a while that she was making an effort to get better.

     

                Maybe she had gotten better in a way, the affair - it was , technically, but Lena knew her marriage was over in a way that was beyond any means to fix - helping to shock her out of getting stuck on Andrea in perhaps the worst way possible. Kara had replaced Andrea as so many lasts that it had made Lena sick at the start. How could the last person she’d kissed, made love to, and slept beside not be her wife? It had forced Lena to come to terms with those things she would never get back again, and that had helped a little but her grief had never been a thing that was a product of the past. She visited Andrea almost every day and left feeling it all again as if it was for the first time.

     

                And it never got easier. No matter how many times Andrea didn’t recognise her, how many meltdowns Lena had to help contain, how many times she was accidentally caught in the middle of an outburst, covering up bruises and bloodshot eyes from her crying as she came home to Kara and her gentle concern for Lena’s purported clumsiness. It only got worse as she watched her wife’s health decline with that hollow horror of knowing it would only continue to get even worse.

     

                Guilt still ate away at her for putting her in there, even though it had been her wife’s wishes. She’d gotten lost one too many times, still clinging to her memories of her wife enough to call Lena to come and pick her up, but it was a terrifying thing for both of them. Lena wondered if she’d wake up to a call in the middle of the night to Andrea blindly walking into traffic as her mind unravelled. She was called to Obsidian North with increasing frequency as meetings took a turn for the worse, as Andrea ranted in the middle of the open office floor in Spanish, an uncomfortable tension filling the space as her employees didn’t know what to do, as her security had to shepherd her back to her office and keep her in there until Lena could collect her, until investors pulled out and clients dropped her and Andrea had to hand the company over to a cousin. 

     

                Even after she’d been forced to give up the thing she loved, she’d try to go back, her key card deactivated so she couldn’t access the elevators, berating security and the receptionists until she was calmed down. Once, she’d gotten the keys to her Audi and been rear-ended as she’d stopped in the middle of the road, forgetting she had been driving for a brief moment. Lena couldn’t cope, not between her own company and the steadily declining mental functioning of her wife. She tried to give up L-Corp, asking Sam if she would leave her life in Metropolis and move back to the west coast to step up as CEO. Andrea wouldn’t let her, still lucid enough most of the time to be present in those decisions, their arguments often leaving them both in tears and Andrea confused and erratic afterwards.

     

                In the end, Lena came home from work one day to find Andrea sitting at the kitchen table with their family lawyer. Pausing in the mouth of the kitchen, Lena felt her throat constrict, eyes immediately filling with tears as she’d shaken her head, stubbornly refusing to allow the conversation she knew was coming to happen. In the end, she’d been made to sit and listen, Andrea sliding pamphlets across to her, detailing the services of the Leviathan Respite Home she’d chosen for herself, listening as her wife’s voice trembled with barely contained fear as she outlined the decision she’d made and then had their lawyer present her with her will and a stack of legal documentation that Lena would refuse to even look at for months.

     

                She’d gotten angry, her own fear manifesting as bitter rage as she’d refused to accept the decision that had already been made. Shutting herself in their bedroom, Lena had sat on the edge of their bed and buried her face in her hands as she’d cried with such agony that she’d thought she might never stop. How could they be discussing her wife moving out, their things becoming just Lena’s, an apartment without Andrea’s things, without her laughter and her nostalgic music and her torrent of Spanish as she called her father or spoke to the dog? She spoke in Spanish more often those days, reverting back to her easily remembered native language, Lena dusting off her rusty skills as she tried to make it easier for her. 

     

                In the end, she’d had to accept it. It wasn’t her decision, she’d had no say in the matter, despite her legal right to make those decisions for her wife. Lena would never have chosen that if it had been up to her. She would have made the apartment fool-proof so Andrea couldn’t escape, couldn’t hurt herself, could live in comfort with Lena. But it wasn’t her choice and she was struggling alone, drowning in the difficulty of helping her wife as she tried to come to terms with their new reality. 

     

                All she could do was help pack her things away, folding cashmere and silk and designer brands that would be wasted on the inside of a care home, setting dozens of Louboutins that Andrea wouldn’t be able to wear anymore aside for donation, cleaning out her half of the bathroom with the products that Andrea was particular about, packing them into toiletry bags and adding them to the stack of cases. Andrea helped as well but there were long stretches where she sat on the edge of the bed, pale with reluctance, instructing Lena.

     

                “You’d better not throw away my Birkin’s. Ever.”

     

                Choking on a breathless laugh, Lena swallowed thickly. “Never.”

     

                “Take care of my Hermès coat-”

     

                “You can take your coat. You might need it.”

     

                “I won’t.”

     

                “You might. What about when you go out? It might be raining.”

     

                “Okay, fine. I’ll take the coat.”

     

                They bickered back and forth about everything, Andrea taking a nihilistic approach to it as Lena tried to make her keep her things. What would she do without her favourite books? She had to take all of her perfumes; Lena was quietly horrified at the thought of her wife no longer smelling like herself, that sickly odour of nursing homes and hospitals settling in if she was left there to waste away. It was a long process with many tears and Lena just wanted it to be over - no, she never wanted to do it in the first place.

     

                A few months past Andrea’s thirty-fourth birthday, Lena buckled her wife into the passenger seat as Andrea sat limply, staring out the window with a hollow look of grief on her face. Lena couldn’t speak past the lump in her throat and her hands shook as she tried to click the seat belt into place.

     

                “Just let me-” Andrea started.

     

                “I’ve got it,” Lena rasped, a click punctuating her insistence.

     

                She’d driven her to Leviathan’s in the middle of Downtown, central to where their whole lives existed. It was a short drive from their penthouse, not far from their office either, but it was still too far. Lena parked in the lot out front and helped Andrea out of the car. Walking on ahead, Andrea’s back was straight and her shoulders were squared with her determination to do it; Lena was left behind, already crying before she stepped foot through the door. She’d refused to come before then, didn’t want to see the place her wife had sentenced herself to, and she didn’t want to go inside now.

     

                “Mrs Rojas,” a man greeted Andrea as she was admitted to the lobby. Lena followed, her face hard with anger as she scowled against her heartbreak, trying not to fall apart.

     

                “This is my wife, Lena,” Andrea introduced them, still knowing her then, although there had been so many times she’d forgotten already.

     

                “Russell Rogers,” the man greeted her, “I’m one of the carers here.”

     

                He was handsome and English, charming to a fault with a soothing manner that made Lena like him immediately. “Lena Luthor.”

     

                They’d been escorted to Andrea’s room, a surprisingly spacious place that almost seemed like a nice hotel, and then he’d given them a tour of the rest of the facility. It had security and a courtyard with a neatly cultivated garden for the residents to get fresh air and enjoy the outdoors, a games room and a cinema theatre, a dining hall where well-rated chefs prepared their meals. It seemed more like the business retreats Lena had been on, the staff seeming less like nurses and carers and more like waiters and assistants to the wealthier clientele who found themselves needing respite care. 

     

                Andrea’s bags were brought up to her room and Lena insisted on unpacking it all herself, lining up her things in the ensuite, which didn’t have a bath and had rails to hold onto and was big enough to fit a wheelchair. It wasn’t lost on her that the entire design of the place was catered to allow for medical care. Even the bed, which looked ordinary, especially once she’d made it in the same sheets that were on their own bed at home, allowed for it to be inclined at the push of a button and had wheels and rails hidden beneath the quilted valance.

     

                The respite centre was one of the most luxurious ones, if a place like that could ever be called such, which meant that the rooms were spacious and there was a veneer of grandeur over the medical equipment that blended in with the wealth of the place. Lena had done what she could to make Andrea’s room appear more homely, more like their penthouse, hoping the familiarity of it would be comforting, even if she didn’t remember why. 

     

                “You’d better go,” Andrea had gently murmured once she’d finished, giving her a wavering smile.

     

                Lena had burst into tears, her feet carrying her forward as she fell into her wife’s arms, sobbing into her shoulder as she grabbed fistfuls of her shirt. Holding her close, Andrea had rocked her slowly as Lena had cried and cried, leaving a wet patch on her clothes, softly murmuring reassurances to her. 

     

                Then her mood had changed and she’d thrust Lena back, gripping her arms tightly as she gave her a sharp shake, startling Lena enough to make her sobs die in her throat. “Stop it,” Andrea snapped, her cheeks colouring with anger as her pale blue eyes clouded with unease at the open display of sudden emotion. “I don’t have time for this, I- I have to be at the office-”

     

                Her sentence had died in her mouth and Andrea had let her go, shoulders slumping as she blinked, rubbing her forehead as she turned away. “I’m sorry.”

     

                “It’s okay,” Lena whispered, reaching out to touch her shoulder.

     

                Andrea had jerked away from her and then hugged her arms to herself, shrinking slightly as she meekly turned and gave her an apologetic smile, wavering as her eyes filled with tears. Lena didn’t want to leave her there, she just wanted to take her home.

     

                “You’d better go,” Andrea softly repeated.

     

                Nodding this time, Lena had kissed her and then hesitated, prolonging the moment before she stepped back. “I’ll see you tomorrow.”

     

                She’d gone home and cried herself to sleep in their bed, alone, with a bottle of whisky, and her life had followed the same monotonous routine of visiting Andrea once, sometimes twice, a day as she tried to remain cheerful, hopeful, which didn’t come naturally to Lena anyway. She worked, she slept, she sometimes ate, she drank far too much and found Andrea’s cigarettes that she hadn’t thrown out, smoking them on occasion. 

     

                And then she’d been given a flyer for a grief group that ran out of a local YMCA across town by Russell, one of Andrea’s bad bouts leaving her sitting in the lobby, crying as she tried to get herself under control. He’d suggested she check it out after a few conversations with Lena about counselling for herself had gone nowhere, and it had sat on the passenger seat of her car until the following Thursday, a month since she’d put Andrea in care, when she’d stopped by for curiosity's sake. And then she had met Kara.

     

                It had been such a sweet reprieve from her overwhelming life that Lena had been drowning in. Those weekly drives home after Group were a chance for her to feel as if she was understood, which turned into drinks and dinners and walks, all of it allowing Lena the opportunity to regain some sense of normalcy. She tried to make sure it didn’t affect her time spent with Andrea, her sole attention always on her wife as she watched Andrea struggle to remember her name, looking upset and angry and then pleased and relieved when she remembered, watched her forget their address and her phone number, the date of their anniversary and their first date, their first kiss. Lena watched with anticipated agony as the years were stripped away, each milestone forgotten as Andrea’s mind found it harder and harder to recall the memories that were still tucked away inside. 

     

                Cognitive decline could be rapid at that stage, heading towards the final stages, but Lena knew it could be years before Andrea forgot how to feed herself, forgot her own name, forgot how to speak and how to find her room. She was young, so painfully young at barely thirty-six, and they’d prepped Lena for the eventuality that she might not make it a few years past her diagnosis, as a lot of Alzheimer’s patients didn’t, but the doctors had also prepared Lena for the outcome that Andrea could very well spend the next twenty years declining until her health finally failed. Not knowing how long she had left was its own torture, and Lena tried to cherish the time she had with Andrea while bitterness ate away at her at the fact that it wasn’t her wife she was spending time with.

     

                There was still so much of Andrea left though, her brusque attitude, her dismissive entitlement, her sharp mind when she was talking about her early projects - less and less these days as she forgot her work - her sarcastic humour and the surety of herself. Even in the face of losing bits of herself, Andrea always seemed to ooze a sense of confidence, even in her erratic bouts of delusion she was always sure she was right, that conviction staying with her, which was maddening but reassuring for Lena, in a sense.

     

                Every day she visited her, and every day Lena felt the guilt grow a little bit bigger. She told Andrea about Kara at the beginning, when she still remembered her diagnosis often enough to react as herself, glad that Lena had a friend, someone to rely on even if Andrea couldn’t remember her name for the life of her. Every time Lena mentioned Kara, she would explain that she was a vet, that they’d met at a grief group, that her husband had died and Lena drove her home on Thursdays. It didn’t matter how many times she repeated herself, Andrea always forgot.

     

                But Kara remembered the things Lena told her, and it was a balm to the frustration of visiting her wife and feeling so helpless, trying to be patient, knowing it was nobody’s fault, but just feeling so angry at the entire situation. It only served to make Lena feel worse every time she resented the cyclical conversation and managing Andrea’s contrary moods, never sure which version of her she’d get the next time she visited. It was draining but she loved her and so she didn’t complain; Lena just drank more and declined alongside her while seeking comfort in her friend in any way she could get it.

     

                She fell asleep in the early hours of the morning, thinking of her wife and her lover and feeling torn in half with the grief of loving both of them and having neither. Crying herself to sleep, Lena was exhausted but still woke early with harsh sunlight spilling through the wide windows. Jolting awake, she threw an arm across her eyes, grumbling as she blinked back the gritty feeling of her tears, sloshing the vodka bottle that was still wedged beside her from where she’d fallen asleep. 

     

                Lena held it up by the neck, finding over half of it gone, and briefly considered finishing the rest of it before breakfast. But she already felt bad enough, grey with a nasty hangover as her head pounded and she tasted the stale cigarettes at the back of her throat. Staggering to her feet, Lena went to have a hot shower instead, vomiting three times before she even made it beneath the steaming water and once more in the shower.

     

                Choking down two Tylenol with a bottle of water after she emerged, Lena dressed down for the day, knowing there was no way in hell she’d make it to the office. All she wanted was the opportunity to talk to Kara properly, without emotions running high and a shouting match, but she knew it would be futile. Instead, she got ready to see Andrea, as usual, donning large sunglasses against the brightness and a coat to hide her casual clothes. 

     

                Making the familiar drive to Leviathan’s, Lena parked and felt a heavy weight in her stomach as she crossed over to the front door. There were two sets of doors to pass through before she was admitted to the hushed lobby and she made her way to the elevator and up to the third floor, where Andrea’s room was located.

     

                “Morning,” Lena wearily greeted Russell, one of the care nurses and the one she was most familiar with.

     

                “Lena. Everything alright?”

     

                Her mouth went dry and she managed a stiff nod, her eyes burning with the building pressure behind them. She swallowed thickly as she fell into step beside him as he moved away from the nurse’s station.

     

                “How is she today?”

     

                “She didn’t sleep well with her arm so she’s a bit restless. She keeps trying to leave for a meeting.”

     

                “Oh,” Lena murmured, her expression clouding. 

     

                She didn’t feel up to pandering to Andrea’s muddled perception of where she was and Lena’s shoulders slumped as she followed the familiar path to Andrea’s room. Russell knocked on the door and then opened it, a warm smile on his face as he stepped inside.

     

                “Mrs Rojas, look who’s here to see you.”

     

                Lena swallowed the lump in her throat and stepped inside, shedding her coat and setting down her bag. “Good morning,” she said with forced levity, giving her wife a pained smile.

     

                Andrea was dressed in the comfortable clothes Lena was constantly replacing, understated designer brands in the darker colours her wife preferred. It was a navy set today, the loose cotton pants and the matching shirt, sleeves rolled up, her hair clipped up but coming loose. Her pale blue eyes were quickly appraising, giving Lena a once over before she nodded to herself.

                

                “You must be the new assistant. You’re late.”

     

                Closing her eyes, Lena’s mouth thinned and then she let out a quiet breath. Opening her eyes, she smiled slightly and ducked her head apologetically. “Sorry. Traffic.”

     

                “Come. Quickly. We have work to do before the conference starts.”

     

                “What are we working on today?” Lena asked, stepping forward as Andrea moved over to the desk, taking a seat.

     

                “We’ll be presenting a prototype for my new VR lenses at the next National City tech expo in two months. Word is a few big money investors are going to be there so we need to make sure it’s impressive if we want the funding to get it past the R and D stage. Here, you take notes.”

     

                She handed Lena a notebook and pen and Lena flipped through the pages, looking at the indecipherable scribbles and half-constructed sentences, most of them in Spanish and unrecognisable from Andrea’s blocky lettering.                 Lena knew this game well, knew what would usually make her less agitated, in a more cooperative mood, and she knew enough of Andrea’s projects to jot down notes unprompted.                 “Let me see,” Andrea demanded a few minutes later, snatching the notebook from Lena and quickly assessing her notes. “You’re doing it all wrong.”

                Climbing to her feet, Lena stepped out of the room and found Russell at the small nurse’s station, where he was locking a medicine cabinet and pocketing the keys. He turned at the sight of her and gave her a small smile.

     

                “Alright?”

                “Something like that.”

                “My phone. She took it.”

                Blinking rapidly as she ran a hand over her hair, more strands coming loose, Andrea perked up slightly and sank down onto the armchair. Picking up the newspaper Lena had brought her, she shook it open.

                “The garden? I’ll need my coat.”

     

                “Yes,” he agreed. “Why don’t you find it in your wardrobe while we wait?”

     

                “My coat. My coat,” Andrea mumbled to herself, jerking open the wardrobe door. She dragged her coat off the hanger and held it before pausing. 

     

                Staring at Lena, her brow puckered, deepened by the scar she’d received a few years ago when it had first started to get bad.                 “I do know you,” Andrea said with soft surprise. Lena’s heart jolted as she looked at her, unbridled hope in her eyes, even though she knew it was foolish to do that to herself. “Mrs Luthor. I- you’re Lena’s mom.”

     

                Stomach plummeting, Lena stiffened.                 “Lillian,” Lena supplied.

     

                “Yes, Lillian. How is Lena? We- we were … friends, weren’t we? I haven’t seen her since graduation.”

                “She did.”

     

                “Oh. It would be good to see her again.”

     

                Eyes limned with tears, Lena swallowed thickly. “I think she’d like that.”

     

                “I have to go, I have a meeting. Here … give her my number.” Andrea dropped her coat to the floor and crossed over to her desk, writing quickly and then tearing the page free. “You’ll give this to her, won’t you?”

     

                She shoved the paper into Lena’s hand and Lena nodded, looking down at the first twelve digits of pi; she couldn’t remember her phone number anymore. Folding it in half, Lena slipped the note into the pocket of her pants and sniffed as she regained her composure.

                “Be more careful,” Lena berated her, panic making her heart pound in her chest.

                “Hey, hey, I’m sorry, I didn’t mean to snap.”

     

                Wiping her tears away as she backed off, Andrea gave her a scornful look, her hitching sobs twisting the knife in Lena’s chest.                 “Go down to the dining room. I’ll bring her down shortly,” Russell murmured to Lena before stepping around her. “Hey, Andrea, it’s okay. It’s alright. What’s the matter?”

     

                Looking confused as she stared at her damp palm, Andrea opened and closed her mouth as Lena pocketed her discarded phone and backed out of the door. She lingered outside as she watched Russell talk Andrea down, her confusion making Lena’s guilt even worse as she watched her wife struggle to pinpoint what was wrong. The reason was gone from her almost immediately and she blinked as she looked around and then spotted her coat.

     

                “I dropped my coat.”

     

                “Well, that’s okay. Look, problem solved. Do you want me to hang it up in your closet for you?”

     

                “It’s cold today,” Andrea mumbled, hugging her arms to herself.

     

                “Is it? Mhm, I think you’re right. It looks like it might rain. Tell you what, I’ll get you a sweater and then we’ll go downstairs for coffee. How does that sound?”

     

                “Coffee? I can’t- I can’t remember what my order is.”

     

                Resentment welled up at how easy it was for Russell to defuse the situation, to coax Andrea into listening to him, spinning the situations to get her to cooperate without her realising. For the better part of a year now, every time Andrea watched Russell walk into a room, her face lit up with delight, like a schoolgirl with a crush, and while Russell was only ever professional, Lena still resented the attention he was given while the most she got was the occasional bewildered look as if Andrea knew she should know her but couldn’t pin down from where.                 She made her way downstairs, to the dining room that looked like it could have been a hotel restaurant from the early 1900s, elegantly furnished in antiques to make for a comfortable area. There were tables evenly spaced, heavily embroidered curtains over the tall windows, covered with grilles on the outside, and a quiet hum of conversation with the other residents and visitors.                 “Why don’t you take a seat with Lena while I go and order drinks? I’m sure you two will get along famously.”

                “I’m an architect.”

                

                “Oh, really? Maybe you can build a new office for me.”

     

                Lena gave her a soft smile, her eyelids shuttering as a sense of peace filled her heart. These moments where she was engaging, almost playful, were a balm to the bad moments, even though she never remembered they were married, that she recognised the woman sitting across from her. Just the lucid presence of her mind was enough to ease some of Lena’s frustration but she knew the bouts never lasted long these days.                 “If you’d like,” Lena lightly replied. “What do you do for work?”

                Lena propped her chin up in her hand and raised her eyebrows, politely inquisitive as she smiled slightly. “Sure, let’s have dinner.”

     

                Russell smiled and ducked his head politely, clasping his hands behind his back as if he was a waiter at The Ritz.                 “So, are we splitting dessert?”

     

                “I- yeah, that sounds nice. Which one do you think we should go for?”

     

                “Might I suggest the coffee cake?” Russell interjected.

                “Listen, once we’re done here … I was thinking maybe we could head back to mine. It’s a bit of a mess - I’ve just moved here,” Andrea said with a sheepish laugh. “But we could have a drink.”

     

                “Oh yeah?” Lena murmured, a dimple appearing on one cheek. “I’d love to.”

     

                Smiling, Andrea ate a bite of the cake and Lena picked up her own fork, feeling queasy as she made herself eat, despite her hangover leaving her clammy and without any appetite.                 “It’s okay, why don’t you sit down?”

                “You alright? What happened?”

                Dropping the paper towels into the sink, she covered her face with her hands and broke down into sobs, full body ones that made her shoulders heave, that hitched in her throat, loud and ragged.                 “I want to take her home,” Lena said to Russell as she extracted herself, her chin wobbling as she quietly sobbed. There was a stubborn set to her jaw as she tried to swallow them. “She shouldn’t be in here.”

                “I understand-”

     

                “No, you don’t! You don’t understand.                 His mouth opened and closed and he blinked, understanding dawning on his face. “That vet …”

     

                Ducking her head down as she ran her tongue over her teeth, Lena smiled bitterly and let out a frayed laugh as she shook her head. “I guess it’s my own fault.”

     

                “Lena.”

     

                Dashing her tears away, she sniffed, plucked the wet paper towels from the sink, and tossed them in the trash. “It’s fine. I should go and check on her.”

     

                “You can’t take her home. You have to know that it would be worse for everyone involved.”

     

                Wrinkling her nose, Lena smiled wanly and met his eyes, her shoulders slumping with defeat. “I know. I just miss her a little bit more today.”

     

                “Just for a minute; she should rest.”

     

                Nodding, Lena made her way upstairs with him and they found Andrea sitting in the armchair and looking out the window. She turned at their arrival and smiled slightly, uncrossing her legs and climbing to her feet as she crossed the room. 

     

                “Hello. I’m … God, sorry, mental blank. I’m Andrea, it’s nice to meet you.” 

     

                She shook Lena’s hand and then Russell’s and instructed them to take a seat. Reclaiming her armchair, Andrea sat down and Lena sank onto the desk chair nearby. Giving her a wan smile, Lena felt her pounding headache returning as the Tylenol wore off.

     

                “I should leave you to it. I’ll be down the hall if you need anything.”

     

                “Coffee would be nice,” Andrea said with a smile. “A latte with oat milk and vanilla for me and … sorry, what was your name?”

     

                “Lena.”

     

                “Lena,” she softly repeated, her voice slightly tender as she smiled. “How funny; I had a friend with that name at school.”

     

                “Did you?”

     

                “Mm, you- oh, you could almost be sisters, now that I’m looking at you. You could be- oh, I don’t- I don’t know if she had any. What was her name? God, what was her name?”

     

                With a wavering smile on her lips, Lena drew in a shuddering breath. “It’s me, Andrea. Lena. Lena Luthor.”

     

                “That was her name! Do you know her?”

     

                “It’s me.”

     

                “I- I don’t understand.”

     

                Russell hovered in the doorway as they watched Andrea’s face crumple. “Tell her,” he prompted Lena. 

     

                One thing they’d always told her was to explain why Andrea was confused when she was lucid enough to understand she couldn’t remember things, but Lena hated this part. Having to tell her what was wrong, having to explain why she was struggling to understand what was going on. She was always advised against reminding her that they were married though, usually making her confusion worse as she tried to comprehend it and failed, that part of her mind completely closed off from her.

     

                “You have Alzheimer’s; you have trouble remembering things but it’s okay. Why don’t we get some coffee and we can talk about it.”

     

                Relief flashed across Andrea’s face and she smiled sheepishly, rolling her eyes. “Oh, you’re here for the interview. Sorry, I don’t know where my head is. I just got back from Switzerland last night; it was a rough trip. I crashed on one of the slopes and … well, now I have this.”
