                She raised her cast and let out a laugh and Lena closed her eyes, her shoulders slumping slightly. Inhaling, she opened her eyes again and smiled. “Right, well, should we get into the questions?”

     

                Pretending to be a reporter, Lena spent the better half of twenty minutes asking questions as Andrea answered in good humour, only tripping up on a few words and a brief stretch of Spanish that blurred back into English without her even realising she’d done it. She started pacing at one point, gesturing animatedly and then falling silent as she paused, then turning and resuming her pacing and ranting. Russell left them to it as he went to check on a few of the other residents, fetching lukewarm teas and coffees and getting a few of the elderly patients out of bed for a turn up and down the hallway as he paused outside their door to check in and carried on.

     

                Lena had to climb to her feet and take her hand when her pacing started getting a little agitated, and Andrea stopped, blinking as she faced her. A shallow crease formed between Andrea’s eyebrows and she gave Lena a searching look for a moment, before Lena looked down at their hands, her wife’s so familiar in her grasp that she wanted to hold onto it forever, leaching what comfort she could from it.

     

                “Look at your nails,” Lena clicked her tongue, holding Andrea’s hand as she eyed the chipped polish. “Let’s get that sorted, shall we?”

     

                She made her sit back in the armchair and fetched a little bottle of acetone locked away in a little safe with the other items deemed too risky to be left lying around. Using cotton balls, Lena wiped away the remains before gently filing them into shape. Then she held up a few bottles of polish.

     

                “Which colour do you think?”

     

                Humming, Andrea cocked her head to the side and then pointed at the beige one. She always picked the same, with an aversion to anything overly bright, save for the cherry red bottoms of the heels she was no longer allowed to wear. Nodding, Lena unscrewed it and held Andrea’s hand gently as she applied the first coat to her pinky. Working slowly, Lena finished the left hand and then moved on to the right, made more difficult with the new, bulky cast.

     

                “Are you okay? You seem upset.”

     

                A choked sob suddenly burst out of Lena as she kept her head ducked down, eyes bright with tears as she tried to swallow the next sob building in her chest. It hurt, a sharp pain cutting through her, and she felt her face redden with the sudden onslaught of emotion.

     

                “Yeah, I’m okay. I just miss you.”

     

                “I miss you.”

     

                Lena let out a strained laugh as Andrea mimicked her. “Thank you.”

     

                “You need help.”

     

                She reached out to touch Lena’s face and the strength went out of Lena as she knelt slumped on the floor, her hand shaking as she held the bottle of nail polish and dipped the brush back in. Touching the tears on Lena’s cheeks, Andrew pulled her hand back and frowned down at her fingertips as she tried to comprehend things. Lena wasn’t sure what she was seeing; she could have been wrapped tightly in a hallucination and not even realised what she was doing, her mind so loud that it overstimulated her as she forgot the thread of their conversation.

     

                “It’s okay,” Lena murmured, giving her knee a gentle squeeze. “Why don’t you let me finish your nails.”

     

                “My nails?” Looking surprised, Andrea blinked down at her nails. “Oh, yes.”

     

                Finishing them off with a second coat, Lena held Andrea’s hands in hers, made difficult by the cast, and made sure she didn’t smudge them for as long as possible. It was a pointless effort, knowing the nails wouldn’t completely dry for hours without curing the polish with UV light, and Andrea would ruin them long before then in one of her frantic bouts of activity. She was docile now though, looking tired and troubled, bewilderment in the vacant look of her eyes as they sat there holding hands until Russell returned.

     

                “She should rest.”

     

                “Okay,” Lena rasped, reluctantly letting go of her hands as she glanced over her shoulder. “Can I come back after dinner?”

     

                Looking apologetic, Russell gave her a grim smile. “It was a long night for her, and an emotional morning. Why don’t you let her rest today and come back in the morning?”

     

                Accepting his suggestion, Lena nodded, gathering up the various nail products and pushing herself to her feet. She put everything back where she’d gotten it from and then pulled on her coat and picked up her handbag. Making sure she had everything, she steeled herself and crossed over to Andrea, sinking down to a crouch as she rested a hand on her knee and gave her a tender smile before taking her hand.

     

                “I have to go but I’ll be back tomorrow, okay?”

     

                “Okay,” Andrea nodded.

     

                “I love you,” Lena fiercely whispered, her eyes bright with tears and her voice fraught with anguish. 

     

                She kissed the knuckles of Andrea’s hand and pushed herself to her feet before ducking down and kissing the top of her head as well, smoothing down her dark hair and stepping back. 

     

                “I’ll see you in the morning.”

     

                “Goodnight.”

     

                Leaving, she quietly conversed with Russell in the hallway for a few minutes as he assured her he’d make sure Andrea ate her food and got enough sleep, that he’d give her painkillers if her arm was bothering her, that he’d play Titanic for her on the TV built into the wall with protective plexiglass covering it if she got restless later.  There was a knot in her chest, a reluctance to leave that plagued her every day when she had to go, even if she was coming back in the evening. Still, she left, saying goodbye to Russell and a few of the other carers she was familiar with before she made her way out to the car park and climbed behind the wheel.

     

                In her car, she dissolved into tears and spent the next forty minutes sitting there, gripping the wheel in white-knuckled hands before she managed to choke her sobs down, wiping her splotchy cheeks dry and then starting her car. She linked one of the mindfulness Podcasts Kara had hooked her on through the car speakers and drove home following the instruction of the guide, inhaling and exhaling as her shaky breaths evened out and the hitching sobs subsided.  Back in her penthouse, her loneliness swallowed her, despite the happy dog that greeted her at the door. Sinking down to a crouch, Lena let out a slightly hysterical laugh as Aristotle tried to lick her cheek and chin, massaging his ears as she cooed over him and then climbed to her feet. 

     

                The living room was a mess and she dropped her bag and coat onto the sofa and sat down heavily. Biting her nails as she stared blankly at the wall with a glazed look in her eyes, Lena felt so empty inside that she didn’t know what to do. The bottle of vodka was there, with enough in it to see her drunk before lunch, and she thought about Andrea’s words, about how she needed help, the shockingly perceptive words of a woman who was starting to forget her own name. And then she reached for the bottle.

    Chapter 22

                She’d cried herself to sleep last night in her sister’s spare room, which was in the midst of a makeover for a children’s room, Kelly quietly confessing they’d started the adoption process in earnest with the wedding out of the way. And now Kara was monopolising the room, derailing her sister’s life once more as her own fell apart. It was her own fault really for being too trusting, too willing to overlook the gaps in the stories, to not ask too many questions, for being so easy and accommodating at the expense of her own feelings.

     

                Brooding and devastated, she’d woken up early for work shortly after Alex had arrived home from her shift at the hospital and hadn’t explained a thing to her. She knew Kelly would have filled her in, her sister-in-law somewhat sheepish as she ate her oats and drank her coffee at the kitchen table. Kara had gotten ready for work and left early, riding the bus - a considerably longer commute now, as a result of her own actions that had led to a new job - and going through the motions. If Jack noticed anything wrong, he tactfully kept it to himself and Kara was as tentatively kind in the staff break room as ever as she ate her lunch and made small talk with the vet nurses and made coffee as they discussed their weekends, despite it now being Wednesday.

     

                After work, she rode the bus home after a day of trying hard not to think about Lena and found Alex packing away things in the spare room. Standing in the doorway, bedraggled and hollow-eyed, Kara had swallowed the lump in her throat, unable to look at her sister.

     

                “Sorry.”

     

                “What happened?”

     

                Shrugging, Kara’s mouth twisted with dismay. “You were right.”

     

                Alex had stared at her with confusion, expecting more, and Kara just stood there for a moment before gesturing helplessly and letting her hands fall back to her sides. Blowing the air out of her cheeks, she let out a small laugh.

     

                “And I guess this is me coming to cry to you.”

     

                Shoulders slumping as a grim look of concern softened her face, Alex crossed over to her and wrapped her in a gentle hug. Propping her chin on her shoulder, Kara’s eyes stung as she blinked rapidly.

     

                “You know you can always stay here.”

     

                “I know, I just- I shouldn’t have let myself become so dependent on her for everything. I … I shouldn’t have moved in. You were right about everything, if that makes you feel happy to hear.”

     

                “Don’t be an ass,” Alex sighed with weary annoyance. “You know I wanted to be wrong more than anything.”

     

                Grimacing, Kara shoved her hands into the pockets of her scrubs and shrugged again. Shoving a box beneath the bed, Alex looked at Kara over her shoulder and raised her eyebrows.

     

                “Can you come with me to get my things? I told her I’d get it all tonight and leave the keys.”

     

                “Sure. Do you want to go there now?”

     

                “Yeah, maybe. She’s usually home late so it’s probably a good time.”

     

                Nodding, Alex got her shoes and her keys and they trekked across town in her car, Kara fiddling with the radio as she tried to settle on a station, restless and nervous. She found it hard to keep her mind focused as Alex inched through rush hour traffic, asking her questions that Kara was too distracted to pay attention to.

     

                Her key rattled in the lock and Kara warily stepped into the silent apartment, listening to the delayed sound of Aristotle’s claws skittering on the floor as he rushed to greet her. Giving him a cursory pat and a quick fuss, Kara moved further inside, her muscles coiled tightly as she anticipated Lena’s presence, but she was nowhere to be seen in the living room.

     

                Alex followed Kara in, just as quietly and cautiously, and shut the door behind her. Walking through to the kitchen, Kara paused again in the doorway, making sure the coast was clear. There was evidence of Lena’s presence there though, a cluster of bottles of vodka, whisky, wine and tequila crowded together and a few more broken in the sink.

     

                “Jesus fucking Christ, surely she hasn’t drunk all this?” Alex muttered, picking up the bottle of whisky and letting out a low whistle. “This is expensive stuff.”

     

                “Leave it alone,” Kara tightly told her.

     

                “Do you think she’s home?”

     

                “Her keys are in the dish in the hallway. I’ll make it quick.”

     

                “Don’t you want to … I don’t know, talk?”

     

                Letting out a huff of laughter, Kara ran a hand over her face, so tired and so heartbroken that the last thing she wanted to be doing was packing up her belongings. Shaking her head, she sighed and carried on.

     

                “No, I don’t want to talk to her.”

     

                Alex shadowed her to the bedroom and Kara glanced at Lena’s shut door, wondering if she was in there listening, or maybe she was in her office at the end of the hallway. Maybe she was passed out in bed, drunk from the selection of bottles in the kitchen. Either way, it wasn’t Kara’s business.

     

                Opening her bedroom door, she murmured directions to Alex to clean out the bathroom cupboards while she tackled the drawers in the bedroom. She didn’t bother with folding, she shoved as much as she could into the suitcase and duffel bag she’d brought with her.

     

                With most of her things in storage at Lena’s office building, in some sub-basement unit, Kara didn’t have a lot to take with her, and she didn’t need the stuff in storage yet. Not that she had anywhere to put it either, but she held onto the opinion that Lena would hold onto it for her for a few weeks until Kara got her own place.

     

                Zipping up the case once she was done, Kara dragged it over to the door and out to the kitchen. Alex was petting Aristotle in the living room, a bag slung over her shoulder with Kara’s toiletries, and she straightened at the appearance of her.

     

                “Is that it?”

     

                “Yep.”

     

                Nodding, her sister moved to take the duffel bag from her and moved towards the front door. Jangling the keys to the buildings, penthouse and Audi in her hand, Kara wheeled the suitcase to the console and dropped the keys into the little bowl. Hesitating a moment, prolonging her departure, she couldn’t help but feel a twinge of disappointment that Lena hadn’t even tried to stop her. 

     

                “I’ll miss you, buddy,” she murmured to Aristotle, giving him one last pat before she slipped out of the apartment and let the door click shut.

     

                They made their way downstairs and packed the suitcase and the bags into the car before Kara climbed into the passenger seat and buckled up. She was silent as Alex drove her home, brimming with questions but keeping them to herself for now as Kara propped her chin up in her hand and stared out the window, deep in thought.

     

                Lugging everything up to her sister’s apartment, Kara made a pile of her bags and then sank down onto the edge of the bed Alex had made up in fresh sheets for her. Shoulders sloping forwards as she hunched over, elbows on her thighs, Kara chewed on her bottom lip, brimming with so much pent-up frustration and confusion as she tried to muddle through it.

     

                Leaning against the doorframe with her arms crossed over her chest, Alex watched her closely. “Are you going to tell me what happened?”

     

                “No,” Kara rasped, her voice cracking as her cheeks heated with embarrassment.

     

                Crossing over to her, Alex sank down onto the small twin bed and pressed a hand against Kara’s back. Turning her head aside, lips pressed into a flat, trembling line, Kara drew in a shuddering breath through her nose as she tried to blink tears away.

     

                “It’s okay.”

     

                “I- I don’t think … it’s my place to say. Um … it just- it’s very messy and … I think maybe I should’ve known better but … anyway, if I could stay here for just a few weeks-“

     

                “I told you, you can stay as long as you want.”

     

                Shaking her head, Kara shaking exhaled as hot tears ran down her cheeks. Hastily wiping them away, she sniffed. “Thanks.”

     

                “I’ll make some coffee,” Alex murmured, cupping Kara’s head and kissing the side of it before pushing to her feet. 

     

                Pressing the heels of her palms into her eyes, Kara let out a shaky breath and raked her fingers through her hair before climbing to her feet. Digging clean clothes out of her bags, she slipped out of the bedroom and into the bathroom, stripping off her scrubs and turning on the hot water. Letting it sluice down her back as her hair was plastered to her face, Kara quietly broke down again, relying on the sound of running water to mask the sound as she tried to be brief, shampooing as she choked down her sobs, soap suds and the sweet smell of vanilla filling the shower stall as she scrubbed herself clean and slowed her breaths.

     

                Stepping out, she wrapped a towel around herself and dried off before dressing in her pyjamas and then wrapping the towel around her wet hair. Leaving her glasses on the counter, she walked out to the open living area and curled up on the sofa with the cup of coffee Alex had made for her. Her sister stared at her, taking in the bloodshot eyes, the pink skin, soft from the shower but with a pinched look of grief.

     

                “I was thinking of Chinese takeout for dinner,” Alex hesitantly suggested.

     

                “Sure,” Kara rasped, sniffing as she sank deeper into the sofa.

     

                “Do you, um, do you want to talk? You don’t have to tell me everything, just … maybe it’ll help to get it off your chest.”

     

                Letting out a strained laugh, Kara took a sip of coffee and remained silent. Running an idle finger around the rim of her coffee mug, she swallowed thickly. “You know how I felt about her.”

     

                “Yes.”

     

                “I guess I- I thought because we both shared the same pain, the differences didn’t matter but … that wasn’t true. It turns out … our circumstances are very different and … I guess we’d both been using each other but I was doing a lot better and she- she was just getting worse. And I think maybe that should’ve been enough of a warning but I ignored it, and … I guess it came back to bite me on the ass.”

     

                “What are you going to do now? I mean … is it salvageable? I thought- sorry if I’ve misunderstood, but … she loves you, right? I thought …”

     

                Wrinkling her nose as fresh pain cut through Kara, she smiled bitterly, her eyes creasing at the corners. “Yeah, I think so but I’ll only ever be the other woman.”

     

                “The other woman. Kara- come on. Can you really blame her for being stuck in a shit situation where she has to get used to the idea that her wife is dead and she loves someone else? You, of all people, after you spent months justifying this mess to me in the first place, knowing the two of you were still grieving.”

     

                The corner of Kara’s mouth twitched at the mention of Lena’s dead wife but she just closed her eyes, her heart in her throat. “It’s not as simple as that.”

     

                “Simple? Yes, because this whole thing has been so simple up until now. Honestly, I’m not trying to be a dick but it’s almost like you’re committed to fucking up your own life too. I don’t think you’re doing any better; you just had her. And that’s not the same thing.”

     

                Nodding in concession to her sister’s words, knowing it was overwhelmingly true, Kara took another sip of her coffee. “Well, now I don’t, so I guess I’ll have to figure out the rest.”

     

                “Kara-”

     

                Uncurling, she rose from the sofa, a tense set to her jaw. “I’m going to lie down for a bit.”

     

                Shutting herself in the spare room, she sat on the edge of the bed and finished off her coffee in peace, breathing in the smell of fresh paint from the new coat on the walls. Setting her mug down on the half-assembled bedside table, Kara stretched out on the bed and rolled over, her back to the door as she tried to quieten her mind enough to sleep. 

     

                Feeling physically and emotionally drained, it shouldn’t have been that difficult, but she couldn’t stop thinking about Lena. All day, it had been an effort to focus on her work as she often found her mind drifting, trying to make sense of it all. It was a shock, to say the least, and Kara didn’t know how to feel. Should she have been more understanding? Should she have given her more time to explain? Was she entitled to feel like she’d been betrayed by a small omission of the truth that had snowballed into something bigger than either of them could have thought? It hurt to talk about Mike, and she had a lot of empathy for how difficult it must be for Lena to talk about her wife, but surely once in eighteen months there had been a good time to tell Kara, and not after they’d slept together, moved in together, loved each other. She felt conflicted by the whole thing, feeling valid in her hurt but at the expense of someone else being hurt in the process.

     

                She didn’t nap at all before the food came, and Kara sat up at the quiet knock on the door after listening to the sound of murmured conversation as Kelly arrived home with dinner. Emerging from the room, her wet hair dried into a tangled mess and a pale look of mournful self-pity on her face, Kara helped set the table and joined them for dinner. She was silent and brooding, picking at her potstickers and pushing lo mein and Peking duck around her plate as she obstinately refused to indulge any attempts to draw her into a conversation.

     

                Going to bed early, Kara slept soundly and woke early the next day for work. Draining two cups of coffee in the kitchen before she left, she fell into her old routine of walking to the bus stop from her sister’s place, riding the bus to work - a slightly different and lengthier trip now - and then walking the rest of the way to the clinic for a day of work with different people, different patients but the same issues. 

     

                It was a Thursday which meant she had Group that evening, and she deliberated all day about whether or not she should go, knowing it wasn’t actually helpful, that she’d only been going because Lena was going, even though Lena was only going because she was going. But she knew without a doubt Lena wouldn’t be going, that she would be angry and avoidant in Kara’s stunned rejection as they both struggled to cope with her wife’s illness. It was a safe bet that she wouldn’t bump into her and Kara didn’t want to go home, didn’t want to sit with her sister and wife while they discussed their plans for adoption, in love and success, their lives on track and simple for them. Kara was unfairly bitter all over again.

     

                There was also that need to get everything off her chest to a group of strangers who she didn’t have to see outside of the walls of the Y, and maybe that was where she’d gone wrong with Lena. They’d met at a low-budget group counselling session and had made it into something far bigger than they ever should have, their pain existing outside of that dingy recreation room and forged into some codependent relationship as the two of them tried to fill the hole. That was all it was, or that was what she needed it to be to look back with some clarity and perspective that didn’t hurt quite so much if she could convince herself it had been a mistake.

     

                She arrived right on time, hastily making a cup of tea and snagging a donut before she took a seat, her eyes anxiously scanning the room for any sign of Lena before she sagged with relief. Her hand was shaking slightly at the adrenaline-fuelled panic that she might have shown up, but Kara knew her - not as well as she’d thought but she knew her all the same. Slowing her breathing as her pounding heart settled, she took small bites of her donut and sipped her tea as she tried to focus on the stories people were telling, but she was visibly restless as she shifted in her chair.

     

                “Kara, you look like you have something on your mind. Would you like to go next?” Thomas asked, earlier than she’d anticipated as she blinked in surprise.

     

                “Me? Um … sure.”

     

                She stopped fidgeting and set her cup down on the floor, slowly smoothing her hands over her thighs before opening her mouth to talk. Nothing came out and she hummed disconcertingly, let out a strained laugh before trying again as she gestured matter-of-factly. 

     

                “I’ve … uh, it’s- it’s been a difficult couple of days. I thought- well … it doesn’t matter,” Kara stammered, rubbing her forehead as she stared at the worn carpet in the middle of the circle. “I think … I’m struggling with the concept of grief.”

     

                “In what way?”

     

                Frowning, she pressed her lips into a flat line, trying to pick her words carefully. “Do you think that … grief is exclusive to people who have lost someone?”

     

                Humming as he shifted back in his seat, folding his arms over his chest, Thomas considered the question. “I think that grief is more complex than that. To view it as something that’s exclusive to one experience is … perhaps very limiting. We all experience loss in different ways, at different speeds and intensities, different stages.” 

     

                “But what about if the person isn’t dead?”

     

                “For some … I think grief can manifest before we’ve even lost the person we’re grieving for. Take for example, which I’m sure a few of our number here can agree with, having a sick parent, spouse, or child. With a diagnosis, the grieving process can begin prematurely as one watches their loved one slip away before the finality of the loss. That slow process of grief can sometimes help with the acceptance of that loss, that sense of relief that a loved one is no longer in pain, but it can be just as debilitating in its difficulty to manage.” 

     

                “I don’t think someone who hasn’t lost a loved one could ever begin to understand it though. Even if they have a sick loved one. It’s not grief , not in the same sense of the word. I understand … people can be upset, and they might prematurely mourn what they’re going to lose, but … it’s nowhere near the same,” Kara objected.

     

                “Why not?”

     

                Frustration making a muscle twitch in her jaw, Kara gestured vaguely. “Because the person is alive. It’s not the same as that shock of having someone ripped away from you.”

     

                “I think … perhaps it’s different for people like you, with a sudden accident. You might have felt like the rug had been pulled out from under you, your grief sudden and intense, but for people who are yet to lose a loved one, maybe they’ve already grieved the loss for six, seven or eight months before the loss occurs, maybe even years . I think perhaps there are also different circumstances for grief that aren’t to do with the ending of life, as such, but the loss of an important relationship. Divorce or breakups and lost friendships can bring a sense of grief with them, at a lower intensity perhaps, but that grief may be very real to that person. That sense of finality, of losing something forever. I think that , more than the nature of the circumstances, is what grief is really about. It’s not necessarily about death.”

     

                “I- but … I don’t think it’s fair-”

     

                “I think grief is very fair. Much like death, it doesn’t discriminate. We all feel that intense sorrow for something at some point in our lives. Loss doesn’t have to happen the same way for us to be allowed to grieve in a way that’s deemed appropriate. You’ve mentioned in the past that your friends and family have struggled with your grief; do you think it’s fair of them to make that judgement?”

     

                Crossing her arms over her chest, Kara’s cheeks heated and she looked away, teeth clenched. Her throat closed up and she couldn’t respond, a shakiness in her chest as she blinked rapidly, eyes bright with a film of tears. 

     

                “I’d be very interested in hearing your perspective on it, Kara,” Thomas gently prompted her.

     

                “No,” she managed to grind out, her voice hoarse.

     

                Blinking in surprise, he echoed her. “No?”

     

                “No. I don’t want to talk to you. I don’t even want to be here . I don’t even know why I bother coming anymore, I just- I come here because at least I can convince myself I’m doing something to get better, but … it’s fucking useless so I don’t even know what the point is anymore.”

     

                The room was silent and she felt embarrassment wash over her, her skin prickling with the feeling of being watched, and Kara ran a hand through her hair before quickly climbing to her feet. Stooping to pick up her half-empty tea and her backpack, she straightened again.

     

                “Um … I think I might go, actually.”

     

                Thomas didn’t try to stop her, just nodded as she gathered her things and stalked out of the room. No one spoke until the door squealed shut behind her and Kara hunched her shoulders as she made a hasty exit. Distant sirens and rushing traffic greeted her with a burst of neon lights from the convenience store across the street. 

     

                Coming to a stop at the bottom of the steps, Kara ran a hand through her hair and blew the air out of her lungs, pacing back and forth for a moment. Closing her eyes, she shook her head and then carried on her way, walking to the bus stop with her backpack and her confusion and grief weighing her down.

     

                Riding the bus back to Alex and Kelly’s, Kara found the apartment silent. Her sister was on a night shift and she assumed Kelly was running errands after catching up on sleep from her night shift. Feeling a little lost, Kara made herself toast for dinner and cracked open a beer before tucking herself away in the spare room.

     

                Looking around at the half-assembled furniture, the new curtains that were still in the packaging as a rod leaned against one wall, flatpack boxes with shelves that needed to be put up where the brackets had been drilled into the wall and then abandoned, Kara needed the distraction. Trying to be helpful, Kara sat on the bedroom floor with its new thick carpet and slowly started to assemble things in between bites of toast and sips of beer. 

     

                She got the end table finished and stood it upright before unveiling a lamp and setting it on top, then she climbed onto the bed and drilled the curtain rod into place with the new drapes looped on, adjusting it over the window. Turning her attention to the shelves next, Kara had them both in place and then unpacked the flat boxes for the new dresser. It was all very neutral and she wondered whether they would have a boy or a girl when they made it to the end of the process, whether it would be a newborn or a toddle, maybe older again, a pre-teen like Kara was, wondered what it would be like to be an aunt with the bitter knowledge she most likely wouldn’t be a mother. 

     

                It was peaceful and fulfilling as she worked until she ran out of things to put together, the burr of the drill falling silent as she looked around at the result of her productivity. Tidying away the boxes and styrofoam padding and vacuuming up the mess, Kara washed her dishes and put them away and retired to her room to listen to a Podcast. She got distracted partway through, the temptation to Google Lena too convincing as she wondered what she’d find. Kara wasn’t big on social media, had no interest in business or the news beyond the major headlines, and so she’d never even considered looking her up before to find a LinkedIn profile or check out L-Corp’s website.

     

                She started there though, clicking through the projects that they’d completed in recent years and the ones that were currently in development. Lena was present in a number of photos and Kara hesitated before quickly swiping to the next one, reading about the initiatives and the recyclable material that Lena had introduced in an effort for greener projects. There was also a page for the partnerships associated with L-Corp and Kara’s stomach lurched at the sight of an Alzheimer’s charity and another for dementia before she got off the website. On Google, she scrolled through a few articles and found one relating to the newly constructed National City Children’s Hospital a few years back, Lena posing for a photo with the new Chief of Surgery, local government officials and her wife, smiling in front of a red ribbon cordoning off the front door of the building as Lena held the oversized scissors.

     

                Reading the names listed beneath the photo, she found Andrea Rojas and searched her up as well. Stomach lurching as the familiar tech company Obsidian North popped up, Kara felt her throat go dry as realisation dawned on her. They’d had this conversation before, so long ago, that time they’d gone to Metropolis together and Kara had mentioned the CEO getting sick and stepping down. She wasn’t involved in the tech world, wouldn’t have known Andrea by sight or name, only picked up on the tidbit in conversation with her more tech-savvy friends, but it was Lena’s wife. Lena’s wife, who she’d constructed the new office building for, her magnum opus, her passion project, the one that meant the most to her. Of course it was, and Kara felt suddenly very idiotic to have not picked up on the trail of breadcrumbs. But how could she have known they were all linked? Even if she had known, she still never could have guessed that Andrea Rojas was alive, tucked away in some respite home for twenty-four-seven care as she steadily deteriorated. 

     

                A knock on the door interrupted her research and she sat up, humming as she removed her headphones and ran a hand through her hair. Kelly cracked open the door and then opened it wider, blinking in surprise as she looked around at the room, which was half put together now, and just needed to be made more homely for a child.

     

                “Oh, you’ve been busy.”

     

                “Mm, needed the distraction.”

     

                “Thanks.”

     

                Nodding, Kara fiddled with her phone. Kelly leaned against the door frame as she cocked her head to the side, looking at her. “You alright?”

     

                “Mhm.”

     

                “You’re home early.”

     

                “Yeah, I, uh … I left Group,” Kara confessed, wrinkling her nose as she smiled tightly. “Doesn’t really feel like it’s helpful so … yeah. It just feels like a bunch of nonsense.”

     

                “Well, I’m making chicken and black bean enchiladas if you want to give me a hand and talk about it.”

     

                Considering it, Kara wearily climbed to her feet and left her phone on the bed as she followed Kelly into the kitchen. They worked beside each other in companionable silence for a while, draining the cans of beans and corn, sauteing onions and bell peppers in a pan and dicing chicken. As she seared the chicken in the pan, Kara felt the burning urge to speak and swallowed the lump in her throat as she nudged the contents of the pan around.

     

                “Hey, can I- can I ask you a question? We were just talking about it in Group and … I’m just curious what your take on it is.”

     

                “Of course,” Kelly lightly murmured.

     

                “Do you think … grief is more about general loss than death?”

     

                Pausing, Kelly glanced over at her, the knife hovering over the bell peppers. Kara met her eyes with a nervously apprehensive look on her face, blue eyes wide and doleful. Mouth thinning as she considered the question, she deliberated for a moment before responding.

     

                “I think … the general perception of grief is to do with death, but it’s not the only reason for grief.”

     

                Nodding, Kara nudged the chicken about, her throat feeling like it was closing up. “If someone lied to you as a product of their grief, do you- do you think that’s like … a good enough excuse?”

     

                Letting out a bewildered laugh, Kelly’s eyebrows drew together as she smiled faintly. “What? No. Absolutely not. Maybe it’s a reason for the lie but I think lying in itself is usually a very negative thing that serves no one but the liar. Why? What did she lie about?”

     

                Shrugging, Kara masked a wince of pain. “Nothing. I mean … it doesn’t really matter anymore so … yeah.”

     

                “Okay.”

     

                The conversation turned to lighter topics after that, Kara asked about work and reassured Kelly she’d be there for drinks tomorrow night, asking about the adoption process and confessing that Alex hadn’t really told her much about the whole thing. They’d been approved a while ago but with Kara and the wedding, they hadn’t really been in a position to pursue it any further but the last few weeks had helped progress it quickly. Kara made a mental note to find somewhere else to stay as soon as possible so she didn’t hold them back from the family that they wanted. She knew Winn would let her sleep on his couch if all else failed.

     

                Alex was home shortly after the enchiladas came out of the oven, and they all sat down for dinner together again, listening to her sister regale them with a story about a surgery that day. It was a strikingly similar process in the crossover between treating humans and animals and Kara was able to keep up with the conversation about the hospital with ease, although there were giant gaps in her knowledge about humans, while she could have detailed the anatomy of multiple breeds of dozens of species to their utter bewilderment. 

     

                Her Friday was occupied with another day of work and then she came home to get ready for drinks. Showering and changing into jeans and a plaid shirt, she waited for Alex and Kelly to get home from their shift and the three of them went to Al’s together. Everyone was there that night and Kara followed her sister inside and made for their usual table.

     

                Ordering two vodkas at the bar, Kara knocked them both down quickly and then ordered a beer as Al gave her a sceptical look. Wedged in between Alex and Nia, Kara was sullen as she nursed her bottle of beer and offered very little to the conversation.

     

                “Where’s Lena tonight?” Querl asked as they started on their second round of drinks.

     

                “I don’t know,” Kara murmured, a glazed look in her eyes.

     

                “Text her; see if she’s coming.”

     

                Shifting uncomfortably, Kara held her bottle between her palms and idly rolled it. “No, it’s alright.”

     

                There was a tense moment as everyone looked at each other, Alex and Kelly tight-lipped as they sipped their drinks while Kara kept her eyes downcast. After a moment, Winn let out a hesitant laugh, looking around.

     

                “Are we missing something?”

     

                “We had a, uh, a bit of a falling out. I … I’m staying with Alex and Kelly for a while,” Kara slowly confessed.

     

                “Wait, what? You got kicked out?” Nia quietly exclaimed, leaning back to look at her properly.

     

                “Lena wouldn’t just kick her out,” Querl objected, shaking his head as he reached for his drink. “She’s nice.”

     

                Letting out a strained laugh, Kara smiled half-heartedly as she shrugged, looking down at the sticky ring stains on the table as she avoided looking anyone in the eye. “No, I- I moved out. Voluntarily.”

     

                “Oh. Why?” Winn asked.

     

                “Um … just a lot going on for her personally. It was for the best.”

     

                “So what, you’ve completely fucked your life over for this woman and that’s it?” James laughed, frowning.

     

                Bristling, Kara grit her teeth with chagrin. “I didn’t-“

     

                Snorting, James shook his head and gestured pointedly. “Kara, you don’t even have a house anymore because you sold it to move in with her. You’ve become so dependent on her in the last year that she had to find you a new job because you lost yours, and now we’re all … what? Supposed to walk on eggshells around you again because you’ve been brought back down to reality and had your heart broken by the widow you were screwing as if we all didn’t warn you against this. Come on.”

     

                “I wasn’t dependent on her and I’m not heartbroken ,” Kara scoffed.

     

                “Yeah, right,” Winn muttered.

     

                “You know what, I’m not having this conversation with you lot. You don’t even know the half of it.”

     

                Raising his eyebrows, James placidly smiled in an infuriating manner. “Of course we don’t; you’ve barely even been around, bailing on us so you can sit at home with her all the time. Can you blame us?”

     

                Scoffing, Kara rolled her eyes. “Don’t act as if that’s the reason you don’t like her. You’re just mad that I had friends outside of us, that I met someone who took up his seat.”

     

                “Well, yeah, Kara, he was our friend. You conveniently forget that when you’re feeling sorry for yourself.”

     

                “Sorry for myself?”

     

                Alex heaved a sigh, reaching out to spread her arms between the two of them as the conversation started to get heated. The two shots had kickstarted the pleasant hum in Kara’s veins and she was already in a foul mood, her patience worn thin, and Alex understood that more than James did.

     

                “Alright, how about we cool it down.”

     

                Holding his hands up defensively, James shook his head. “Alright, okay, I’m not doing this. You’re mad, I get that but I was patient with you and you took advantage of it and that’s not my fault. You’re not innocent here; you never showed up for work, you slept with William-“

     

                There were exclamations of surprise and Kara’s face reddened as she spluttered. “Not that it’s any of your business-“

     

                “He liked you and you fucking used him!” James said with an exasperated laugh, shaking his head. “That’s what you do. And that’s probably what happened with Lena as well because there’s only so long you can live rent-free in someone’s house, driving her flash car every day - yes, I noticed - and having everything catered to you because she’s lonely enough to give you all of that in exchange for getting laid. It’s pathetic.”

     

                “James,” Kelly tightly interjected, giving her brother a warning look.

     

                He shrugged helplessly, looking mildly surprised that his sister was jumping to Kara’s defence. “Seriously? You can’t be happy with this; you’re about to adopt a fucking child, Kelly. Except you already have a thirty-five-year-old one living with you.”

     

                Slipping off her stool, Kara jerked it back with a loud grating sound, aware that they were attracting looks from the other patrons now. Nia also climbed to her feet, wrapping an arm around Kara’s shoulders as she loudly suggested a game of pool. Querl quickly agreed and slipped away to set the table but Kara just shrugged Nia’s arm off, brimming with hurt and anger. Eyes bright with tears and her face red, Kara’s voice wobbled as she sharply replied.

     

                “Sorry that everything went to shit because my husband fucking died and left a shitload of debt behind without any life insurance because he thought he was fucking invincible, and remortgaging our apartment could barely cover it, and I couldn’t pay the bills by myself on the shit wages you paid me before you fucking fired me.”

     

                “You called out sick for your friend’s dead wife’s birthday. Do you hear how fucking insane that sounds? Do you, Kara? You were willing to lose your job to sit at home with the woman you were screwing because she was sad -“

     

                “Wait, what?” Alex spluttered, turning to look at Kara. “That’s why you got fired?”

     

                Ignoring her sister, Kara curled her hands into fists. “Does it fucking matter why? It’s more than you did for me. I would have loved it if you could’ve been there for me for things like that. We’ve been friends since I was in college, you’ve been there for my entire career; did I get a text from you on Mike’s birthday to see how I was doing? No. You know who sent me flowers on every occasion? Every anniversary or holiday? Lena . I would do it all again to help her if she needed it because I know she’d do the same for me, and it’s more than I can say for you. And for the record, her wife’s not fucking dead.”

     

                “What?” Alex and Kelly exclaimed at the same time.

     

                “But you don’t give a shit about that, do you? Not a shred of empathy for anyone. You are in your forties with some vendetta against a woman you don’t even fucking know.”

     

                “Yeah, well, to be honest Kara, I don’t think you knew her all that well either,” James said with a pitying laugh as he shrugged.

     

                “You’re a fucking asshole.”

     

                Nia murmured something unintelligible and touched Kara’s shoulder but was roughly shrugged off again. Snatching her jacket from the stool, Kara stormed off to pleading protests following after her and the sound of the argument resuming. Pushing open the bar door, she barged out into the cool night air, running a hand over her face as she paced the sidewalk and then sagged against the brick wall of the bar.

     

                Sinking to a crouch, she hung her head and choked on a ragged sob as the tears that had been threatening to spill finally did. Anger choked her up and Kara tried to stamp it down - angry with James, angry with Lena, angry with herself - but it was useless and she felt smothered by it as she dragged in sharp lungfuls, trying to rein it back in.

     

                The door burst open a minute later and Alex stalked out, bristling as she stopped on the sidewalk and then looked around. Spotting Kara, she rushed to her side and then slowed. Leaning against the wall, she slowly sank down beside her sister, stretching her legs out in front of her as she slumped.

     

                “You alright?”

     

                “Yeah,” Kara croaked, wiping her cheeks. “It’s just- it’s been a shit week.”

     

                “Um … when you said her wife isn’t dead …“

     

                “She’s sick. She’s been in a respite centre this whole time.”

     

                “What is it?”

     

                “Alzheimer’s.”

     

                “Alzheimer’s? How old is her wife?”

     

                “Thirty-six,” Kara whispered, pain rippling across her face.

     

                “Thirty-si- surely not. It happens, rarely, but … no, that’s not right. That’s- that’s … fuck. You never said-“

     

                Shrugging, Kara blew the air out of her lungs and sniffed. “I only found out three nights ago.”

     

                “Oh. That’s what happened?”

     

                Kara let out a thin laugh, wiping her nose on her sleeve. “Guess I should’ve known better.”

     

                “You couldn’t have,” Alex murmured. “God, poor Lena.”

     

                Glancing down at her sister, Kara’s brow furrowed and her mouth turned down at the corners with grim agreement. Alex glanced up at her, brown eyes full of pity and concern.

     

                “I was jealous of her. Of course I was but I wasn’t going to admit that to you . I mean, I was worried she’d break your heart too but … yeah, I was jealous. This beautiful, rich woman who was smart and funny and kind as well just showing up and stealing all of your attention? But God, knowing that’s what her life is like … I wouldn’t swap places with her for all the money in the world.”

     

                Kara blinked at her, the corners of her mouth turning down slightly. “What, because her wife is sick?”

     

                “Yeah. We saw them sometimes on our rotations during our Residency, the dementia patients, and … I would not want to go through that. Especially at such a young age. Fuck. Give me a quick death any day.”

     

                “Because that’s so easy,” Kara quietly scoffed.

     

                “Kara.”

     

                “What?”

     

                “I- what? You- I- come on. You’re mad at her for lying? Is that what this is about? Fine, be mad . But I can guarantee you if you spent five minutes living her life, you’d be fucking grateful. If that’s all that’s wrong, that you’re pissed you didn’t know … I don’t know, maybe reevaluate your priorities a bit and find a way to forgive her.”

     

                Jerking away, Kara stammered speechlessly. “Are you kidding me? Now you decide it’s a- a great idea for me to see her? Considering you were so caught up on the fact that she was an emotionally unavailable widow, you’d think the fact that she’s legally married would be more of an issue.”

     

                Shrugging nonchalantly, Alex heaved a sigh and snorted with grim amusement. “Yeah, you’d think, but … I don’t know. I think I just got used to the idea of you moving on with someone else, watched you do a lot better with her, and now … I’m worried if you’re too proud to tell her how you feel, you’re going to be a lot worse. And that’s a shame because … I think I really liked her, actually. I was just scared for you but I think … I’d be more scared if you ended up alone, really.”

                

                Wrinkling her nose, Kara ran a hand through her hair. “I did tell her how I feel.”

     

                “Really?”

     

                Nodding, Kara pursed her lips in a brooding manner as she fiddled with her fingers. Alex nudged her and raised her eyebrows when Kara glanced over at her.

     

                “And? How’d it go?”

     

                “She said she felt the same way,” she admitted, her throat closing up with thick emotion as her vision blurred and she choked on a sob. Clapping a hand over her mouth, Kara closed her eyes and hot tears dropped onto the knees of her jeans. It all started coming out then, a tearful torrent of confusion, hurt and guilt.

     

                “It got serious between us. I didn’t tell you because it was new and … I guess it only lasted a week anyway. She said we needed to discuss some things but … I told her it was fine, to- to take her time because … I knew it would be difficult for us because I- I thought we’d both lost our partners and we were still getting over that. I didn’t know it would be that. And then she got a call from the place her wife is in and … she asked me to go with her and started to explain and I- I got out of the elevator. I know I’m being an asshole by leaving her when she probably needs me the most but I just- I don’t know what to do, Alex. She has a wife. She pretended that she knew what it was like and I- I know it must be so hard for her, I know that, but … I feel like I deserved to know. We weren’t together but … she let me believe her wife was dead so I thought maybe there was a chance but now I- her wife is alive and I will never be able to understand that and I feel so bitter now. What am I supposed to do?”

     

                Wrapping an arm around her shoulder, Alex tipped her head against Kara’s. “It’s a shit position. For both of you. I mean … I can see why she did it, and I don’t know, maybe if I was struggling a lot and I had someone who made me forget for a second … maybe I’d do the same. I’m not saying you didn’t deserve to know, but … now you do. What happens next is your choice. I love you and want you to be happy; God, I want that for you so badly. The truth is, Kara, I don’t think you were happy for a long, long time. Even before Mike’s accident. And that’s okay, I know you were going through your own shit and … who knows what might’ve happened if things had turned out differently, but losing him … or really I should say meeting her, it shocked you back to life a bit. James isn’t wrong about that; you’ve been so consumed by her that you’ve distanced yourself from your friends, and I know you’ll always have time for me, even when I’m on your back about things and you push me away, but … honestly, I think you needed to get over him without the people who loved him holding you back. Maybe Kelly will say differently from a professional standpoint, but I think Winn and James and their constant reminiscing about what a great guy he was wouldn’t have helped you realise that it’s okay for you to move on. You’ve been a fucking pain about it, you’ve had me and mom stressed out about all these big, sudden changes that were bound to end in disaster, but at the end of the day … you’ve been so much happier for the last six months; not any better but at least you were happier in your misery. I don’t have to look very far to find out why. And if you think you’ve been happier, and life’s going to be empty without her, I don’t know … I know what I would do.”

     

                Sighing heavily, feeling empty and tired with her emotions running high and confusion knotting her stomach tightly, Kara sagged against her sister. “Mom said … we had to decide if our futures were going to have each other in it, but either way it wouldn’t have them. And I guess she’s wrong, to an extent, but … I guess she’s a little bit right too.”

     

                The door burst open then, Kelly fuming as she slowed, cool air tempering some of the visible tension in the lines of her body. She spotted them then, her shoulders sagging, and she smiled, drawing in closer.

     

                “You doing alright?” Kelly asked, sinking to a crouch in front of Kara, giving her a once over.

     

                Sniffing, Kara wrinkled her nose and swiped her fingertips over her cheeks. “I’m okay.”

     

                “Come on, let’s go home,” Alex whispered, patting her knee. “Just think about it some more before you decide.”

     

                Leaning over to kiss her sister’s temple, Kara reached for the wall and pushed herself to her feet. “I will.”

    Chapter 23

                “So … it’s been two weeks; have you given it much thought?”

     

                Looking up as her sister perched on the arm of the sofa, Kara’s mouth turned down at the corners. Her expression clouded as she shrugged cluelessly. “I have but … I don’t know.”

     

                “Bullshit.”

     

                Sighing, she rolled her eyes and gestured helplessly. “What do you want me to say, huh? That I miss her? Of course I do.”

     

                “Then call her. You don’t have to decide anything but you could at least talk about it. Maybe it’ll clear some things up, make it a cleaner break if that’s what you want. You know, some closure; that would make a change for you.”

     

                Rubbing her forehead as her face furrowed with agonised indecision, Kara squeezed her eyes shut. “I don’t know, I’m not sure that’s a good idea.”

     

                “I could call her for you. See how she’s doing.”

     

                Looking up, Kara’s expression softened with aching hope. “Would you?”

     

                Snorting, Alex arched an eyebrow, messing Kara’s hair as her sister grumbled. “No. I just wanted to see if you really want to know how she is or not. Now stop being stubborn and call her yourself.”

     

                “Asshole.”

     

                “Coward.”

     

                “Coward?” Kara choked out, blinking in surprise. “I’m not a coward. I’m just- I’m allowed to be upset, you know. My feelings shouldn’t be dismissed just because she has it worse off. She still lied to me. This whole time.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Alex’s mouth thinned with exasperation and she rolled her apple between her palms. “I know, I know. I just don’t want pride to be the only reason why you’re going cold turkey. If you were scared-“

     

                “Of course I’m scared,” Kara admitted, the words coming out as a defeated sigh as she sagged on the sofa. “This is a lot more than I bargained for.”

     

                “Relationships usually are.”

     

                “Yeah, well, I’ve already gone through hell for one of them. I don’t feel like doing it again. And … I don’t know if I can be there for her through this.”

     

                “Haven’t you already been? Inadvertently.”

     

                “I- yeah, but … that was different. I thought the worst of it was over but it’s not and I- what, am I supposed to be her girlfriend while I wait for her wife to die? That’s what’s going to happen. She’s going to die and I don’t- I can’t watch her go through that. I don’t want to.”

     

                Shrugging, tossing her apple and catching it, Alex gave her a withering look. “Suit yourself.”

     

                Rolling her eyes, Kara sank down lower on the sofa and continued scrolling through her phone, looking at apartment listings. There were a few that looked promising to rent, and within budget, thanks to her new salary, and Kara showed Alex her screen.

     

                “What do you think about this one?”

     

                “Where is it? Midtown? Way too far and you know it.”

     

                “Yeah, but rent will be cheaper.”

     

                “You’re already on the outskirts of the city; if you go any further you’ll be in the suburbs.”

     

                “God forbid I make it to the suburbs,” Kara sarcastically replied with mock horror. “I’m surprised you didn’t move out there to have a kid.”

     

                Taking a bite of her apple, Alex wrinkled her nose, “not my kind of scene.”

     

                “What, no white picket fence? Kissing your wife off to work while you stay home baking a pie? No shit. It’s the done thing though; it’s what Mike wanted to do.”

     

                “And you?”

     

                “I don’t know. We never really got to the point of seriously discussing it. I used to agree but … I don’t know, I like the city. Midtown isn’t that far. I used to head out the way for work anyway.”

     

                “But it’ll be a nightmare getting a bus in every day for work. It’s already a trek to the new clinic from here. You should buy a car instead.”

     

                “Mm, I do miss the car.”

     

                “Yeah, that’s why you miss Lena. For the use of her car. What car was it? You never told me she gave you one.”

     

                Scoffing, Kara’s mouth thinned with annoyance as she continued to scroll through viable apartment options, shrinking the location to within the confines of Downtown. “I can’t imagine why, and I didn’t tell anyone. Also, she didn’t give me one, but it was an Audi. An expensive one . It was her wife’s, just … sitting there, so … she insisted.”

     

                “God, I wish I had someone who would insist on giving me an Audi and letting me stay in their penthouse.”

     

                “Yeah, because that’s why I was friends with her. What about this one?”

     

                Leaning in, Alex’s mouth turned down at the corners. “Too prison cell block. Have you considered just-”

     

                “I swear to God if you tell me to just call-”

     

                “Just call her!”

     

                “I’m thinking. Can you just quit it while I think about it? I don’t know what I’m doing yet.”

     

                “What you’re doing is avoiding the problem. It’s not going to magically fix itself if you don’t do anything about it. I don’t give a shit if you call her and give her an earful, but at least rip off the bandaid and get it over and done with. You see how waiting for something to happen doesn’t give you the same closure as something being over?”

     

                “Don’t rush me!”

     

                “If this is what rushing you is like, a fucking snail could get there faster.”

     

                “What do you want me to do? Call her and demand that she only love me? She loves her wife. Present tense. She talks about her like she’s her everything and I can’t compete with that. It’s me that has no one.”

     

                “Just … make the chilli.”

     

                “What?” Kara scoffed, her expression crumpling.

     

                “Make the chilli.”

     

                “What the fuck are you talking about? I don’t even like chilli.”

     

                Gesturing helplessly, Alex spluttered. “I- you- I don’t know! Whatever that shitty metaphor is that you tried using on me that one time you got mad at me. About not wanting to make the chilli. It’s about going out of-“

     

                “Oh,” Kara softly exclaimed, the memory coming back to her now. “Going out of your way for someone you love to make them happy.”

     

                “Yeah, that’s the one. So make the chilli.”

     

                “I- different situation, actually.”

     

                “And?”

     

                Clicking her tongue in annoyance, Kara pursed her lips. “You’re irritating me now.”

     

                “Likewise. Figure your shit out.”

     

                Taking her sister’s words to heart, Kara resolved to make a conscious choice in the direction her life was leading, although she still dragged her feet where Lena was concerned. Within the next week, she’d visited two apartments and hadn’t liked either of them and then another four the following week. Far too soon, it had been a month since she’d moved out of Lena’s with no resolution in sight for their mutual determination to ignore each other. 

     

                A part of Kara was hoping she’d get a call from Lena with another apology, further explanation, a plea to move back in. Maybe it was pride, or maybe it was the desire to be wanted, but Kara didn’t want to make the first move, although she winced whenever she thought about how callously cold she’d reacted. Would she have called Lena if she’d been on the receiving end of such an abrupt rejection?

     

                By the end of that month, she’d found somewhere within her budget that was close enough to work without it being in Lena’s close vicinity - not that Kara had to worry about that much, with the wide gulf between their tax brackets that left them in completely different spheres of society, with her never being able to afford an apartment near Lena’s - and was decent enough to be made homely once she moved in her furniture. She knew she’d have to bite the bullet soon and call Lena to get her furniture back , but that was a bridge Kara was all too happy to cross once she came to it. For now, it was enough that she’d found somewhere and would be able to move in at the end of July, just a couple of months shy of two years since Mike had died. It would be a fresh start over two losses.

     

                Kelly was happy for her and Alex was too, to a lesser extent, still somewhat disapproving of Kara’s refusal to speak to Lena before she made any rash decisions. Still, they’d been set up with meetings about a little girl called Esme, so Alex didn’t push Kara too hard about the apartment situation, all three of them aware that they’d most likely need the use of the spare room soon if things went well. Kara hoped they did, wanted that for her sister, even if she couldn’t have what she wanted for herself. Although maybe she could have but it would never be the way she wanted it, and that seemed a big enough difference for Kara to put it to bed.

     

                Still, in the late hours of the night, she couldn’t help but think of Lena. She would wake sometimes reaching for her, something she’d never done with Mike, never slept pressed up against him, wrapped around him, but she missed Lena from the handful of nights they’d fallen asleep together and woken up that way. It felt odd that something that had been so small and short, and seemingly unimportant at the time, could have left such a lasting impact. But Kara retreated inside herself and grew more defeated as she struggled to come to terms with the fact that it was over. It didn’t feel finished , didn’t feel like she had that closure she needed to move on, and she knew that Alex was right and she needed to call Lena and hash it out properly, for better or worse, but she hesitated at that.

     

                Quicker than she would have thought possible for such an infinitely agonising moment of her life, six weeks passed by and Kara found herself home with Alex and Kelly on Saturday night, ever-present as she joined them for dinner and planned on watching a movie with them afterwards. She’d become the awkward third party of their relationship, seemingly always present, and while she tried to give the newlyweds their space, they pitied her too much to not include her. 

     

                Picking at her food with little relish, a thing that had concerned her sister more than anything of late, Kara was only half-listening to the conversation, practically spoken in shorthand between the wives, in that intimate manner of partners or best friends. She’d used to feel that way with Lena, little anecdotes that explained a whole story, little quips that would have them laughing together while everyone else was clueless. 

     

                Brooding and frustrated, Kara picked at her lasagna and felt a restless urge to do something. It had been plaguing her for weeks now, and she’d thought packing up her things, which she’d never fully unpacked, would help take the edge off that lost indecisiveness, but it had never been about living with Alex. It had been about Lena, and Kara had stuck her head in the sand and let time pass her by without even attempting to make things better for herself on that front. It hadn’t gotten any easier, no matter how she tried to rationalise it to herself, how much she tried to feel that initial anger, which had simmered to confusion over time, to feel vindicated. 

     

                All three of their phones buzzed with texts a moment later, intruding on Kara’s bleak thoughts and she reached for hers, tilting the screen to read it as Alex and Kelly looked at theirs as well. They’d assumed it was a message to the group chat, Nia or Winn asking after their Saturday night plans, seeing who was around for drinks or making plans for another game night. It wasn’t.

     

    Emergency Alert

    Silver Alert in Downtown National City. Woman, Andrea Rojas, 36. Last known location West Cordova Street. If observed please call 911. Click for details.

     

                Kara’s stomach jolted at the silver alert text that came through on her phone, her hand shaking as she clicked the link. It opened to a database with a photo of Andrea and a description but Kara already knew it was her before seeing the photo, from the name alone. Her vision blurred slightly, everything suddenly seeming so far away as panic constricted her chest.

                

                “Did everyone else just get that? Another silver alert,” Alex said, clicking her tongue as she set her phone down. 

     

                “Mm, I got one the other day as well when I was driving out past Midtown. I hope they find her; most of them turn up fine within twenty-four hours.”

     

                The chatter fell on deaf ears as Kara’s throat felt tight around the sudden feeling of dread that crept over her. Jerking her chair back, the legs scraping the floor, she staggered to her feet, phone clutched tightly in a white-knuckled grip.

     

                “Can I borrow your car?” Kara blurted out, her voice a hoarse rasp.

     

                “What? Now?” Alex asked, glancing at her and then doing a double-take. “Are you okay? You’ve gone white.”

     

                “Where are your car keys?”

     

                Her voice was sharper this time, laced with urgency, and Alex’s brow puckered as she gestured towards the kitchen counters. “Over there. What’s going on?”

     

                Crossing the room quickly, Kara snatched them up and headed towards the door, throwing a quick explanation over her shoulder as she left without even pausing to find shoes. “It’s Lena’s wife.”

     

                The exclamations of surprise and barrage of questions were cut off by the apartment door shutting behind her and Kara was in the elevator before she could really give it much thought. All she knew was that Lena’s very much alive wife was missing, and she would search all night if it helped. She wasn’t so deep in her own self-pity that she couldn’t recognise the gravity of the situation.

     

                In Alex’s car, she started the engine and tore off without hesitation, speeding towards the street detailed in the silver alert text message. It was lined with closed businesses and residential apartments and a few highrises of varying offices and Kara drove the entire length of it with no luck. Her phone kept buzzing with calls from Alex and Kelly but she ignored them all she searched.

     

                “Come on, come on,” Kara murmured to herself as she squinted through the dark, trying to catch a glimpse of faces as she passed by pedestrians, trying not to slow down traffic as she went.

     

                She scrambled for places Andrea might be, based on the very limited information Lena had revealed since they’d met. All she knew was that they both spent an awful lot of time at their offices and she didn’t remember Lena, so chances were that she didn’t remember L-Corp either. That left Obsidian North, not too far away in a car but a lengthy walk on foot, and Kara input it into Maps and followed the directions as she continued to scan the streets.

     

                Slowing outside the office, she found the lobby dimly lit and security guards milling about and it occurred to her that if Andrea had gone there, they would’ve called either Lena or the police. Cursing, Kara slapped her palm against the wheel and ground her teeth together before biting the bullet and calling Lena to see if she’d been picked up yet.

     

                The call rang four times before she got Lena’s voicemail. Biting back an impatient sigh, Kara raked a hand through her hair and braked at the next intersection.

     

                “Hey, it’s, uh, it’s me. Look, I got the silver alert. I just wanted to see if she’s been found yet and to check how you are.”

     

                Hanging up, Kara waited for the light to turn green and accelerated, doing laps around the block and spiralling outwards as she tried to canvas the area. With no luck, she decided to check the apartment next, pulling up haphazardly outside the front door and running up the steps to the lobby, where she couldn’t get in so settled for slapping her palm against the front door until the security guard got up from behind the desk.

     

                He knew her and unlocked the door, arching an eyebrow at her panic. “You know Lena?” Kara breathlessly asked. “From the penthouse. And her wife, Andrea, who used to live there?”

     

                “Yeah?”

     

                “Have you- have you seen Andrea?”

     

                “No. Didn’t they get divorced or something? I thought you- ”

     

                “Fuck,” Kara exclaimed, raking her hands through her hair and grabbing fistfuls. “Thanks. Sorry.”

     

                Rushing back down the steps as she ignored the man’s questions, she climbed back behind the wheel and started the car. Peeling out into late-night traffic, Kara continued her search for another hour, driving up and down blocks and asking in a few convenience stores that were open 24/7. She had a photo of Andrea on her phone from the alert and was desperate and frazzled as she asked around to no avail.

     

                Climbing back into the car after trying a pizza parlour on the off chance Andrea had been hungry in her lost state of confusion, Kara clenched the wheel in her hands and closed her eyes. Thinking hard about any other places, she murmured to herself.

     

                “Come on. Think, think. Where could she be? The office, the apartment. Late-night business dinners. Il Palazzo - that’s too far. She liked to walk Aristotle in the park- the park.”

     

                The thought jolted through Kara, remembering Lena talking about how that was where they’d walked Aristotle, how it was one of Andrea’s favourite places in the city, her idea of getting into nature. She’d been searching for hours now, almost midnight with the tank of gas running low, and Kara wasn’t sure if she was grasping at straws but it seemed like a good shot.

     

                Starting the car, she sped through the emptying streets and made a few reckless turns as she tried to envision the route. She hadn’t spent a lot of time on the harbour side of Downtown until she’d moved in with Lena and she made a wrong turn before looking on Maps and getting back on track. At the first sign of the enclosed sprawling mass of dark trees, Kara jerked the wheel and abruptly parked, yanking up the handbrake and killing the engine.

     

                Out of the car within seconds, she made for the first path disappearing into the acres of greenery nestled in the heart of the city and set off quickly. It was far too big to canvas herself with speed but Kara would comb every inch of it before she gave up. And it wasn’t just for Lena’s sake, but the fact that she was Lena’s wife, and Kara loved her for that too. Even though they’d never met, even though they would never know each other properly, Kara cared for this sick woman because the woman she loved loved her. She knew Lena would be out of her mind and the thought wrenched Kara’s heart.

     

                Running through the park, her phone’s flashlight illuminating the dark between the periodically placed lamp posts along the paths, Kara shouted her name.

     

                “Andrea?”

     

                There was no response from the dark but she saw a few people as she ran, pausing each time as she spoke to them, some of the homeless, others drunk, others lovers walking home, but none of them had seen Andrea. They probably thought she was a little crazy, no shoes, breathless and wild-eyed, running through the park in the early hours of the morning, alone.

     

                She didn’t give up though, searching for more than an hour, until the night was cold enough that even the warmth of running couldn’t stop her from shivering - although that might have been the adrenaline - her voice growing husky as she shouted herself hoarse.

     

                “Aristotle?”

     

                Kara thought she’d imagined it at first, a distant shout as a sharp wind ran through the trees, rustling the leaves and branches. Pausing, her hands on her knees as she breathed heavily, each breath like a knife as a stitch formed in her side, she listened intently.

     

                Just as she thought she’d imagined it, she heard it again and straightened, alert and eagle-eyed. “Aristotle. Ven aquì, mijo.”

     

                Almost tripping over her feet in her haste, the breath hitched in Kara’s throat and she followed the sound of Spanish coming from between the trees. Off the trail, she crunched leaves beneath her feet, the damp seeping into the soles of her socks, and she listened to the halting calls get louder. It was still another five minutes of stumbling through the park before her flashlight glanced over the form of a woman amidst the trees.

     

                “Hello?” Kara called out. “Um … hola. Estás bien?”

     

                The woman turned sharply, stumbling away as panic and fear crossed her face, the brightness of Kara’s flashlight as she approached making her seem ghastly. Leached of any colour as the light made her a monochrome figure in the dark, making hollows and shadows of her face, she was still shockingly familiar to Kara, which was an odd sensation considering they’d never met before.

     

                Giving her a hesitant smile as she lowered her phone, Kara warily approached, wondering what the rules were for dealing with dementia patients. She decided to treat her like a skittish animal was the best bet, and after years of soothing animals to treat them, Kara felt more at ease.

     

                “Estás bien?”

     

                “Mi perro,” Andrea pitifully replied, her face slack with devastation.

     

                Scrambling for her high school Spanish, Kara opened and closed her mouth. “Perro? Your dog? Your dog is missing? Perdido?”

     

                “Sí, mi perro esta perdido.”

     

                “Oh, well, I can help you look, if you’d like,” Kara offered. “Uh … ayuda. Mí.”

     

                “Your Spanish is terrible,” Andrea laughed, her brow creasing, perplexed but amused.

     

                A surprised bark of laughter escaped Kara as she blinked, taken aback by the response, so normal, so clear and present. Wrinkling her nose, Kara couldn’t help but smile, a tightness in her chest.

     

                “It is. Sorry. I’m- I’m Kara.”

     

                “My dog-“

     

                “Aristotle, isn’t it?”

     

                Face brightening with delight, Andrea smiled, lighting her up. “Aristotle, yes. How did you know?”

     

                “I heard you calling him.”

     

                “Oh. I was walking and then … I don’t know what happened but he’s gone.”

     

                “Oh, well, I could help you look.”

                

                A shiver ran through Andrea and she hunched her shoulders as she hugged her arms to herself, a thick cast on the right arm from her almost healed fracture. Swallowing the lump in her throat, Kara took a cautious step forward.

     

                “Are you- are you cold?”

     

                “Cold?” Andrea laughed. “The weather’s gorgeous today.”

     

                “Oh, um, okay,” Kara faltered, slowly removing her sweatshirt and inching closer. “I think- I think you dropped this though. When you were looking for Aristotle.”

     

                “Aristotle,” Andrea softly sighed, her expression turning tender as a faint smile crossed her lips. “I have a dog called that.”

     

                “If you … if you put this on, I’ll help you look for him. We can look together,” Kara coaxed her, holding out the sweatshirt.
