She didn’t want to cry, didn’t want to waste the moment of the longing that suffused her every waking moment but she couldn’t help herself. Lena was inconsolable, even by the one woman who was the source of that pain.

     

                “I love you too,” Andrea told her, her fingers sliding down the side of her face, thumb reaching across her cheek to wipe away the tears. “Don’t cry. I’m right here. Even if I can’t reach you, I’m always thinking of you. I’m with you.”

     

                Covering Andrea’s hands with her own, Lena closed her eyes, drawing in a hitching breath. “I just miss you so much.”

     

                “I know but … tell me how you are. What have I missed?”

     

                Where did Lena even begin? So much had changed in her life in the months between the last bout of lucidity and she didn’t know how to tell her. Glancing over at Kara, mouth opening and closing as she struggled, she turned back to Andrea and her shoulders caved. Fingers cupping her chin, Andrea smiled slightly.

     

                “It's okay. Tell me about her.”

     

                Lena’s eyes slid back over to Kara, who looked restless as she watched with a mournful ache on her face, dwelling in the horrible feeling of helplessness. Looking back at her wife, Lena’s smile was pained, and she took Andrea’s hands in her own and squeezed them tightly.

     

                “Her name is Kara. She’s thirty-five. Her husband passed away two years ago. She’s a vet. Aristotle loves her; I think you would too.”

     

                “That’s good,” Andrea replied, her voice wavering.

                

                “She looks after me.”

     

                “I wish it could have been me.”

     

                Tears spilt over, running down Lena’s cheeks, carving paths through her makeup as her bottom lip trembled. She’d told her all of this before, of course, or some variation of it, but it hurt every time to watch Andrea be brave about her wife being with another woman. 

     

                “I’m sorry.”

     

                “I’m happy you’re not alone,” Andrea firmly replied, even as her blue eyes shone with unshed tears. “I’m happy you have someone to look after you. You should- you should be happy. That’s good. It makes it … easier. Thank her for me.”

     

                “I will.”

     

                “How much time do we have?”

     

                “Not long.”

     

                Knowing from experience, Lena was sure they had minutes, if that. These bouts of remembrance rarely lasted long and last time it had been all of five minutes before that fog had crept back in, stealing away any familiarity in Andrea’s mind. But even a single second of clarity was a gift, to know her wife remembered to love her even for a moment. Lena clung to it so tightly that she was almost desperate in her desire to never let it go.

     

                Nodding, Andrea dropped her hands and drew in a shaky breath, confused and upset but putting on a brave face in spite of that. Lena wanted to hold her tight, to be held tightly by her, and it was all she could do to rein in her self-control and rest her forehead against her wife’s. Cupping the side of her face, Andrea kissed her again, slowly, as if savouring it, knowing she wouldn’t remember.

     

                Lena’s cheeks were a splotchy mess as cried freely, devastated and elatedly relieved in equal parts. Andrea tried to pull away but Lena wouldn’t let her go, holding her face in her hands and peppering her cheeks, her forehead, her chin, her jaw with kisses. She kissed the scar between her eyebrows, the tip of her nose, her closed eyelids, before pulling her close. She couldn’t quite shake the feeling that it was goodbye.

     

                The breaths couldn’t come quick enough, each one a sharp pain in her chest as she was left gasping for air in between the breathless sobs of someone trying her best to not fall apart. Andrea cradled Lena’s head to her chest and rubbed her back, talking freely, her voice a hoarse rasp that trembled occasionally as she tried to comfort her wife the only way she could, with the gift of their memories.

     

                She haltingly cobbled together anecdotes of dates and mishaps, laughing at the memories as Lena managed choked sobs, her face crumpling with amusement, and she reminisced over their wedding day, the two of them and their witnesses, about the time Lena had gotten food poisoning in Cabo and Andrea had gotten stung by a jellyfish in Australia. There were a few that she got muddled up with, the places, the people, but it was enough for Lena that she remembered even a sliver of their life together.

     

                After a few minutes, she fell silent and Lena listened to the sound of her heart beating, so strong, so familiar. Lena would’ve been content to stay that way forever but the threads of Andrea’s mind were already blurring, the details starting to escape her, and Lena knew what came next.

     

                “My Lena,” Andrea softly sighed, holding her tightly, “I’m sorry to go so soon.”

     

                “It’s okay,” Lena whispered, her voice a weary wisp of agony, her head in the crook of Andrea’s neck and shoulder, her eyes swollen and red. “You go. I’ll be okay; I’ll be right here with you.”

     

                “You won’t leave me?”

     

                “I won’t leave you. Not ever.”

     

                “Thank you.”

     

                “I love you.”

     

                “I love you too. You should- you should visit again soon.”

     

                “I will.”

     

                “Really?”

     

                Sniffing, Lena closed her eyes, the breath gusting out of her as she sagged, feeling her wife retreating back in on herself. “Always. Every day.”

     

                “I’m glad you moved here. It’s been so lonely.”

     

                “You won’t ever be alone. I promise.”

     

                “How long has it been now? I missed you. We were best friends … weren’t we? It’s been so many years. I can’t believe you’re here.”

     

                And then she was drifting even further away, Lena’s words coming out hollow as she replied to Andrea’s questions about the past, dragged back down into it until she didn’t know she was talking to her wife, until she didn’t know she was talking to her best friend, the woman who’d loved her with every shred of herself. By the time she fell quiet, mid-sentence of a work query, Lena was depleted of every ounce of energy, spent in the emotion-fuelled few minutes that had been afforded to her.

     

                Shrugging Lena’s head off her shoulder, Andrea blinked at her, forehead creasing. “I’m tired.”

     

                Nodding, her throat so tight she could barely speak, Lena wiped at her pallid cheeks with shaky fingers. She was slumped in a heap on the blanket and couldn’t even force a goodbye out past the lump lodged behind her sternum, her lungs aching with the effort it was taking to keep the breathless sobs inside her chest. Andrea looked at her, eyes a burning blue as she smiled warmly.

     

                “Thank you for coming.”

     

                She was on her feet a moment later, quickly crossing over to Russell. He glanced at Lena, who nodded, unable to stand to go with her, and led Andrea inside. 

     

                Kara lingered near the door for a moment before crossing over to Lena, her face tense with concern. She stopped a few feet away and then all but fell to her knees beside Lena, hesitating before reaching out to cover the back of her hand with her own. Lena’s skin was cold to the touch and she drew in a ragged breath, her eyes rising to meet Kara’s, bloodshot and puffy, her heartbreak plain to see.

     

                “How can I help?” Kara murmured, her expression pleading as she desperately wanted to do something to take away her pain, that guilty feeling of relief stealing over her once again at the clean cut of loss she’d suffered herself.

     

                Letting out a shaky breath, Lena slowly tipped into Kara, her head finding the space between her neck and shoulder, a different fit to the home of her wife’s but no less comforting. Wrapping her arms around Lena, Kara held her close, a comforting presence in the absence of the one she craved.

     

                “She said thank you,” Lena whispered, her voice breaking.

     

                “For what?”

     

                “For looking after me.”

     

                “You- you told her about me? Us?”

     

                “Yes. She’s happy I’m not alone.”

     

                Eyes stinging with tears, Kara’s voice wobbled slightly as she managed to force out an, “oh.”

     

                Closing her eyes, Lena felt the feeble tremor of her grief in her chest and pressed her lips into a flat line as she fought for her composure. “I’ll be alright, you know. Don’t worry. I didn’t think I- … I got to have her again for a few minutes; if this is goodbye, then I’m lucky.”

     

                “You’ll have her again,” Kara whispered, so sure of herself. “You will always have her. And you’ll have me too. And between the two of us, you’ll never be alone.”

     

                Lena made a frayed sound at the back of her throat, pitiful and small, and Kara held her as they sat in the courtyard, alone beneath the shade of the tree with the ghosts of their grief for company. Turning her head slightly, Lena’s lips grazed the side of Kara’s neck in a light kiss before she sighed, her breath a warm gust of resignation.  “All’s well that ends well.”

     

                But there was no ending for Lena that would be well. The most she would have would be Kara to see her through it, and that was enough. The same way it had been enough for Kara to have Lena through her darkest hours. And as her own complex struggle with grief came to a close, Kara had so much clarity about her past that she wished so desperately for Lena when the time came. That space to hold her grief and feel it all and pull through it to the other side, even if it would never truly leave either of them. 

     

                They made the world bearable for each other and as they sat there, side by side, Lena’s head on Kara’s shoulder, they both knew she’d get through it. Maybe not for a long while but she would. With a soft sigh, Kara turned her head slightly and brushed a kiss against Lena’s dark head as she gave her the closure she needed.

     

                “All’s well that ends well.”
